وأكثر العُرَّاف أضافوا معرفة الله – تعالى – إلى فناء الوجود وفناء الفناء – وذلك غلط وسهو واضح: فإن معرفة الله – تعالى – لا تحتاج إلى فناء الوجود ولا إلى فناء فنائه، لأن الشيء لا وجود له، وما لا وجود له لا فناء له؛ فإن الفناء بعد إثبات الوجود. فإذا عرفت نفسك بلا وجود ولا فناء فقد عرفتَ الله. – وإلا فلا.

وفي إضافة معرفة الله – تعالى – إلى فناء الوجود وإلى فناء فنائه إثباتُ الشرك، لأنك إذا أضفت معرفة الله إلى فناء الوجود وفناء الفناء، كان الوجود لغير الله ونقيضه – وهناك شرك واضح، لأن النبي – صلى الله عليه وسلم – قال: "مَن عرف نفسَه فقد عرف ربَّه"، ولم يقل: "مَن فني عن نفسه عرف ربَّه." فإن إثبات الغير يناقض فناءه، وما لا يجوز ثبوتُه لا يجوز فناؤه. وجودك لا شيء، واللاشيء لا يُضاف إلى شيء، لا فانٍ ولا غير فانٍ، ولا موجود ولا معدوم. «أنت» الآن كما كنتَ معدَمًا قبل التكوين. فالآن الأزل، والآن الأبد، والآن القِدَم. فالله هو وجود الأزل ووجود الأبد ووجود القِدَم؛ فإنه بلا وجود الأزل والأبد والقِدَم لم يكن كذلك ما كان وحده لا شريك له. وواجب أن يكون وحده لا شريك له: فإن "شريكه" هو الذي يكون وجودُه بذاته، لا بوجود الله؛ ومَن يكن كذلك لم يكن محتاجًا إليه، فيكون إذًا ربًّا ثانيًا – وذلك محال: فليس لله شريك ولا ندٌّ ولا كفؤ. ومَن رأى شيئًا مع الله أو من الله أو في الله – وذلك الشيء يحتاج إلى الله بالربوبية – فقد جعل ذلك الشيء أيضًا شريكًا يحتاج إلى الله بالربوبية. ومن جوَّزَ أن يكون مع الله شيءٌ يقوم بنفسه، أو يقوم به، أو هو فانٍ عن وجوده أو عن فنائه، فهو بعدُ ما شمَّ رائحة معرفة النفس، لأن مَن جوَّزَ أن يكون موجودًا سواه، قائمًا به، فيه يصير فانيًا في فنائه، فتسلسل الفناء بالفناء، – وذلك شِرْك بعد شِرْك، وليس بمعرفة النفس، – هو مُشْرِك، لا عارف بالله ولا بنفسه.
sanskrit_iast:
wa akthar al-ʿurrāf ʾaḍāfū maʿrifat Allāh – taʿālā – ilā fanāʾ al-wujūd wa fanāʾ al-fanāʾ – wa dhālika ghalṭ wa sahw wāḍiḥ: faʾinna maʿrifat Allāh – taʿālā – lā taḥtāj ilā fanāʾ al-wujūd wa lā ilā fanāʾ fanāʾih, liʾanna al-shayʾ lā wujūd lahu, wa mā lā wujūd lahu lā fanāʾ lahu; faʾinna al-fanāʾ baʿda ʾithbāt al-wujūd. fa-idhā ʿarafta nafsak bilā wujūd wa lā fanāʾ faqad ʿarafta Allāh. – wa illā fa-lā.

wa fī ʾiḍāfat maʿrifat Allāh – taʿālā – ilā fanāʾ al-wujūd wa ilā fanāʾ fanāʾih ʾithbāt al-shirk, liʾannak idhā ʾaḍafta maʿrifat Allāh ilā fanāʾ al-wujūd wa fanāʾ al-fanāʾ, kāna al-wujūd li-ghayr Allāh wa naqīḍuh – wa hunāka shirk wāḍiḥ, liʾanna al-nabī – ṣallā Allāh ʿalayh wa sallam – qāla: "man ʿarafa nafsahu faqad ʿarafa rabbahu," wa lam yaqūl: "man fanī ʿan nafsihi ʿarafa rabbahu." faʾinna ʾithbāt al-ghayr yunāqiḍ fanāʾahu, wa mā lā yajāz thubūtuh lā yajāz fanāʾuh. wujūdak lā shayʾ, wa al-lā shayʾ lā yuḍāf ilā shayʾ, lā fān wa lā ghayr fān, wa lā mawjūd wa lā maʿdūm. "anta" al-ān kamā kunta maʿdaman qabla al-takwīn. fa-al-ān al-ʾazal, wa al-ān al-ʾabad, wa al-ān al-qidam. fa-Allāh huwa wujūd al-ʾazal wa wujūd al-ʾabad wa wujūd al-qidam; fa-innahu bilā wujūd al-ʾazal wa al-ʾabad wa al-qidam lam yakun kathālika mā kāna waḥdahu lā sharīk lahu. wa wājib an yakūna waḥdahu lā sharīk lahu: fa-ʾinna "sharīkuhu" huwa alladhī yakūn wujūduhu bi-dhātihi, lā bi-wujūd Allāh; wa man yakun kathālika lam yakun muḥtājān ilayh, fa-yakūn idhān rabbān thānī – wa dhālika muḥāl: fa-laysa li-Allāh sharīk wa lā nadd wa lā kufūʾ. wa man rāʾa shayʾan maʿ Allāh aw min Allāh aw fī Allāh – wa dhālika al-shayʾ yaḥtāj ilā Allāh bi-l-rubūbiyya – faqad jaʿala dhālika al-shayʾ ayḍan sharīkan yaḥtāj ilā Allāh bi-l-rubūbiyya. wa man jawwaza an yakūna maʿ Allāh shayʾun yaqūm binafsihi, aw yaqūm bihi, aw huwa fān ʿan wujūdihi aw ʿan fanāʾih, fa-huwa baʿdū mā shamma rāʾiḥat maʿrifat al-nafs, liʾanna man jawwaza an yakūna mawjūdān siwāh, qāʾimān bihi, fīhi yaṣīr fānīan fī fanāʾih, fa-tasalsal al-fanāʾ bi-l-fanāʾ, – wa dhālika shirk baʿda shirk, wa laysa bi-maʿrifat al-nafs, – huwa mushrik, lā ʿārif bi-Allāh wa lā bi-nafsihi.

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body: If you know yourself without existing and passing away, then you know God, and if not, then not. By making the knowledge of God dependent on the passing away of your existence and the passing away of that passing away, there is an affirmation of something other than God.

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.

items.definition: Arabic fanāʾ ‘passing away, evanescence’ → passing-away of the egoic claim before the Real Here: Knowing God Through Annihilation of Self Pearl #30 If you know yourself without existing and passing away, then you know God, and if not, then not. Trap: self-erasure as quietism or dissociation rather than clearing of false independence

‘self/soul/breath’ → the claiming self that must be known so its independence can be seen through Here: Knowing God Through Annihilation of Self Pearl #30 If you know yourself without existing and passing away, then you know God, and if not, then not. Trap: psychologizing as ego-therapy without ontological stakes

Arabic wujūd ‘finding/being found; existence’ → being as what is found in God alone; creatures have no independent wujūd Here: By making the knowledge of God dependent on the passing away of your existence and the passing away of that passing away, there is an affirmation of something… Trap: treating ‘existence’ as a neutral metaphysical predicate shared equally by God and world
‘association/partnership’ → ascribing independent power or being to what is other-than-God Trap: narrowing to idol-worship while missing subtle self-ascription of agency

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.citation: Plotinus Enneads — Ennead VI, Tractate 9, Section 7
items.resonance: Both texts locate knowledge in a reorientation of attention away from external objects toward an inner principle that is always present but obscured by habitual perception. The move is identical: turn inward, and what was hidden becomes known.
items.divergence: Ibn Arabi grounds this inward turn in the paradox of self-knowledge without ontological persistence (fana), while Plotinus grounds it in the soul's continuous intelligible activity that sense-perception merely obscures.

items.resonance: Both texts collapse the distinction between attention and knowledge: sustained or focused attention is itself the act of knowing, not a means to it. The knower and the knowing are unified through the quality of attention itself.
items.divergence: The Siva Sutra formulates this as a metaphysical principle of consciousness (Śāktopāya), while Ibn Arabi frames it as a paradoxical condition of self-annihilation (fana) that reveals divine knowledge.

title: Self-Knowledge as the Gateway to Divine Knowledge
thesis: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
source_excerpt: By making the knowledge of God dependent on the passing away of your existence and the passing away of that passing away, there is an affirmation of something other than God. The Prophet said, Whoever knows their self, knows their Lord.
translation_literal: By making the knowledge of God dependent on the passing away of your existence and the passing away of that passing away, there is an affirmation of something other than God. The Prophet said, Whoever knows their self, knows their Lord.

"anta" al-ān kamā kunta maʿdaman qabla al-takwīn. fa-al-ān al-ʾazal, wa al-ān al-ʾabad, wa al-ān al-qidam. fa-Allāh huwa wujūd al-ʾazal wa wujūd al-ʾabad wa wujūd al-qidam; fa-innahu bilā wujūd al-ʾazal wa al-ʾabad wa al-qidam lam yakun kathālika mā kāna waḥdahu lā sharīk lahu. wa wājib an yakūna waḥdahu lā sharīk lahu: fa-ʾinna "sharīkuhu" huwa alladhī yakūn wujūduhu bi-dhātihi, lā bi-wujūd Allāh; wa man yakun kathālika lam yakun muḥtājān ilayh, fa-yakūn idhān rabbān thānī – wa dhālika muḥāl: fa-laysa li-Allāh sharīk wa lā nadd wa lā kufūʾ. wa man rāʾa shayʾan maʿ Allāh aw min Allāh aw fī Allāh – wa dhālika al-shayʾ yaḥtāj ilā Allāh bi-l-rubūbiyya – faqad jaʿala dhālika al-shayʾ ayḍan sharīkan yaḥtāj ilā Allāh bi-l-rubūbiyya. wa man jawwaza an yakūna maʿ Allāh shayʾun yaqūm binafsihi, aw yaqūm bihi, aw huwa fān ʿan wujūdihi aw ʿan fanāʾih, fa-huwa baʿdū mā shamma rāʾiḥat maʿrifat al-nafs, liʾanna man jawwaza an yakūna mawjūdān siwāh, qāʾimān bihi, fīhi yaṣīr fānīan fī fanāʾih, fa-tasalsal al-fanāʾ bi-l-fanāʾ, – wa dhālika shirk baʿda shirk, wa laysa bi-maʿrifat al-nafs, – huwa mushrik, lā ʿārif bi-Allāh wa lā bi-nafsihi.

pratibha_layers.label: Original (Arabic)
pratibha_layers.body:
وأكثر العُرَّاف أضافوا معرفة الله – تعالى – إلى فناء الوجود وفناء الفناء – وذلك غلط وسهو واضح: فإن معرفة الله – تعالى – لا تحتاج إلى فناء الوجود ولا إلى فناء فنائه، لأن الشيء لا وجود له، وما لا وجود له لا فناء له؛ فإن الفناء بعد إثبات الوجود. فإذا عرفت نفسك بلا وجود ولا فناء فقد عرفتَ الله. – وإلا فلا.

وفي إضافة معرفة الله – تعالى – إلى فناء الوجود وإلى فناء فنائه إثباتُ الشرك، لأنك إذا أضفت معرفة الله إلى فناء الوجود وفناء الفناء، كان الوجود لغير الله ونقيضه – وهناك شرك واضح، لأن النبي – صلى الله عليه وسلم – قال: "مَن عرف نفسَه فقد عرف ربَّه"، ولم يقل: "مَن فني عن نفسه عرف ربَّه." فإن إثبات الغير يناقض فناءه، وما لا يجوز ثبوتُه لا يجوز فناؤه. وجودك لا شيء، واللاشيء لا يُضاف إلى شيء، لا فانٍ ولا غير فانٍ، ولا موجود ولا معدوم. «أنت» الآن كما كنتَ معدَمًا قبل التكوين. فالآن الأزل، والآن الأبد، والآن القِدَم. فالله هو وجود الأزل ووجود الأبد ووجود القِدَم؛ فإنه بلا وجود الأزل والأبد والقِدَم لم يكن كذلك ما كان وحده لا شريك له. وواجب أن يكون وحده لا شريك له: فإن "شريكه" هو الذي يكون وجودُه بذاته، لا بوجود الله؛ ومَن يكن كذلك لم يكن محتاجًا إليه، فيكون إذًا ربًّا ثانيًا – وذلك محال: فليس لله شريك ولا ندٌّ ولا كفؤ. ومَن رأى شيئًا مع الله أو من الله أو في الله – وذلك الشيء يحتاج إلى الله بالربوبية – فقد جعل ذلك الشيء أيضًا شريكًا يحتاج إلى الله بالربوبية. ومن جوَّزَ أن يكون مع الله شيءٌ يقوم بنفسه، أو يقوم به، أو هو فانٍ عن وجوده أو عن فنائه، فهو بعدُ ما شمَّ رائحة معرفة النفس، لأن مَن جوَّزَ أن يكون موجودًا سواه، قائمًا به، فيه يصير فانيًا في فنائه، فتسلسل الفناء بالفناء، – وذلك شِرْك بعد شِرْك، وليس بمعرفة النفس، – هو مُشْرِك، لا عارف بالله ولا بنفسه.

items.definition: Arabic fanāʾ ‘passing away, evanescence’ → passing-away of the egoic claim before the Real Here: Balyānī critiques the notion of fanāʾ as a *precondition* for divine knowledge, since it presupposes a real self that must be destroyed. Trap: self-erasure as quietism or dissociation rather than clearing of false independence

Arabic wujūd ‘finding/being found; existence’ → being as what is found in God alone; creatures have no independent wujūd Here: The teaching rests on the radical claim of waḥdat al-wujūd (oneness of being): there is only one existence, God's existence, and what you call 'your' existence… Trap: treating ‘existence’ as a neutral metaphysical predicate shared equally by God and world

‘unity of being/finding’ → the Real’s being is one; multiplicity is relational appearance, not rival substances Here: The teaching rests on the radical claim of waḥdat al-wujūd (oneness of being): there is only one existence, God's existence, and what you call 'your' existence… Trap: pantheist collapse that erases servant/Lord distinction

‘association/partnership’ → ascribing independent power or being to what is other-than-God Here: Balyānī argues that this doctrine, however pious it sounds, secretly smuggles in polytheism (shirk). Trap: narrowing to idol-worship while missing subtle self-ascription of agency

Arabic tawḥīd from waḥḥada ‘to make/declare one’ → absolute oneness of the Real, radicalized here as sole agency and sole being Here: The teaching rests on the radical claim of waḥdat al-wujūd (oneness of being): there is only one existence, God's existence, and what you call 'your' existence… Trap: hearing a creedal slogan rather than ontological exclusivity of wujūd

title: Knowing Self Reveals the Lord Within
thesis: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
source_excerpt: The Prophet said, Whoever knows their self, knows their Lord. He did not say, Whoever annihilates their self, knows their Lord. Your being is nothing and whatever is nothing cannot be placed in relationship to anything else, whether it is capable of passing away or not and whether it is existent or nonexistent.
translation_literal: The Prophet said, Whoever knows their self, knows their Lord. He did not say, Whoever annihilates their self, knows their Lord. Your being is nothing and whatever is nothing cannot be placed in relationship to anything else, whether it is capable of passing away or not and whether it is existent or nonexistent.
commentary: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

وفي إضافة معرفة الله – تعالى – إلى فناء الوجود وإلى فناء فنائه إثباتُ الشرك، لأنك إذا أضفت معرفة الله إلى فناء الوجود وفناء الفناء، كان الوجود لغير الله ونقيضه – وهناك شرك واضح، لأن النبي – صلى الله عليه وسلم – قال: "مَن عرف نفسَه فقد عرف ربَّه"، ولم يقل: "مَن فني عن نفسه عرف ربَّه." فإن إثبات الغير يناقض فناءه، وما لا يجوز ثبوتُه لا يجوز فناؤه. وجودك لا شيء، واللاشيء لا يُضاف إلى شيء، لا فانٍ ولا غير فانٍ، ولا موجود ولا معدوم. «أنت» الآن كما كنتَ معدَمًا قبل التكوين. فالآن الأزل، والآن الأبد، والآن القِدَم. فالله هو وجود الأزل ووجود الأبد ووجود القِدَم؛ فإنه بلا وجود الأزل والأبد والقِدَم لم يكن كذلك ما كان وحده لا شريك له. وواجب أن يكون وحده لا شريك له: فإن "شريكه" هو الذي يكون وجودُه بذاته، لا بوجود الله؛ ومَن يكن كذلك لم يكن محتاجًا إليه، فيكون إذًا ربًّا ثانيًا – وذلك محال: فليس لله شريك ولا ندٌّ ولا كفؤ. ومَن رأى شيئًا مع الله أو من الله أو في الله – وذلك الشيء يحتاج إلى الله بالربوبية – فقد جعل ذلك الشيء أيضًا شريكًا يحتاج إلى الله بالربوبية. ومن جوَّزَ أن يكون مع الله شيءٌ يقوم بنفسه، أو يقوم به، أو هو فانٍ عن وجوده أو عن فنائه، فهو بعدُ ما شمَّ رائحة معرفة النفس، لأن مَن جوَّزَ أن يكون موجودًا سواه، قائمًا به، فيه يصير فانيًا في فنائه، فتسلسل الفناء بالفناء، – وذلك شِرْك بعد شِرْك، وليس بمعرفة النفس، – هو مُشْرِك، لا عارف بالله ولا بنفسه.

pratibha_layers.label: Transliteration (ALA-LC)
pratibha_layers.body:
wa akthar al-ʿurrāf ʾaḍāfū maʿrifat Allāh – taʿālā – ilā fanāʾ al-wujūd wa fanāʾ al-fanāʾ – wa dhālika ghalṭ wa sahw wāḍiḥ: faʾinna maʿrifat Allāh – taʿālā – lā taḥtāj ilā fanāʾ al-wujūd wa lā ilā fanāʾ fanāʾih, liʾanna al-shayʾ lā wujūd lahu, wa mā lā wujūd lahu lā fanāʾ lahu; faʾinna al-fanāʾ baʿda ʾithbāt al-wujūd. fa-idhā ʿarafta nafsak bilā wujūd wa lā fanāʾ faqad ʿarafta Allāh. – wa illā fa-lā.

wa fī ʾiḍāfat maʿrifat Allāh – taʿālā – ilā fanāʾ al-wujūd wa ilā fanāʾ fanāʾih ʾithbāt al-shirk, liʾannak idhā ʾaḍafta maʿrifat Allāh ilā fanāʾ al-wujūd wa fanāʾ al-fanāʾ, kāna al-wujūd li-ghayr Allāh wa naqīḍuh – wa hunāka shirk wāḍiḥ, liʾanna al-nabī – ṣallā Allāh ʿalayh wa sallam – qāla: "man ʿarafa nafsahu faqad ʿarafa rabbahu," wa lam yaqūl: "man fanī ʿan nafsihi ʿarafa rabbahu." faʾinna ʾithbāt al-ghayr yunāqiḍ fanāʾahu, wa mā lā yajāz thubūtuh lā yajāz fanāʾuh. wujūdak lā shayʾ, wa al-lā shayʾ lā yuḍāf ilā shayʾ, lā fān wa lā ghayr fān, wa lā mawjūd wa lā maʿdūm. "anta" al-ān kamā kunta maʿdaman qabla al-takwīn. fa-al-ān al-ʾazal, wa al-ān al-ʾabad, wa al-ān al-qidam. fa-Allāh huwa wujūd al-ʾazal wa wujūd al-ʾabad wa wujūd al-qidam; fa-innahu bilā wujūd al-ʾazal wa al-ʾabad wa al-qidam lam yakun kathālika mā kāna waḥdahu lā sharīk lahu. wa wājib an yakūna waḥdahu lā sharīk lahu: fa-ʾinna "sharīkuhu" huwa alladhī yakūn wujūduhu bi-dhātihi, lā bi-wujūd Allāh; wa man yakun kathālika lam yakun muḥtājān ilayh, fa-yakūn idhān rabbān thānī – wa dhālika muḥāl: fa-laysa li-Allāh sharīk wa lā nadd wa lā kufūʾ. wa man rāʾa shayʾan maʿ Allāh aw min Allāh aw fī Allāh – wa dhālika al-shayʾ yaḥtāj ilā Allāh bi-l-rubūbiyya – faqad jaʿala dhālika al-shayʾ ayḍan sharīkan yaḥtāj ilā Allāh bi-l-rubūbiyya. wa man jawwaza an yakūna maʿ Allāh shayʾun yaqūm binafsihi, aw yaqūm bihi, aw huwa fān ʿan wujūdihi aw ʿan fanāʾih, fa-huwa baʿdū mā shamma rāʾiḥat maʿrifat al-nafs, liʾanna man jawwaza an yakūna mawjūdān siwāh, qāʾimān bihi, fīhi yaṣīr fānīan fī fanāʾih, fa-tasalsal al-fanāʾ bi-l-fanāʾ, – wa dhālika shirk baʿda shirk, wa laysa bi-maʿrifat al-nafs, – huwa mushrik, lā ʿārif bi-Allāh wa lā bi-nafsihi.

items.definition: Arabic wujūd ‘finding/being found; existence’ → being as what is found in God alone; creatures have no independent wujūd Here: This is waḥdat al-wujūd (the oneness of being) applied rigorously—not a merging of two things into one, but the recognition that there was never a second thing… Trap: treating ‘existence’ as a neutral metaphysical predicate shared equally by God and world

‘unity of being/finding’ → the Real’s being is one; multiplicity is relational appearance, not rival substances Here: This is waḥdat al-wujūd (the oneness of being) applied rigorously—not a merging of two things into one, but the recognition that there was never a second thing… Trap: pantheist collapse that erases servant/Lord distinction

Arabic tawḥīd from waḥḥada ‘to make/declare one’ → absolute oneness of the Real, radicalized here as sole agency and sole being Here: This passage strikes at the very heart of the treatise's teaching on tawḥīd and self-knowledge. Trap: hearing a creedal slogan rather than ontological exclusivity of wujūd

Arabic fanāʾ ‘passing away, evanescence’ → passing-away of the egoic claim before the Real Here: The author is critiquing a common Sufi misreading whereby the path requires 'ceasing to be' (fanāʾ) and then the 'ceasing of that ceasing. Trap: self-erasure as quietism or dissociation rather than clearing of false independence

‘association/partnership’ → ascribing independent power or being to what is other-than-God Here: ' His argument is subtle but decisive: to speak of annihilating something is first to affirm that it truly exists—and to affirm an existence alongside God is p… Trap: narrowing to idol-worship while missing subtle self-ascription of agency

title: Nothingness Cannot Relate to Anything
thesis: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
source_excerpt: He did not say, Whoever annihilates their self, knows their Lord. Your being is nothing and whatever is nothing cannot be placed in relationship to anything else, whether it is capable of passing away or not and whether it is existent or nonexistent.
translation_literal: He did not say, Whoever annihilates their self, knows their Lord. Your being is nothing and whatever is nothing cannot be placed in relationship to anything else, whether it is capable of passing away or not and whether it is existent or nonexistent.

"anta" al-ān kamā kunta maʿdaman qabla al-takwīn. fa-al-ān al-ʾazal, wa al-ān al-ʾabad, wa al-ān al-qidam. fa-Allāh huwa wujūd al-ʾazal wa wujūd al-ʾabad wa wujūd al-qidam; fa-innahu bilā wujūd al-ʾazal wa al-ʾabad wa al-qidam lam yakun kathālika mā kāna waḥdahu lā sharīk lahu. wa wājib an yakūna waḥdahu lā sharīk lahu: fa-ʾinna "sharīkuhu" huwa alladhī yakūn wujūduhu bi-dhātihi, lā bi-wujūd Allāh; wa man yakun kathālika lam yakun muḥtājān ilayh, fa-yakūn idhān rabbān thānī – wa dhālika muḥāl: fa-laysa li-Allāh sharīk wa lā nadd wa lā kufūʾ. wa man rāʾa shayʾan maʿ Allāh aw min Allāh aw fī Allāh – wa dhālika al-shayʾ yaḥtāj ilā Allāh bi-l-rubūbiyya – faqad jaʿala dhālika al-shayʾ ayḍan sharīkan yaḥtāj ilā Allāh bi-l-rubūbiyya. wa man jawwaza an yakūna maʿ Allāh shayʾun yaqūm binafsihi, aw yaqūm bihi, aw huwa fān ʿan wujūdihi aw ʿan fanāʾih, fa-huwa baʿdū mā shamma rāʾiḥat maʿrifat al-nafs, liʾanna man jawwaza an yakūna mawjūdān siwāh, qāʾimān bihi, fīhi yaṣīr fānīan fī fanāʾih, fa-tasalsal al-fanāʾ bi-l-fanāʾ, – wa dhālika shirk baʿda shirk, wa laysa bi-maʿrifat al-nafs, – huwa mushrik, lā ʿārif bi-Allāh wa lā bi-nafsihi.

items.definition: Arabic fanāʾ ‘passing away, evanescence’ → passing-away of the egoic claim before the Real Here: To insist on annihilation is therefore to smuggle in a second existence alongside God — a hidden polytheism (shirk). Trap: self-erasure as quietism or dissociation rather than clearing of false independence

Arabic wujūd ‘finding/being found; existence’ → being as what is found in God alone; creatures have no independent wujūd Here: This passage strikes at the heart of the treatise's teaching on waḥdat al-wujūd, the oneness of being. Trap: treating ‘existence’ as a neutral metaphysical predicate shared equally by God and world

‘unity of being/finding’ → the Real’s being is one; multiplicity is relational appearance, not rival substances Here: This passage strikes at the heart of the treatise's teaching on waḥdat al-wujūd, the oneness of being. Trap: pantheist collapse that erases servant/Lord distinction

Arabic tawḥīd from waḥḥada ‘to make/declare one’ → absolute oneness of the Real, radicalized here as sole agency and sole being Here: But such affirmation is exactly what tawḥīd forbids. Trap: hearing a creedal slogan rather than ontological exclusivity of wujūd

‘association/partnership’ → ascribing independent power or being to what is other-than-God Here: To insist on annihilation is therefore to smuggle in a second existence alongside God — a hidden polytheism (shirk). Trap: narrowing to idol-worship while missing subtle self-ascription of agency

title: Your Being Cannot Relate to Anything
thesis: Your being is nothing and whatever is nothing cannot be placed in relationship to anything else, whether it is capable of passing away or not and whether it is existent or nonexistent.
source_excerpt: Your being is nothing and whatever is nothing cannot be placed in relationship to anything else, whether it is capable of passing away or not and whether it is existent or nonexistent. The Prophet alluded to the fact that you are nonexistent now as you were nonexistent before creation, because now is eternity-without-beginning and now is eternity-without-end and now is timelessness. God is the very being of eternity-without-beginning, eternity-without-end and timelessness even though in reality there is no eternity

God is the very being of eternity-without-beginning, eternity-without-end and timelessness even though in reality there is no eternity
commentary: Your being is nothing and whatever is nothing cannot be placed in relationship to anything else, whether it is capable of passing away or not and whether it is existent or nonexistent. sanskrit_devanagari:
وأكثر العُرَّاف أضافوا معرفة الله – تعالى – إلى فناء الوجود وفناء الفناء – وذلك غلط وسهو واضح: فإن معرفة الله – تعالى – لا تحتاج إلى فناء الوجود ولا إلى فناء فنائه، لأن الشيء لا وجود له، وما لا وجود له لا فناء له؛ فإن الفناء بعد إثبات الوجود. فإذا عرفت نفسك بلا وجود ولا فناء فقد عرفتَ الله. – وإلا فلا.

وفي إضافة معرفة الله – تعالى – إلى فناء الوجود وإلى فناء فنائه إثباتُ الشرك، لأنك إذا أضفت معرفة الله إلى فناء الوجود وفناء الفناء، كان الوجود لغير الله ونقيضه – وهناك شرك واضح، لأن النبي – صلى الله عليه وسلم – قال: "مَن عرف نفسَه فقد عرف ربَّه"، ولم يقل: "مَن فني عن نفسه عرف ربَّه." فإن إثبات الغير يناقض فناءه، وما لا يجوز ثبوتُه لا يجوز فناؤه. وجودك لا شيء، واللاشيء لا يُضاف إلى شيء، لا فانٍ ولا غير فانٍ، ولا موجود ولا معدوم. «أنت» الآن كما كنتَ معدَمًا قبل التكوين. فالآن الأزل، والآن الأبد، والآن القِدَم. فالله هو وجود الأزل ووجود الأبد ووجود القِدَم؛ فإنه بلا وجود الأزل والأبد والقِدَم لم يكن كذلك ما كان وحده لا شريك له. وواجب أن يكون وحده لا شريك له: فإن "شريكه" هو الذي يكون وجودُه بذاته، لا بوجود الله؛ ومَن يكن كذلك لم يكن محتاجًا إليه، فيكون إذًا ربًّا ثانيًا – وذلك محال: فليس لله شريك ولا ندٌّ ولا كفؤ. ومَن رأى شيئًا مع الله أو من الله أو في الله – وذلك الشيء يحتاج إلى الله بالربوبية – فقد جعل ذلك الشيء أيضًا شريكًا يحتاج إلى الله بالربوبية. ومن جوَّزَ أن يكون مع الله شيءٌ يقوم بنفسه، أو يقوم به، أو هو فانٍ عن وجوده أو عن فنائه، فهو بعدُ ما شمَّ رائحة معرفة النفس، لأن مَن جوَّزَ أن يكون موجودًا سواه، قائمًا به، فيه يصير فانيًا في فنائه، فتسلسل الفناء بالفناء، – وذلك شِرْك بعد شِرْك، وليس بمعرفة النفس، – هو مُشْرِك، لا عارف بالله ولا بنفسه.

وأكثر العُرَّاف أضافوا معرفة الله – تعالى – إلى فناء الوجود وفناء الفناء – وذلك غلط وسهو واضح: فإن معرفة الله – تعالى – لا تحتاج إلى فناء الوجود ولا إلى فناء فنائه، لأن الشيء لا وجود له، وما لا وجود له لا فناء له؛ فإن الفناء بعد إثبات الوجود. فإذا عرفت نفسك بلا وجود ولا فناء فقد عرفتَ الله. – وإلا فلا.

وفي إضافة معرفة الله – تعالى – إلى فناء الوجود وإلى فناء فنائه إثباتُ الشرك، لأنك إذا أضفت معرفة الله إلى فناء الوجود وفناء الفناء، كان الوجود لغير الله ونقيضه – وهناك شرك واضح، لأن النبي – صلى الله عليه وسلم – قال: "مَن عرف نفسَه فقد عرف ربَّه"، ولم يقل: "مَن فني عن نفسه عرف ربَّه." فإن إثبات الغير يناقض فناءه، وما لا يجوز ثبوتُه لا يجوز فناؤه. وجودك لا شيء، واللاشيء لا يُضاف إلى شيء، لا فانٍ ولا غير فانٍ، ولا موجود ولا معدوم. «أنت» الآن كما كنتَ معدَمًا قبل التكوين. فالآن الأزل، والآن الأبد، والآن القِدَم. فالله هو وجود الأزل ووجود الأبد ووجود القِدَم؛ فإنه بلا وجود الأزل والأبد والقِدَم لم يكن كذلك ما كان وحده لا شريك له. وواجب أن يكون وحده لا شريك له: فإن "شريكه" هو الذي يكون وجودُه بذاته، لا بوجود الله؛ ومَن يكن كذلك لم يكن محتاجًا إليه، فيكون إذًا ربًّا ثانيًا – وذلك محال: فليس لله شريك ولا ندٌّ ولا كفؤ. ومَن رأى شيئًا مع الله أو من الله أو في الله – وذلك الشيء يحتاج إلى الله بالربوبية – فقد جعل ذلك الشيء أيضًا شريكًا يحتاج إلى الله بالربوبية. ومن جوَّزَ أن يكون مع الله شيءٌ يقوم بنفسه، أو يقوم به، أو هو فانٍ عن وجوده أو عن فنائه، فهو بعدُ ما شمَّ رائحة معرفة النفس، لأن مَن جوَّزَ أن يكون موجودًا سواه، قائمًا به، فيه يصير فانيًا في فنائه، فتسلسل الفناء بالفناء، – وذلك شِرْك بعد شِرْك، وليس بمعرفة النفس، – هو مُشْرِك، لا عارف بالله ولا بنفسه.
sanskrit_iast:
wa akthar al-ʿurrāf ʾaḍāfū maʿrifat Allāh – taʿālā – ilā fanāʾ al-wujūd wa fanāʾ al-fanāʾ – wa dhālika ghalṭ wa sahw wāḍiḥ: faʾinna maʿrifat Allāh – taʿālā – lā taḥtāj ilā fanāʾ al-wujūd wa lā ilā fanāʾ fanāʾih, liʾanna al-shayʾ lā wujūd lahu, wa mā lā wujūd lahu lā fanāʾ lahu; faʾinna al-fanāʾ baʿda ʾithbāt al-wujūd. fa-idhā ʿarafta nafsak bilā wujūd wa lā fanāʾ faqad ʿarafta Allāh. – wa illā fa-lā.

wa fī ʾiḍāfat maʿrifat Allāh – taʿālā – ilā fanāʾ al-wujūd wa ilā fanāʾ fanāʾih ʾithbāt al-shirk, liʾannak idhā ʾaḍafta maʿrifat Allāh ilā fanāʾ al-wujūd wa fanāʾ al-fanāʾ, kāna al-wujūd li-ghayr Allāh wa naqīḍuh – wa hunāka shirk wāḍiḥ, liʾanna al-nabī – ṣallā Allāh ʿalayh wa sallam – qāla: "man ʿarafa nafsahu faqad ʿarafa rabbahu," wa lam yaqūl: "man fanī ʿan nafsihi ʿarafa rabbahu." faʾinna ʾithbāt al-ghayr yunāqiḍ fanāʾahu, wa mā lā yajāz thubūtuh lā yajāz fanāʾuh. wujūdak lā shayʾ, wa al-lā shayʾ lā yuḍāf ilā shayʾ, lā fān wa lā ghayr fān, wa lā mawjūd wa lā maʿdūm. "anta" al-ān kamā kunta maʿdaman qabla al-takwīn. fa-al-ān al-ʾazal, wa al-ān al-ʾabad, wa al-ān al-qidam. fa-Allāh huwa wujūd al-ʾazal wa wujūd al-ʾabad wa wujūd al-qidam; fa-innahu bilā wujūd al-ʾazal wa al-ʾabad wa al-qidam lam yakun kathālika mā kāna waḥdahu lā sharīk lahu. wa wājib an yakūna waḥdahu lā sharīk lahu: fa-ʾinna "sharīkuhu" huwa alladhī yakūn wujūduhu bi-dhātihi, lā bi-wujūd Allāh; wa man yakun kathālika lam yakun muḥtājān ilayh, fa-yakūn idhān rabbān thānī – wa dhālika muḥāl: fa-laysa li-Allāh sharīk wa lā nadd wa lā kufūʾ. wa man rāʾa shayʾan maʿ Allāh aw min Allāh aw fī Allāh – wa dhālika al-shayʾ yaḥtāj ilā Allāh bi-l-rubūbiyya – faqad jaʿala dhālika al-shayʾ ayḍan sharīkan yaḥtāj ilā Allāh bi-l-rubūbiyya. wa man jawwaza an yakūna maʿ Allāh shayʾun yaqūm binafsihi, aw yaqūm bihi, aw huwa fān ʿan wujūdihi aw ʿan fanāʾih, fa-huwa baʿdū mā shamma rāʾiḥat maʿrifat al-nafs, liʾanna man jawwaza an yakūna mawjūdān siwāh, qāʾimān bihi, fīhi yaṣīr fānīan fī fanāʾih, fa-tasalsal al-fanāʾ bi-l-fanāʾ, – wa dhālika shirk baʿda shirk, wa laysa bi-maʿrifat al-nafs, – huwa mushrik, lā ʿārif bi-Allāh wa lā bi-nafsihi.

items.definition: Arabic wujūd ‘finding/being found; existence’ → being as what is found in God alone; creatures have no independent wujūd Here: This is the heart of waḥdat al-wujūd: there is only one existence, the Real's, and what we call time, self, and world are its self-disclosures, not rival being… Trap: treating ‘existence’ as a neutral metaphysical predicate shared equally by God and world

Arabic tawḥīd from waḥḥada ‘to make/declare one’ → absolute oneness of the Real, radicalized here as sole agency and sole being Here: The logic is protective of tawḥīd: if any created thing possessed existence rooted in its own essence, it would be self-subsistent, independent of God, and the… Trap: hearing a creedal slogan rather than ontological exclusivity of wujūd

‘unity of being/finding’ → the Real’s being is one; multiplicity is relational appearance, not rival substances Here: This is the heart of waḥdat al-wujūd: there is only one existence, the Real's, and what we call time, self, and world are its self-disclosures, not rival being… Trap: pantheist collapse that erases servant/Lord distinction

‘association/partnership’ → ascribing independent power or being to what is other-than-God Here: The logic is protective of tawḥīd: if any created thing possessed existence rooted in its own essence, it would be self-subsistent, independent of God, and the… Trap: narrowing to idol-worship while missing subtle self-ascription of agency

from ʿarafa ‘to know/recognize’ → gnosis as recognition of the Real’s sole agency, not informational theology Here: The affirmation of divine oneness; in this treatise, the recognition that there is only one existence—God's—so that attributing independent being to any creatu… Trap: equating mystical knowing with accumulated doctrine

title: Eternity Dissolves When Truly Known
thesis: Read this line as a contemplative pointer: pause interpretation for a moment and let the insight disclose itself directly.
source_excerpt: God is the very being of eternity-without-beginning, eternity-without-end and timelessness even though in reality there is no eternity-without-beginning, eternity-with-out-end or timelessness. If it were otherwise, He would not be alone, without any associate.
translation_literal: God is the very being of eternity-without-beginning, eternity-without-end and timelessness even though in reality there is no eternity-without-beginning, eternity-with-out-end or timelessness. If it were otherwise, He would not be alone, without any associate.

"anta" al-ān kamā kunta maʿdaman qabla al-takwīn. fa-al-ān al-ʾazal, wa al-ān al-ʾabad, wa al-ān al-qidam. fa-Allāh huwa wujūd al-ʾazal wa wujūd al-ʾabad wa wujūd al-qidam; fa-innahu bilā wujūd al-ʾazal wa al-ʾabad wa al-qidam lam yakun kathālika mā kāna waḥdahu lā sharīk lahu. wa wājib an yakūna waḥdahu lā sharīk lahu: fa-ʾinna "sharīkuhu" huwa alladhī yakūn wujūduhu bi-dhātihi, lā bi-wujūd Allāh; wa man yakun kathālika lam yakun muḥtājān ilayh, fa-yakūn idhān rabbān thānī – wa dhālika muḥāl: fa-laysa li-Allāh sharīk wa lā nadd wa lā kufūʾ. wa man rāʾa shayʾan maʿ Allāh aw min Allāh aw fī Allāh – wa dhālika al-shayʾ yaḥtāj ilā Allāh bi-l-rubūbiyya – faqad jaʿala dhālika al-shayʾ ayḍan sharīkan yaḥtāj ilā Allāh bi-l-rubūbiyya. wa man jawwaza an yakūna maʿ Allāh shayʾun yaqūm binafsihi, aw yaqūm bihi, aw huwa fān ʿan wujūdihi aw ʿan fanāʾih, fa-huwa baʿdū mā shamma rāʾiḥat maʿrifat al-nafs, liʾanna man jawwaza an yakūna mawjūdān siwāh, qāʾimān bihi, fīhi yaṣīr fānīan fī fanāʾih, fa-tasalsal al-fanāʾ bi-l-fanāʾ, – wa dhālika shirk baʿda shirk, wa laysa bi-maʿrifat al-nafs, – huwa mushrik, lā ʿārif bi-Allāh wa lā bi-nafsihi.

pratibha_layers.label: Original (Arabic)
pratibha_layers.body:
وأكثر العُرَّاف أضافوا معرفة الله – تعالى – إلى فناء الوجود وفناء الفناء – وذلك غلط وسهو واضح: فإن معرفة الله – تعالى – لا تحتاج إلى فناء الوجود ولا إلى فناء فنائه، لأن الشيء لا وجود له، وما لا وجود له لا فناء له؛ فإن الفناء بعد إثبات الوجود. فإذا عرفت نفسك بلا وجود ولا فناء فقد عرفتَ الله. – وإلا فلا.

وفي إضافة معرفة الله – تعالى – إلى فناء الوجود وإلى فناء فنائه إثباتُ الشرك، لأنك إذا أضفت معرفة الله إلى فناء الوجود وفناء الفناء، كان الوجود لغير الله ونقيضه – وهناك شرك واضح، لأن النبي – صلى الله عليه وسلم – قال: "مَن عرف نفسَه فقد عرف ربَّه"، ولم يقل: "مَن فني عن نفسه عرف ربَّه." فإن إثبات الغير يناقض فناءه، وما لا يجوز ثبوتُه لا يجوز فناؤه. وجودك لا شيء، واللاشيء لا يُضاف إلى شيء، لا فانٍ ولا غير فانٍ، ولا موجود ولا معدوم. «أنت» الآن كما كنتَ معدَمًا قبل التكوين. فالآن الأزل، والآن الأبد، والآن القِدَم. فالله هو وجود الأزل ووجود الأبد ووجود القِدَم؛ فإنه بلا وجود الأزل والأبد والقِدَم لم يكن كذلك ما كان وحده لا شريك له. وواجب أن يكون وحده لا شريك له: فإن "شريكه" هو الذي يكون وجودُه بذاته، لا بوجود الله؛ ومَن يكن كذلك لم يكن محتاجًا إليه، فيكون إذًا ربًّا ثانيًا – وذلك محال: فليس لله شريك ولا ندٌّ ولا كفؤ. ومَن رأى شيئًا مع الله أو من الله أو في الله – وذلك الشيء يحتاج إلى الله بالربوبية – فقد جعل ذلك الشيء أيضًا شريكًا يحتاج إلى الله بالربوبية. ومن جوَّزَ أن يكون مع الله شيءٌ يقوم بنفسه، أو يقوم به، أو هو فانٍ عن وجوده أو عن فنائه، فهو بعدُ ما شمَّ رائحة معرفة النفس، لأن مَن جوَّزَ أن يكون موجودًا سواه، قائمًا به، فيه يصير فانيًا في فنائه، فتسلسل الفناء بالفناء، – وذلك شِرْك بعد شِرْك، وليس بمعرفة النفس، – هو مُشْرِك، لا عارف بالله ولا بنفسه.

‘association/partnership’ → ascribing independent power or being to what is other-than-God Here: For if it were not so, He would not be by Himself without any partner, and it is indispensable that He should be by Himself without any partner. Trap: narrowing to idol-worship while missing subtle self-ascription of agency

Arabic wujūd ‘finding/being found; existence’ → being as what is found in God alone; creatures have no independent wujūd Here: And God (whose name be exalted) is the very existence of past eternity and the existence of future eternity and the existence of past time — yet without past e… Trap: treating ‘existence’ as a neutral metaphysical predicate shared equally by God and world

title: All Existence Contained in One Syllable
sanskrit_devanagari: हरिः ॐ । ओमित्येतदक्षरमिदं सर्वं तस्योपव्याख्यानं भूतं भवद्भविष्यदिति सर्वमोङ्कार एव । यच्चान्यत्त्रिकालातीतं तदप्योङ्कार एव ॥ १ ॥
sanskrit_iast: hariḥ oṃ | om ity etad akṣaram idaṃ sarvaṃ tasyopavyākhyānaṃ bhūtaṃ bhavad bhaviṣyad iti sarvam oṅkāra eva | yac cānyat trikālātītaṃ tad apy oṅkāra eva || 1 ||
translation_literal: Hari Om. Om — this syllable is all this. What follows is an exposition of it. Whatever is past, present, and future — all of that is Om alone. And whatever lies beyond the three divisions of time — that too is Om alone.
commentary:
The text opens not with an argument but with a declaration so total it can barely be contained in grammar. *Idam sarvam* — all this — is the universe of phenomenal experience in its entirety. The claim is not that Om *represents* everything, or *symbolizes* reality, but that it *is* everything. The distinction is not metaphor but identity. Śaṅkara notes that since all diversified objects are not different from their names, and since all names are not different from Om, therefore all this is verily Om.

The temporal sweep is meticulous: past (*bhūtam*), present (*bhavat*), future (*bhaviṣyat*) — the entire field of conditioned time. Then the text adds: *yac ca anyat trikālātītam* — and whatever else lies beyond the threefold time. This points to the unconditioned, the *avyākṛta* (the unmanifested), the ground that is not itself temporal. That too is Om. The syllable thus contains both the temporal and the atemporal, both the conditioned and its ground.

*Akṣara* carries a deliberate double meaning: "syllable" and "imperishable." The imperishable is being revealed through the syllable — not as its symbol but as its very nature.

Key Terms:

- **oṃkāra** — the syllable Om as both sonic form and ontological ground; not a name *for* Brahman but Brahman as sound-form
- **akṣara** — syllable, and: imperishable, indestructible; the sonic and the eternal in one word
- **trikālātīta** — beyond the three times; the unconditioned ground that is not itself past, present, or future
- **upavyākhyāna** — exposition, detailed explanation; what follows is an unpacking of what the first sentence declares
insight: The text opens not with an argument but with a declaration so total it can barely be contained in grammar.
practice: Sit in silence. Internally sound the syllable Om without vocal effort — just the internal resonance. Notice the three components: the opening of A (arising, manifestation), the middle of U (sustaining, the dream-like interior), and the closing of M (dissolution, gathering back). Then notice the silence that follows, into which the sound dissolves. That silence is not the absence of Om but its fullness. The text is inviting you to recognize that you already live in that silence.

items.resonance: *citiḥ svatantrā viśvasiddhihetuḥ* — the sovereign Śakti is the cause of the universe's manifestation. Both texts open by locating the entire universe in consciousness; the Māṇḍūkya does it through Om as ground, the PHH through Citi as cause.
"The Tao that can be named is not the eternal Tao." The Māṇḍūkya takes the opposite risk: naming everything.
items.divergence: But "Om" as the name that contains all names approaches the same paradox from the other side.

items.resonance: "Listening not to me but to the Logos, it is wise to agree that all things are one." The Logos as the structural equivalent of Om — the unifying ground beneath apparent multiplicity.

title: The Self Recognizes Its Undivided Ground
sanskrit_devanagari: सर्वं ह्येतद् ब्रह्म अयमात्मा ब्रह्म सोऽयमात्मा चतुष्पात् ॥ २ ॥
sanskrit_iast: sarvaṃ hy etad brahma ayam ātmā brahma so 'yam ātmā catuṣpāt || 2 ||
translation_literal: All this is indeed Brahman. This Ātman is Brahman. This Ātman has four quarters.
commentary:
Three sentences that could each be the sole content of a philosophical tradition. *Sarvaṃ hy etad brahma* — all this is indeed Brahman — is a declaration of non-separation: the apparent multiplicity of the world is not other than the one undivided ground. *Ayam ātmā brahma* — this Ātman is Brahman — is the great identity statement, the *mahāvākya* that grounds Advaita: the individual principle of self-awareness and the universal ground of being are identical. Not similar. Not derivative. Identical.

Then: *so 'yam ātmā catuṣpāt* — this Ātman has four quarters. The apparent tension between the absolute declaration of unity and the analytical division into four is deliberate. The four-quarter analysis is not a description of how the Self actually is — it is a pedagogical instrument. Like a coin divided into four quarters: the coin is one, but the quarters serve to make it exchangeable, usable, comprehensible. Śaṅkara is explicit: the four quarters are *imagined* in Ātman to facilitate understanding. The point of the entire analysis that follows is to dissolve itself — to show that when the first three quarters are fully seen through, the fourth (Turīya) reveals itself as what was always the case.

Key Terms:

- **brahma** — the absolute ground of being; from *bṛh* (to expand, to be great); that which is greatest and expands infinitely
- **ātmā** — the Self; reflexive principle of self-awareness; here equated with Brahman, dissolving the distinction between individual and universal
- **catuṣpāt** — four-footed, four-quartered; *catuṣ* (four) + *pāt* (foot/quarter); the fourfold analytical schema
insight: Three sentences that could each be the sole content of a philosophical tradition.
practice: Before any experience arises — before thought, before sensation — there is the simple fact of being aware. This bare awareness, which you cannot step outside of and examine as an object, is *ātmā*. The text says this is *brahma* — the ground of all existence. Not similar to it. Not a part of it. Identical. Sit with "this is that" for five minutes. Not as a belief to maintain but as a recognition to allow.

pratibha_layers.label: Original
pratibha_layers.body: सर्वं ह्येतद् ब्रह्म अयमात्मा ब्रह्म सोऽयमात्मा चतुष्पात् ॥ २ ॥

pratibha_layers.label: IAST
pratibha_layers.body: sarvaṃ hy etad brahma ayam ātmā brahma so 'yam ātmā catuṣpāt || 2 ||

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body: All this is indeed Brahman. This Ātman is Brahman. This Ātman has four quarters.

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body:
Three sentences that could each be the sole content of a philosophical tradition. *Sarvaṃ hy etad brahma* — all this is indeed Brahman — is a declaration of non-separation: the apparent multiplicity of the world is not other than the one undivided ground. *Ayam ātmā brahma* — this Ātman is Brahman — is the great identity statement, the *mahāvākya* that grounds Advaita: the individual principle of self-awareness and the universal ground of being are identical. Not similar. Not derivative. Identical.

Then: *so 'yam ātmā catuṣpāt* — this Ātman has four quarters. The apparent tension between the absolute declaration of unity and the analytical division into four is deliberate. The four-quarter analysis is not a description of how the Self actually is — it is a pedagogical instrument. Like a coin divided into four quarters: the coin is one, but the quarters serve to make it exchangeable, usable, comprehensible. Śaṅkara is explicit: the four quarters are *imagined* in Ātman to facilitate understanding. The point of the entire analysis that follows is to dissolve itself — to show that when the first three quarters are fully seen through, the fourth (Turīya) reveals itself as what was always the case.

- **ātmā** — the Self; reflexive principle of self-awareness; here equated with Brahman, dissolving the distinction between individual and universal
- **catuṣpāt** — four-footed, four-quartered; *catuṣ* (four) + *pāt* (foot/quarter); the fourfold analytical schema

title: Verse 3 · Jāgrat — The Waking State
sanskrit_devanagari: जागरितस्थानो बहिष्प्रज्ञः सप्ताङ्ग एकोनविंशतिमुखः स्थूलभुग्वैश्वानरः प्रथमः पादः ॥ ३ ॥
sanskrit_iast: jāgaritasthāno bahiṣprajñaḥ saptāṅga ekonaviṃśatimukhaḥ sthūlabhug vaiśvānaraḥ prathamaḥ pādaḥ || 3 ||
translation_literal: The first quarter is Vaiśvānara — whose sphere is the waking state, who is conscious of the external, who has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, and who experiences gross objects.
commentary:
*Vaiśvānara* — "belonging to all people" or "universal" — names waking consciousness in its cosmic dimension. Even ordinary waking experience participates in something that exceeds the individual. The seven limbs (*saptāṅga*) are the cosmic body of which the individual body is a localization: heaven as head, sun as eye, air as breath, space as trunk, water as lower region, earth as feet, fire as mouth. The nineteen mouths (*ekonaviṃśatimukha*) are the complete apparatus through which consciousness experiences the waking world: five organs of perception, five organs of action, five vital airs, mind, intellect, ego-sense, and memory.

The philosophical implication is significant: individual waking consciousness is *cosmic consciousness functioning at a particular aperture*. The sense of being a separate individual in a world of objects is the result of identifying consciousness with this nineteen-mouthed apparatus rather than recognizing it as the field in which all apparatuses appear.

*Sthūlabhuk* — "experiencer of the gross" — names the mode: consciousness engaged with dense, relatively stable objects. The word *sthūla* (gross/dense) already signals that this is a relative description; the dream state's objects are *sūkṣma* (subtle/refined), but equally real from within their own register.

Key Terms:

- **vaiśvānara** — universal, all-pervasive; the cosmic name for waking consciousness; from *viśva* (all) + *nara* (human/being)
- **bahiṣprajña** — outwardly conscious; *bahis* (outside) + *prajña* (consciousness); awareness oriented toward external objects
- **saptāṅga** — seven-limbed; the cosmic body enumerated in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.2
- **ekonaviṃśatimukha** — nineteen-mouthed; the complete experiential apparatus
- **sthūlabhuk** — enjoyer of the gross; *sthūla* (gross, dense, material) + *bhuj* (to enjoy, to experience)
insight: *Vaiśvānara* — "belonging to all people" or "universal" — names waking consciousness in its cosmic dimension.
practice: Right now, in this waking moment: notice the nineteen mouths at work — some senses receiving, some organs ready for action, breath moving, mind interpreting, intellect judging, memory cross-referencing. All of this is happening. Now notice: all of this is appearing *in* awareness. The apparatus is within consciousness, not the other way around. This recognition — brief, light, repeated — is the beginning of *jāgrat* being seen through rather than merely lived in.

title: Verse 4 · Svapna — The Dream State
sanskrit_devanagari: स्वप्नस्थानोऽन्तःप्रज्ञः सप्ताङ्ग एकोनविंशतिमुखः प्रविविक्तभुक्तैजसो द्वितीयः पादः ॥ ४ ॥
sanskrit_iast: svapnasthāno 'ntaḥprajñaḥ saptāṅga ekonaviṃśatimukhaḥ praviviktabhuk taijaso dvitīyaḥ pādaḥ || 4 ||
translation_literal: The second quarter is Taijasa — whose sphere is the dream state, who is conscious of the internal, who has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, and who experiences subtle objects.
commentary:
*Taijasa* — "the luminous one," from *tejas* (light, radiance) — names the dream-state consciousness by its most salient characteristic: it is self-illuminating. In dream, consciousness needs no external light source. It creates its worlds from its own radiance, using the impressions (*vāsanā*) left by waking experience as its raw material.

The identical structure — seven limbs, nineteen mouths — operating now at the *sūkṣma* (subtle) level makes the philosophical point precisely. Dream is not a deficient form of waking; it is the same consciousness operating at a different register. This is the setup for the *Vaitathya Prakaraṇa*'s central argument: if dream objects can appear completely real during the dream, and are retrospectively recognized as unreal only from the waking state, then what guarantees that waking objects are not similarly real-appearing-and-ultimately-unreal when viewed from a higher epistemic standpoint?

*Antaḥprajña* — "inwardly conscious" — names the reversal: what was oriented outward in waking turns inward. The source of objects shifts from the shared material world to individual impressional content. Śaṅkara: "like a piece of canvas with pictures painted on it" — the dream mind holds the impressional material of waking experience and projects it as experience.

Key Terms:

- **taijasa** — the luminous one; from *tejas* (fire, radiance); consciousness as self-illuminating creator of its dream-world
- **svapnasthāna** — whose sphere is dream; *svapna* (dream, from *svap*, to sleep) + *sthāna* (sphere, place)
- **antaḥprajña** — inwardly conscious; the reversal of the outward orientation of waking
- **praviviktabhuk** — experiencer of the refined/subtle/discriminated; *pravivikta* (well-distinguished, subtle) + *bhuj*
insight: *Taijasa* — "the luminous one," from *tejas* (light, radiance) — names the dream-state consciousness by its most salient characteristic: it is self-illuminating.
practice: Tonight, before sleep: notice the moment of transition. As the waking state dissolves and dream begins to form, what is it that witnesses both? The transition is brief, but something is present through it. This witness — which is not itself waking or dreaming — is the thread the Māṇḍūkya is pulling. In the morning, notice the reverse transition: something was aware of deep sleep as well, since you remember having slept.

title: Verse 5 · Suṣupti — Deep Sleep
sanskrit_devanagari: यत्र सुप्तो न कञ्चन कामं कामयते न कञ्चन स्वप्नं पश्यति तत्सुषुप्तम् । सुषुप्तस्थान एकीभूतः प्रज्ञानघन एवानन्दमयो ह्यानन्दभुक् चेतोमुखः प्राज्ञस्तृतीयः पादः ॥ ५ ॥
sanskrit_iast: yatra supto na kañcana kāmaṃ kāmayate na kañcana svapnaṃ paśyati tat suṣuptam | suṣuptasthāna ekībhūtaḥ prajñānaghana evānandamayo hy ānandabhuk cetomukhaḥ prājñas tṛtīyaḥ pādaḥ || 5 ||
translation_literal: That is deep sleep wherein the sleeper desires no desire and sees no dream. The third quarter is Prājña — whose sphere is deep sleep, in whom all experience is unified, who is verily a mass of consciousness, full of bliss, who experiences bliss, and who is the door to the knowing of the other two states.
commentary:
The verse begins by defining deep sleep negatively — through absence of desire and dream — then immediately pivots to positive characterization. This is methodologically important: the text refuses to let deep sleep be merely an absence. The four positive descriptions are carefully chosen:

*Ekībhūtaḥ* — "become one" — names the unification of experience. The multiplicity of waking and dreaming collapses into undifferentiated unity. This is not the unity of recognition but the unity of non-differentiation — which is why it is not liberation.

*Prajñānaghana* — "mass of consciousness" — *ghana* means dense, massive, consolidated. Consciousness in deep sleep is not dispersed across objects but concentrated in undivided mass. The image is of space that becomes apparent *density* when no objects divide it — the space itself hasn't changed but the differentiation has ceased.

*Ānandamaya* — "full of bliss" — not the bliss of pleasant experience (which requires subject-object duality) but the inherent ease of consciousness not fragmented by desire and object. This is why sleep is restorative: in returning to the causal state, something of one's original nature is recovered.

*Cetomukha* — "having consciousness as its mouth/door" — Prājña is the gateway through which the other two states emerge and into which they return. The causal state contains the other states in seed form (*bīja*). This is also why Prājña is the doorway to understanding: by examining what is present in deep sleep (consciousness without objects) and absent (desire, duality), one can begin to sense what Turīya is.

Key Terms:

- **suṣupti** — deep sleep; from *su* (well) + *supti* (sleeping); fully, properly asleep
- **prājña** — the knowing one; the third-quarter experiencer; from *prajñā* (comprehensive knowing); paradoxically named "the knower" in the state where ordinary knowing is absent
- **ekībhūta** — become one, unified; the collapse of multiplicity into undifferentiated unity
- **prajñānaghana** — mass of consciousness; the density metaphor for unified, objectless awareness
- **ānandamaya** — made of bliss, full of bliss; the inherent ease of undivided consciousness
- **cetomukha** — having consciousness as its door; Prājña as the causal gateway
insight: The verse begins by defining deep sleep negatively — through absence of desire and dream — then immediately pivots to positive characterization.
practice: In the moment of waking from deep sleep, before the waking mind has fully consolidated, there is a brief window where something is present that belongs to neither sleep nor waking — a bare, contentless awareness. This is the closest most people come to sensing Turīya experientially. Cultivate the habit of pausing in this threshold moment. Not to grasp it — that immediately collapses it into the waking state — but to allow a recognition that was not absent during sleep.

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body: That is deep sleep wherein the sleeper desires no desire and sees no dream. The third quarter is Prājña — whose sphere is deep sleep, in whom all experience is unified, who is verily a mass of consciousness, full of bliss, who experiences bliss, and who is the door to the knowing of the other two states.

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body:
The verse begins by defining deep sleep negatively — through absence of desire and dream — then immediately pivots to positive characterization. This is methodologically important: the text refuses to let deep sleep be merely an absence. The four positive descriptions are carefully chosen:

*Ekībhūtaḥ* — "become one" — names the unification of experience. The multiplicity of waking and dreaming collapses into undifferentiated unity. This is not the unity of recognition but the unity of non-differentiation — which is why it is not liberation.

*Prajñānaghana* — "mass of consciousness" — *ghana* means dense, massive, consolidated. Consciousness in deep sleep is not dispersed across objects but concentrated in undivided mass. The image is of space that becomes apparent *density* when no objects divide it — the space itself hasn't changed but the differentiation has ceased.

*Ānandamaya* — "full of bliss" — not the bliss of pleasant experience (which requires subject-object duality) but the inherent ease of consciousness not fragmented by desire and object. This is why sleep is restorative: in returning to the causal state, something of one's original nature is recovered.

*Cetomukha* — "having consciousness as its mouth/door" — Prājña is the gateway through which the other two states emerge and into which they return. The causal state contains the other states in seed form (*bīja*). This is also why Prājña is the doorway to understanding: by examining what is present in deep sleep (consciousness without objects) and absent (desire, duality), one can begin to sense what Turīya is.

Key Terms:

- **suṣupti** — deep sleep; from *su* (well) + *supti* (sleeping); fully, properly asleep
- **prājña** — the knowing one; the third-quarter experiencer; from *prajñā* (comprehensive knowing); paradoxically named "the knower" in the state where ordinary knowing is absent
- **ekībhūta** — become one, unified; the collapse of multiplicity into undifferentiated unity
- **prajñānaghana** — mass of consciousness; the density metaphor for unified, objectless awareness
- **ānandamaya** — made of bliss, full of bliss; the inherent ease of undivided consciousness
- **cetomukha** — having consciousness as its door; Prājña as the causal gateway

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: In the moment of waking from deep sleep, before the waking mind has fully consolidated, there is a brief window where something is present that belongs to neither sleep nor waking — a bare, contentless awareness. This is the closest most people come to sensing Turīya experientially. Cultivate the habit of pausing in this threshold moment. Not to grasp it — that immediately collapses it into the waking state — but to allow a recognition that was not absent during sleep.

title: Verse 6 · Prājña as Cosmic Ground
sanskrit_devanagari: एष सर्वेश्वरः एष सर्वज्ञ एषोऽन्तर्याम्येष योनिः सर्वस्य प्रभवाप्ययौ हि भूतानाम् ॥ ६ ॥
sanskrit_iast: eṣa sarveśvaraḥ eṣa sarvajñaḥ eṣo 'ntaryāmy eṣa yoniḥ sarvasya prabhavāpyayau hi bhūtānām || 6 ||
translation_literal: This is the Lord of all; this is the knower of all; this is the inner controller; this is the source of all — for this is the origin and dissolution of all beings.
commentary:
The verse makes a cosmic claim: the same Prājña that is the deep-sleep state of the individual is also the ground of universal manifestation. *Sarveśvara* — Lord of all — not as theistic ruler but as the substratum on which all sovereignty rests. *Sarvajña* — knower of all — not omniscience as a faculty but as the consciousness that is the field in which all knowing occurs. *Antaryāmin* — the inner controller — the principle that governs all functions from within while remaining unaffected by them: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad's great image of the one who dwells in earth, in water, in fire, in mind, controlling each from within, yet unknown to each.

*Yoni* — source, womb, creative matrix — names the generative function. Prājña is not just where things end up (dissolution) but where they come from (origin). *Prabhavāpyayau hi bhūtānām* — origin and dissolution of all beings — establishes the eternal rhythm: multiplicity emerges from the causal ground and returns to it, in cosmic cycles and in the daily rhythm of waking-sleeping-waking.

What is extraordinary is that this verse makes the individual's nightly experience of deep sleep into a microcosmic participation in cosmic reality. You return to the ground of being every night. The question the Upaniṣad is building toward is: what if you could recognize this ground while awake?

Key Terms:

- **sarveśvara** — Lord of all; *sarva* (all) + *īśvara* (lord, controller); not theistic kingship but ontological priority
- **sarvajña** — omniscient; knowing all things by being the medium in which all knowing occurs
- **antaryāmin** — inner controller; from *antar* (within) + *yam* (to control, restrain); the governing principle within all things
- **yoni** — source, womb, creative matrix; the generative ground of existence
- **prabhavāpyaya** — origin and dissolution; *prabhava* (arising, emergence) + *apyaya* (merging back, dissolution)
insight: The verse makes a cosmic claim: the same Prājña that is the deep-sleep state of the individual is also the ground of universal manifestation.
practice: For 2 minutes, observe inner speech as sound only. Return to the silent awareness that hears it.

title: Verse 7 · Turīya — The Fourth
sanskrit_devanagari: नान्तःप्रज्ञं न बहिःप्रज्ञं नोभयतःप्रज्ञं न प्रज्ञानघनं न प्रज्ञं नाप्रज्ञम् । अदृष्टमव्यवहार्यमग्राह्यमलक्षणमचिन्त्यमव्यपदेश्यमेकात्मप्रत्ययसारं प्रपञ्चोपशमं शान्तं शिवमद्वैतं चतुर्थं मन्यन्ते स आत्मा स विज्ञेयः ॥ ७ ॥
sanskrit_iast: nāntaḥprajñaṃ na bahiṣprajñaṃ nobhayataḥprajñaṃ na prajñānaghanaṃ na prajñaṃ nāprajñam | adṛṣṭam avyavahāryam agrāhyam alakṣaṇam acintyam avyapadeśyam ekātmapratyayasāraṃ prapañcopaśamaṃ śāntaṃ śivam advaitaṃ caturthaṃ manyante sa ātmā sa vijñeyaḥ || 7 ||
translation_literal: It is not that which is inwardly conscious, not that which is outwardly conscious, not that which is conscious in both directions, not a mass of consciousness, not consciousness, not non-consciousness. It is unseen, beyond practical dealings, beyond grasp, without characteristics, unthinkable, indescribable — the essence of the recognition of the single Self, the cessation of phenomena, peaceful, auspicious, without a second. This is what is known as the Fourth. This is the Ātman. This is to be known.
commentary:
This is the most important verse in the Upaniṣad — arguably one of the most important single passages in the entire history of philosophy — and its method is pure *apophasis*: systematic negation of every possible characterization.

**The six negations** strip away each of the three states and every possible modifier:
- *na antaḥprajñam* — not inwardly conscious (eliminates Taijasa/dream)
- *na bahiṣprajñam* — not outwardly conscious (eliminates Vaiśvānara/waking)
- *na ubhayataḥprajñam* — not conscious in both directions (eliminates any combination)
- *na prajñānaghanaṃ* — not a mass of consciousness (eliminates Prājña/deep sleep)
- *na prajñam* — not consciousness (eliminates any remaining cognitive function)
- *na aprajñam* — not non-consciousness (eliminates inertness or unconsciousness)

Six negations that exhaust every logical possibility. After these, nothing can be said. What remains?

**The positive characterizations** then follow — not as descriptions of *what* Turīya is but as pointers to *how it functions* in relation to experience:

*Ekātmapratyayasāra* — "the essence of the recognition of the single Self" — the one constant that runs through all three states as the witnessing principle. Not a new thing to be discovered but the very substance of what has been present throughout.

*Prapañcopaśama* — "the cessation of phenomena" — not the destruction of appearances but their *upaśama*: settling down, coming to rest, recognizing their nature as appearances in consciousness. The world doesn't disappear; its independent-reality status does.

*Śāntam* — peaceful; *śivam* — auspicious; *advaitam* — without a second. These three together name the quality of Turīya: the peace that is not the opposite of disturbance but prior to the distinction, the auspiciousness that is not a quality but the intrinsic character of what-is, the non-duality that is not a relationship ("these two are actually one") but a recognition ("there was never a second").

The verse ends: *sa ātmā sa vijñeyaḥ* — that is the Ātman, that is to be known. The paradox of saying "this beyond-description is to be known" is deliberate: *vijñeya* here doesn't mean propositional knowledge-about but the direct recognition that Śaṅkara calls *aparokṣajñāna* — non-mediated knowing.

Key Terms:

- **turīya** — the fourth; *tur* (to cross over) + nominal suffix; that which crosses beyond the three; also written *turya*
- **apophatic negations** — *adṛṣṭa* (unseen), *avyavahārya* (beyond practical dealings), *agrāhya* (beyond grasp), *alakṣaṇa* (without characteristics), *acintya* (unthinkable), *avyapadeśya* (indescribable)
- **ekātmapratyayasāra** — the essence of the recognition of the single Self; *eka* (one) + *ātman* (Self) + *pratyaya* (recognition, conviction) + *sāra* (essence, core)
- **prapañcopaśama** — the cessation/settling of phenomena; *prapañca* (the phenomenal world, expansion) + *upaśama* (cessation, settling, coming to rest)
- **advaita** — without a second, non-dual; not a doctrine but a recognition: *a* (without) + *dvaita* (two-ness)
- **vijñeya** — to be known; not propositionally but through direct recognition
insight: This is the most important verse in the Upaniṣad — arguably one of the most important single passages in the entire history of philosophy — and its method is pure *apophasis*: systematic negation of every possible characterization.
practice: The six negations of Verse 7 can be used as a meditation. In sitting practice: *nāntaḥprajñam* — I am not this inward dream. *Na bahiṣprajñam* — I am not this outward waking. *Na prajñānaghanaṃ* — I am not even the unified blankness of deep sleep. *Na prajñam* — I am not any form of consciousness-as-faculty. *Na aprajñam* — I am not unconsciousness. Then sit in what remains after each negation. Not emptiness — *prapañcopaśama*: the settling. Not absence — *śāntam*: the peace. This is the practice the verse encodes.

items.resonance: the convergence point. Nāgārjuna's *śūnyavāda* (doctrine of emptiness) and Gauḍapāda's *ajātivāda* arrive at structurally similar positions — all phenomena lack independent origination
items.divergence: but from opposite directions. Nāgārjuna deconstructs from the phenomenal side; Gauḍapāda proceeds from the standpoint of consciousness as ground. This is the most productive dialogue in the Pratibhā corpus.

items.resonance: "The simple absolute and immutable mysteries of divine knowledge... are hidden in the transcendent darkness of hidden silence." Six apophatic negations followed by silence — the same method as Māṇḍūkya 7, arriving at the same impossibility of predication.

"What we cannot speak about we must pass over in silence." The limit of language as the door to what lies beyond — Wittgenstein as negative theologian arriving at the same boundary the Upaniṣad names *avyapadeśya*.

*na sukhī na ca vā duḥkhī na virakto na saṅgavān | na mumukṣur na vā muktā na kiñcin na ca kiñcana ||* — the liberated one refuses every binary predication. Aṣṭāvakra is describing the lived phenomenology of what Māṇḍūkya 7 describes ontologically.

unit_label: Verses 8–12 · Om and the Fourfold Correspondence
title: Verses 8–12 · Om and the Fourfold Correspondence
thesis: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
source_excerpt:
Overview
The second movement of the Upaniṣad maps the four-quarter analysis of the Self onto the phonetic analysis of Om, establishing a correspondence that transforms sound-meditation into a complete method of Self-inquiry.
translation_literal:
Overview
The second movement of the Upaniṣad maps the four-quarter analysis of the Self onto the phonetic analysis of Om, establishing a correspondence that transforms sound-meditation into a complete method of Self-inquiry.
commentary: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.resonance: Both texts establish a progressive dissolution of subject-object duality through meditative focus: the Mandukya maps the knower's attention inward through Om's quarters until the distinction between observer and observed collapses; Patañjali describes concentration on subtle objects culminating in merger where 'the object ceases to be a distinct entity and merges with the observer.'
items.divergence: The Mandukya uses phonetic-structural correspondence (Om's sound-form as gateway to Self), while Patañjali employs graduated object-focus as the mechanism; the Upanishad emphasizes the knower's return to itself, whereas Yoga Sutras emphasizes the object's refinement into subtlety.

items.citation: Svetasvatara Upanishad — Fire by Friction, Self by Om
items.resonance: Both employ a latency-and-manifestation structure: the Mandukya's Om analysis reveals the Self already present but unrecognized through inattention; Svetasvatara's fire-in-wood metaphor describes the hidden Self requiring 'the right means' to be brought forth—both posit that clarity comes through proper method applied to what is already there.
items.divergence: The Mandukya's method is strictly meditative-phonetic (the four quarters of Om), while Svetasvatara remains more general about 'right means'; the Upanishad emphasizes structural correspondence between sound and Self, whereas Svetasvatara uses natural analogy (fire/wood) without claiming isomorphic mapping.

items.citation: Plotinus Enneads — Ennead VI, Tractate 9, Section 8
items.resonance: Both describe a turning of attention toward an interior center as the condition for Self-recognition: the Mandukya's inward movement through Om's quarters culminates in the knower recognizing itself; Plotinus describes the soul's 'natural movement' revolving around 'its own centre, which is the source of its being'—both make centeredness the locus of self-knowledge.
items.divergence: The Mandukya uses a concrete phonetic scaffold (Om's structure) to guide this inward turn, while Plotinus appeals to the soul's inherent circular motion as self-evident; the Upanishad treats the center as discoverable through method, whereas Plotinus treats it as the soul's natural trajectory.

title: Verse 8 · The Mapping
sanskrit_devanagari: सोऽयमात्माध्यक्षरमोङ्कारोऽधिमात्रं पादा मात्रा मात्राश्च पादा अकार उकारो मकार इति ॥ ८ ॥
sanskrit_iast: so 'yam ātmādhyakṣaram oṅkāro 'dhimātraṃ pādā mātrā mātrāś ca pādā akāra ukāro makāra iti || 8 ||
translation_literal: This same Ātman, with reference to the syllable, is Om. With reference to the elements, the quarters are the elements and the elements are the quarters. The letters here are A, U, and M.
commentary:
A pivotal structural verse: the fourfold Self (*catuṣpāt*) and the fourfold Om (A, U, M + silence) are identified as the same reality approached through two different analyses. *Pādā mātrā mātrāś ca pādā* — "the quarters are the elements and the elements are the quarters" — establishes a two-way correspondence: each of the first three quarters *is* one of the phonetic elements of Om, and each element *is* one of the quarters. The fourth — silence — corresponds to Turīya.

This identification is not arbitrary mnemonic but reflects a genuine structural homology: A (the first, most open vowel, produced without obstruction) corresponds to Vaiśvānara (the most externally manifest, least differentiated from its ground); U (the middle vowel, connecting, produced in the middle of the mouth) corresponds to Taijasa (the intermediate state between gross and subtle); M (the closing consonant, gathering sound back to silence) corresponds to Prājña (the causal state that gathers waking and dreaming back to their source). The silence following Om — *amātrā* (the elementless) — corresponds to Turīya.

The practical consequence: meditation on Om, understood through this correspondence, becomes meditation on the structure of consciousness itself. Each sounding of Om enacts the entire movement from manifestation through dreaming through causal ground to unconditioned silence.
insight: A pivotal structural verse: the fourfold Self (*catuṣpāt*) and the fourfold Om (A, U, M + silence) are identified as the same reality approached through two different analyses.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.citation: Heart Sutra — Form Is Emptiness, Emptiness Is Form
items.resonance: Both texts establish identity between two apparently opposite categories through a reversible equation: Mandukya identifies Ātman with Om by mapping the fourfold Self onto the fourfold syllable; Heart Sutra identifies form with emptiness through the same bidirectional structure (form *is* emptiness, emptiness *is* form). Each uses symbolic/phenomenological analysis to reveal non-duality.
items.divergence: Mandukya grounds the identity in a single transcendent reality (Ātman) accessed through phonetic-meditative correspondence; Heart Sutra grounds it in the mutual emptiness of both terms, making neither primary—a distinctly Buddhist negation rather than Vedantic affirmation.

items.resonance: Both make a stark identity claim between consciousness and the ultimate Self, collapsing the distinction between knower and known into a single statement. Mandukya's 'Ātman is Om' and Śiva Sūtra's 'Consciousness is the Self' both use apposition to assert non-dual recognition.
items.divergence: Mandukya requires a fourfold structural analysis (catuṣpāt) to justify the identity; Śiva Sūtra asserts it directly without mediation, reflecting Kashmir Śaivism's emphasis on immediate recognition (pratyabhijñā) over systematic correspondence.

items.resonance: Both employ a contemplative inversion: Mandukya maps individual consciousness through the syllable Om to recognize the universal Ātman; Vijnana Bhairava Yukti 77 contemplates the presence of consciousness in all things to experience oneself as all-pervasive. Each uses meditation on a universal principle to dissolve the boundary between particular and infinite.
items.divergence: Mandukya works through symbolic correspondence (syllable as ladder); Vijnana Bhairava works through direct phenomenological extension (consciousness already present everywhere, needing only recognition), reflecting Tantra's emphasis on immanence over transcendent mapping.

title: Verse 9 · A — Waking Consciousness
sanskrit_devanagari: जागरितस्थानो वैश्वानरोऽकारः प्रथमा मात्राऽऽप्तेरादिमत्त्वाद्वाऽऽप्नोति ह वै सर्वान्कामानादिश्च भवति य एवं वेद ॥ ९ ॥
sanskrit_iast: jāgaritasthāno vaiśvānaro 'kāraḥ prathamā mātrā āpter ādimattvād vā āpnoti ha vai sarvān kāmān ādiś ca bhavati ya evaṃ veda || 9 ||
translation_literal: Vaiśvānara, whose sphere is the waking state, is A — the first element — on account of its pervasiveness or on account of being the first. One who knows this obtains all desires and becomes the first.
commentary:
The A vowel opens the mouth and generates the fundamental space from which all speech emerges. As the first vowel, it is prior to all differentiation — no other sound precedes it. This structural primacy mirrors Vaiśvānara's role: waking consciousness is the most immediately available state, the one from which the others are known and described. It is also the most *āpta* (pervading) — the A sound pervades all other sounds as their substrate, just as waking consciousness pervades and contains our ordinary understanding of the other states.

The "fruits" described (*āpnoti sarvān kāmān* — attains all desires) are traditional pedagogical incentives but have an inner meaning: to know the waking state as the first expression of the one Self is to recognize oneself as the source from which all desires arise. One does not attain desires as objects; one recognizes oneself as the creative ground of desire's arising.
insight: The A vowel opens the mouth and generates the fundamental space from which all speech emerges.
practice: For 2 minutes, observe inner speech as sound only. Return to the silent awareness that hears it.

items.resonance: Both texts identify consciousness as the fundamental principle that generates or encompasses all manifestation: the Mandukya locates the first vowel A as the generative opening from which speech emerges, while the Siva Sutra declares 'The mind is the Self'—establishing consciousness as the primary, all-containing reality.

items.resonance: Both passages establish pervasiveness as the defining characteristic of consciousness: the Mandukya names Vaiśvānara's pervasiveness (vyāpti) as the reason for its primacy, and the Pratyabhijnahrdayam describes the individual experient as containing the universe in contracted form—consciousness as the all-pervading substrate that appears in graduated manifestations.
items.divergence: The Mandukya emphasizes pervasiveness as the logical ground for naming the waking state, while the Pratyabhijnahrdayam emphasizes the paradox of contraction within the infinite—a Tantric inversion of scale rather than a naming principle.

title: Verse 10 · U — Dream Consciousness
sanskrit_devanagari: स्वप्नस्थानस्तैजस उकारो द्वितीया मात्रोत्कर्षादुभयत्वाद्वोत्कर्षति ह वै ज्ञानसन्ततिं समानश्च भवति नास्याब्रह्मवित्कुले भवति य एवं वेद ॥ १० ॥
sanskrit_iast: svapnasthānas taijasa ukāro dvitīyā mātrā utkarṣād ubhayatvād vā utkarṣati ha vai jñānasantatiṃ samānaś ca bhavati nāsyābrahmavit kule bhavati ya evaṃ veda || 10 ||
translation_literal: Taijasa, whose sphere is the dream state, is U — the second element — on account of its superiority or its intermediate position. One who knows this elevates the stream of knowledge, becomes balanced, and in their lineage no one is born without knowledge of Brahman.
commentary:
U is the middle vowel — between the open A and the closed M — and this medial position is its defining characteristic. *Utkarṣa* (superiority, elevation): U has a naturally rising, elevating quality; its sound lifts from the position of A toward the closure of M. This mirrors Taijasa's relationship to the other states: it rises from the gross engagement of waking toward the subtle interiority of deep sleep, while maintaining the complete cognitive apparatus in subtle form.

*Ubhayatva* (being in between, intermediate): U participates in both extremes — it has the openness of A and the interiority that approaches M. Taijasa similarly participates in both the external orientation of waking and the internal orientation of deep sleep.

The promise that "no one in the lineage is born without Brahman-knowledge" carries an important implication: genuine recognition does not stay bounded within one individual. The field of consciousness in which recognition occurs is not private property.
insight: U is the middle vowel — between the open A and the closed M — and this medial position is its defining characteristic.
practice: Choose one ordinary action today and perform it without haste or self-narration. End with one breath of gratitude.

title: Verse 11 · M — Deep Sleep Consciousness
sanskrit_devanagari: सुषुप्तस्थानः प्राज्ञो मकारस्तृतीया मात्रा मितेरपीतेर्वा मिनोति ह वा इदं सर्वमपीतिश्च भवति य एवं वेद ॥ ११ ॥
sanskrit_iast: suṣuptasthānaḥ prājño makāras tṛtīyā mātrā miter apīter vā minoti ha vā idaṃ sarvam apītiś ca bhavati ya evaṃ veda || 11 ||
translation_literal: Prājña, whose sphere is deep sleep, is M — the third element — on account of its measuring or its dissolution. One who knows this measures all this and becomes that in which all dissolves.
commentary:
M closes the lips and ends the sounding of Om. It is the consonant of closure, gathering, return. *Miti* (measuring): M provides the container, the measure, the limit within which the other sounds are defined. *Apīti* (dissolution, becoming-one-in): all the preceding sounds merge into M as their concluding resolution.

Prājña as the causal state is similarly the measure of the other two — it is the matrix from which they emerge and into which they return. Each day's waking and dreaming life is measured out from the deep-sleep causal ground and returns to it each night. The practitioner who truly knows this — not intellectually but through recognition — becomes *apīti* itself: the one in whom all dissolves, which is to say: the one who is recognized as the ground rather than as one of the states that arise in it.
insight: M closes the lips and ends the sounding of Om.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.resonance: Both texts identify a unified ground beneath the multiplicity of states: the Mandukya locates prājña as the measuring principle that dissolves distinctions in deep sleep, while the Spandakarika describes how 'relative notions tied to the ego rediscover their peaceful source deeply buried under all the different states.' items.resonance: Both passages structure recognition as a return to what is already known: the Mandukya's M 'measures' or completes the Om by closing what was opened, implying a cyclical recognition of the whole; Plotinus describes the soul's perception of beauty as 'an ancient recognition,' a resonance with what it already is. Each makes recognition a structural act of closure or homecoming.
items.divergence: The Mandukya grounds recognition in the dissolution of all content (deep sleep), while Plotinus grounds it in the soul's encounter with transcendent beauty—a positive attraction rather than a negation of multiplicity.
