unit_label: Verse 12 · The Silence — Turīya as Amātrā
title: Verse 12 · The Silence — Turīya as Amātrā
sanskrit_devanagari: अमात्रश्चतुर्थोऽव्यवहार्यः प्रपञ्चोपशमः शिवोऽद्वैत एवमोङ्कार आत्मैव संविशत्यात्मनाऽऽत्मानं य एवं वेद ॥ १२ ॥
sanskrit_iast: amātras caturtho 'vyavahāryaḥ prapañcopaśamaḥ śivo 'dvaita evam oṅkāra ātmaiva saṃviśaty ātmanātmānaṃ ya evaṃ veda || 12 ||
translation_literal: The fourth is without measure (*amātrā*), beyond practical dealings, the cessation of phenomena, auspicious, without a second. Thus Om is the very Ātman. One who knows this merges the Self into the Self by the Self.
commentary:
*Amātra* — without element, without measure, without syllabic weight. The silence following the sounding of A-U-M is not an element of Om the way A, U, M are elements. It is the ground from which they arise and into which they return. This asymmetry is crucial: the three sounds are *within* the silence; the silence is not within or alongside them. Similarly, Turīya is not a fourth state *alongside* waking, dreaming, and deep sleep but the unconditioned ground in which all three appear.

*Saṃviśaty ātmanātmānaṃ* — "merges the Self into the Self by the Self" — the final phrase is the most remarkable in the Upaniṣad. Three uses of *ātman* in one sentence, each playing a different grammatical role: the individual Self merges (*saṃviśati*) into the universal Self (*ātmānam*, accusative — the destination) by means of the Self (*ātmanā*, instrumental — the means). Subject, object, and instrument are all the same — the Self. This is not absorption of the individual into an other; it is the recognition that the individual and the universal were never two things requiring a merger.

The Upaniṣad concludes not with liberation as a future event but with the structure of recognition described in the present tense: *ya evaṃ veda* — "one who knows this thus" — it is present, immediate, now.

Key Terms:

- **amātrā** — without element/measure; the silence following AUM; the unconditioned ground not among the three elements but their source
- **saṃviśati** — enters, merges; but the merger is recognition of prior identity, not the achieving of a new unity
- **ātmanātmānam** — Self into Self; the double Ātman is grammatically and philosophically precise: no external destination
insight: *Amātra* — without element, without measure, without syllabic weight.
practice: Sound Om fully — A arising from the open throat, U rolling forward, M closing and humming through the skull — and then hold the silence afterward. Not making silence; it is already there. Notice that the silence is not empty: it is full with the same awareness that heard the sound. The sound dissolved into silence; the awareness in which the sound appeared did not dissolve. *Amātrā* — the measureless — is not an experience to be had but the ground of all experience to be recognized. Every sounding of Om, understood this way, is a complete recapitulation of the Upaniṣad.

Every sounding of Om, understood this way, is a complete recapitulation of the Upaniṣad.

items.resonance: Both passages define the ultimate reality by negation of ordinary attributes: Turīya is 'without measure' (amātrā), 'beyond practical dealings,' 'without a second'; the Self is 'inactive,' 'free,' 'all-pervading'—each strips away predicates to isolate a non-relational, non-functional ground of awareness.
items.divergence: Mandukya emphasizes the *silence* and *cessation* of phenomena as the mode of Turīya's transcendence, while Astavakra stresses the Self's eternal *witness-consciousness* and fullness—a difference between apophatic negation and positive non-dual presence.

items.citation: Tilopa Mahamudra — Mind Is Like the Open Sky
items.resonance: Both use spatial negation to indicate the ungraspable nature of consciousness: Turīya is 'without measure' (amātrā—literally without dimension), and mind 'has no center and no circumference'—each refuses to locate or bound the ultimate within conceptual or spatial coordinates.
items.divergence: The Mandukya passage treats amātrā as a property of Turīya's transcendence of all measure, while Tilopa uses spatial metaphor (open sky) to evoke the mind's intrinsic freedom from form—one is ontological negation, the other phenomenological openness.

items.citation: Plotinus Enneads — Ennead V, Tractate 1, Section 12
items.resonance: Both identify a gap between the soul's continuous self-activity and ordinary awareness: Turīya is the 'cessation of phenomena' yet the ground of all states; the soul 'continuously executes its characteristic act, but we remain unaware'—each posits an ever-present reality obscured by misdirected perception.
items.divergence: Mandukya locates this gap in the fourth state beyond waking, dream, and sleep (a state-based framework), while Plotinus locates it in the soul's perpetual activity masked by sense-focused attention (a perceptual-habit framework).

title: Gauḍapāda's Kārikā: Extended Philosophical Commentary
thesis: The first prakaraṇa closely follows the Upaniṣad's analysis.
source_excerpt: Āgama Prakaraṇa — Tradition · 29 Verses
translation_literal: Āgama Prakaraṇa — Tradition · 29 Verses
commentary:
The first prakaraṇa closely follows the Upaniṣad's analysis. Its distinctive contributions are:

The causality diagnosis (I.11–12): establishing that the first three quarters are conditioned (by cause and effect, or cause alone) while Turīya alone is uncaused — not one term in the causal chain but the ground in which causality appears.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.citation: Svetasvatara Upanishad — Knowledge and Ignorance in the Imperishable
items.resonance: Both texts posit a fundamental duality—knowledge and ignorance—as co-present within the ultimate ground (Brahman/imperishable). Gaudapada's analysis of consciousness requires examining how ignorance and knowledge structure awareness itself, mirroring the Svetasvatara's claim that both are 'hidden' in the imperishable.
items.divergence: Svetasvatara treats knowledge and ignorance as metaphysical principles hidden within Brahman; Gaudapada emphasizes their role in the phenomenology of consciousness and the path to freedom through discriminative awareness.

items.resonance: Both texts describe a progressive removal or dissolution of obscuring layers—Patañjali's 'coverings of knowledge' and Gaudapada's analysis of how ignorance veils the Self—culminating in a knowledge that is paradoxically 'almost nothing' or non-dual emptiness.
items.divergence: Patañjali frames this within the Yoga framework of mental transformation and samadhi; Gaudapada grounds it in Advaita Vedanta's non-dual recognition that the Self is eternally free and unbound.

items.resonance: Both texts invert the conventional value of knowledge, declaring that conceptual or dualistic knowledge itself becomes a form of bondage—a radical critique of the knower's assumption that accumulating knowledge liberates.
items.divergence: The Siva Sutra states this as a paradoxical aphorism within Kashmir Shaivism's recognition of consciousness; Gaudapada develops this through the Mandukya's analysis of the four states of consciousness to show how ignorance of non-duality perpetuates bondage.

title: Nothing Is Uncomfortable
sanskrit_devanagari:
mar pa la gu phyag 'tshal/
'jig rten gyi dgos pa spang bar byin gyis rlols/

brag dkar mtsho'i dbu phug tu/
ras pa bod kyi rnal 'byor pas/
zang zing med par bsgom/

steng 'og gi shing rta bde/
bal gos bde/
bsam gtan gyi sgyings thag bde/
lus zas bde/
sems gsal ba bde/
ci yang mi bde ba med/

ngas myur du 'chi/
sang rgyas thob par bya/
gtam du med par ting nge 'dzin la 'jug
sanskrit_iast: *rnal 'byor pa* / *re pa* (yogin Repa), *ting nge 'dzin* (samādhi), *sang rgyas* (buddhahood), *bsam gtan gyi sgyings thag* (meditation strap). Five comforts (bde ba lnga) song.
commentary:
Milarepa lists five comforts—hard mattress, cotton quilt, meditation strap, moderated body, clear mind—then declares nothing uncomfortable remains. The counterintuitive claim is ascetic comfort: hardship reframed as ease because the goal (*sang rgyas*) redefines the scale of evaluation. He dismisses pity from worldly visitors ("Spare me your misplaced pity") because pity measures comfort against ego's error, not against buddhahood's trajectory. Dragkar-Taso's cave is the laboratory: renunciation of food, clothing, and worldly aims is not deprivation but alignment. When the sun passes and visitors return home, Milarepa enters *ting nge 'dzin*—no time for useless talk. Kagyü hagiography uses this song to invert bourgeois sympathy for the green-skinned yogin: his comfort exceeds palace softness because clinging has been evacuated. Existentially: discomfort is not sensation but conflict between sensation and aim.

Key Terms:

**ting nge 'dzin** — Etymology: samādhi, meditative fixation, absorbed concentration. Closing refusal of "useless talk" enters *ting nge 'dzin*—not escapism but the quiescent state visitors cannot share. Default "samadhi" misses the Tibetan emphasis on unwavering fixity.
**bde ba lnga** — Etymology: five comforts. Enumerated ascetic satisfactions—mat, quilt, strap, body, mind—each "comfortable" by yogic standards. The song plays on *bde ba* (ease, pleasure) to scandalize worldly pity.
**rnal 'byor pa / re pa** — Etymology: yogin; *re pa* (cotton-clad one). Self-designation "Tibetan yogin called Repa"—identity tied to Marpa's lineage and cotton robe, not household status.
**sang rgyas** — Etymology: awakened, expanded. Self-set task of winning buddhahood reorganizes time: uncertain hour of death makes small talk wasteful. Comfort is measured against awakening, not cushions.
insight: Milarepa lists five comforts—hard mattress, cotton quilt, meditation strap, moderated body, clear mind—then declares nothing uncomfortable remains.
practice: Notice one physical inconvenience today—cold, hunger, stiffness. Before fixing it, ask whether it obstructs your real aim or only your preference. If the latter, bow once mentally and return to your task as Milarepa returns to samādhi when visitors leave.

pratibha_layers.body:
Tord! Gracious Marpa! I bow down at Thy Feet !
Enable me to give up worldly aims.

Here in the Dragkar-Taso’s Middle Cave,
On this the topmost summit of the Middle Cave,
I, the Yogz Tibetan called Repa,
Relinquishing all thoughts of what to eat or wear, and this
life’s aims,
Have settled down to win the perfect Buddhahood.

Comfortable is the hard mattress underneath me,
Comfortable is the Nepalese cotton-padded quilt above me,
Comfortable is the single meditation-band which holdeth up
my knee,!
Comfortable is the body, to a diet temperate inured,
Comfortable is the Lucid Mind which discerneth present
clingings and the Final Goal ;
Nought is there uncomfortable; everything is comfortable.

If all of ye can do so, try to imitate me;
But if inspired ye be not with the aim of the ascetic life,
And to the error of the Ego Doctrine? will hold fast,
I pray that ye spare me your misplaced pity ;
For I a Yogt am, upon the Path of the Acquirement of
Eternal Bliss.

The sun’s last rays are passing o’er the mountain tops ;
Return ye to your own abodes.
And as for me, who soon must die, uncertain of the hour of
death,

With self-set task of winning perfect Buddhahood,
No time have I to waste on useless talk ;
Therefore shall I into the State Quiescent of Samadhi

unit_label: A Demoness in the Body of an Aunt
title: A Demoness in the Body of an Aunt
thesis: Unlike the wisdom song's gift of property, this persecution song memorizes injury without immediate reconciliation—yet still ends with disciplined withdrawal rather than hail-magic.
source_excerpt:
Q Kind and Gracious Father, compassionate to all,
O Marpa the Translator, I bow down at Thy Feet!
Be Thou a Kindred unto me, who am bereft of kindred !
translation_literal:
Kind gracious father, compassionate to all—
Marpa the Translator, I bow at your feet!
Be kin to me, who am bereft of kin!

Aunt, do you recall all you have done?
If not, this song of mine will refresh your memory;
Listen attentively, and repent sincerely.

There in the wretched land of Kyanga-Tsa,
When our noble father died, he left us three—
A widowed mother and two orphans;
You defrauded us of all our wealth and brought us to misery.
Like peas struck from a staff we were scattered—
By you, aunt, and by our uncle too—
So our attachment to kin was severed.

Later, when I wandered long in distant lands,
Longing to see my sister and mother, I returned home
And found my mother dead and my sister gone.

Pierced with anguish, I turned to religion;
Finding it my sole solace, I chose the religious life.

Compelled by hunger to beg for alms,
I came before your door, aunt;
Recognizing me, a helpless devotee,
You burst out in spiteful anger.

Crying "Cho! Cho!" you set your dogs on me;
With your tent-pole you beat me heavily,
As though I were a sheaf of grain for threshing.
I fell face-down in a pool of water
And nearly lost my precious life.

In your fury you called me "Trafficker in Lives"
And "Disgrace to my clan";
Those words wounded my heart;
Overwhelmed with despair and misery,
My breath stopped and I was speechless.

Then, though I had no need of them,
You cheated me by various wiles of house and field.

You are a demoness in the body of an aunt,
Who severed all my love for you, aunt.

Later, at my uncle's door,
I met malicious thoughts, harmful acts, vile words.
"The destroying demon of the country comes!" was his cry;
He called the neighbors to help kill me;
Abusive words flew;
He pelted me with showers of stones
And sought to transfix me with a rain of small sharp arrows;
He filled my heart with an incurable sickness.
There too I nearly lost my life.
O butcher's heart in an uncle's form!
All respect for an uncle I lost then.

When I was poor and helpless, my kin were crueler than enemies.

Later, to the hill where I was meditating,
My constant Zesay came to see me out of love;
With gentle words she consoled me,
Comforted my sorrow-stricken heart,
Brought nourishing tasty food,
And saved me from starvation.
Kind indeed is she—more kind than I can say;
Yet since even she is not devoted to religion,
I see little need to meet her when she comes;
And as for you, aunt, far less need to meet you.
Return now as you came;
Better to go early while there is still time.
commentary:
Unlike the wisdom song's gift of property, this persecution song memorizes injury without immediate reconciliation—yet still ends with disciplined withdrawal rather than hail-magic. Milarepa catalogs fraud, beatings, near-drowning, forged land theft, uncle's mob, and Zesay's kindly but unreligious visits. The doctrinal naming—*bdud mo* in aunt's body, *srog lcags* severing kin-love—transforms relatives into afflictive forces without denying their humanity. Counterintuitive: he tells aunt to repent and listen, but also sends her away early; compassion here is truthful recollection, not sentimental merge. Zesay's nourishment saved his life yet he minimizes meetings because attachment to kin who reject dharma extends samsara's leash. The song closes Chapter X's persecution arc: kin cruelty forged his path; kin cannot be his resting place. Marpa's kinship (*nged med pas khyed nged du gyis*) frames the orphan's only family as guru-lineage.

Key Terms:

**bdud mo** — Etymology: demoness, female obstructing force. "You are a demoness in the body of an aunt"—afflictive function named without canceling kinship biology. Māra wears familiar faces.
**srog lcags** — Etymology: iron hook of life, life-rope. Kin attachment severed like cut life-cord—persecution destroys familial love that would bind him to revenge cycles.
**lo tsA ba** — Etymology: translator—Marpa Lotsawa. Opening homage to Marpa as kin-substitute for the bereft (*nged med*). Guru-lineage replaces clan after clan failed.
**a zhang** — Etymology: paternal aunt. Central persecutor throughout Chapter X; here invited to repent and remember. Familiar title (*a zhang*) persists even after demoness naming—complexity of real kin.
practice: Write one sentence recording a past injury without embellishment or revenge fantasy. Write one sentence on what practice that injury inadvertently forced. If the first sentence only reheats anger, destroy it; keep the second only if it genuinely turns poison into path.

If thou can not, this song of mine will refresh thy memory ;
Attentively give ear to it, and in repentance be sincere.

'“« There in the wretched land of Kyanga-Tsa,

Our noble father dying, left us, the three, a widowed mother
and two orphans ;

Of all our wealth thou didst defraud us, and brought us unto
misery.

And, as peas are by a staff, we were scattered then,

By thee, O aunt, and by our uncle, too.

So our attachment unto kith and kin was sundered.

'“ Thereafter, when in distant lands I wandered long,
Anxious to behold my sister and my mother, I returnéd
home,
And found my mother dead, and my sister gone.

With anguish pierced, I sought religion, and finding it my
sole solace,

The life religious thenceforth chose.

Compelled by lack of food to seek for alms,

Before thy door, O aunt, I came to beg,

And thou, in recognizing me, the helpless devotee,

Didst burst forth in a storm of spiteful anger.

With cries of ‘Cho! Cho!’ thou didst set thy dogs upon me;

With thy tent-pole thou didst belabour me most heavily,

As though I were a sheaf of corn for threshing.

I fell face downward in a pool of water,

Wherein I almost lost my precious life.

Amidst thy fury, thou didst cal] me ‘ Trafficker in Lives’;

And likewise, too, ‘Disgrace unto my Clan’.

With these rude words my heart was wounded ;

And, with despair and misery overwhelmed,

My breath was stopped and I was speechless.

And then, although I had no need of them,

Thou didst, by various wiles, defraud me of my house and
field.

A demoness thou art, in the body of an aunt,

That sundered me from all my love for thee, O aunt.

'« Thereafter, when I reached mine uncle’s door,
Malicious thoughts, injurious acts, vile words I met.
'The destroying demon of the country cometh,’ was his cry ;
He called the neighbours forth to help in killing me;
And, words abusive uttering,
He pelted me with showers of stones,
And sought to transfix me with a rain of small keen arrows;
With a malady incurable he filled my heart.
There, too, I almost lost my life.
O butcher’s heart in an uncle’s form!
All my respect for an uncle I lost then.

'When I was poor and helpless, my kinsfolk were more cruel
to me than enemies,
Thereafter, to the hill, where I was meditating,
My constant Zesay came to see me, out of love;

And she, with pleasant words, consoled me;

She comforted my sorrow-stricken heart ;

She brought me nourishing and tasty food ;

And from starvation saved me then.

Kind, indeed, is she, more kind than I can say;

Yet since e’en she is not devoted to religion,

Little need I see to meet her when she cometh ;

And as for thee, mine aunt, far less I need to meet thee.
Return e’en now, in the manner thou hast come ;

'Tis better to go early, while there is still the time

title: Ride the Mind-Horse to Buddhahood
thesis: The mind-horse metaphor systematizes mahāmudrā mind-training as equestrian craft: *gcig tu 'dzin* as lasso, meditation-post as tether, guru's teaching as feed, consciousness-stream as water, emptiness as cold enclosure.
source_excerpt: T bow down at the Feet of my Gracious Father Marpa!
translation_literal:
I bow at the feet of my gracious father Marpa!

Within the temple of the bodhi hill—my body—
Within my breast, where the altar stands,
Within the upper triangular chamber of my heart,
The horse of mind, moving like the wind, prances about.

What lasso must be used to catch this horse?
And to what post must it be tied when caught?
What food is given it when hungry?
What drink when thirsty?
In what enclosure is it kept when cold?

To catch the horse, use singleness of purpose as the lasso;
When caught, tie it to the post of meditation;
When hungry, feed it the guru's teachings;
When thirsty, give it the stream of consciousness;
When cold, keep it in the enclosure of emptiness.

For saddle use the will; for bridle, intellect;
Attach fixed immovability as girth and crupper;
Pass the vital winds as headstall and nose-band.

Its rider is the youth of keen watchfulness:
His helmet is Mahayana altruism;
His coat of mail is learning, thought, and contemplation;
On his back he carries the shield of patience;
In his hand the long spear of aspiration;
At his side hangs the sword of intelligence.

The smoothed reed of universal mind—
Straightened by freedom from wrath and hatred,
Barbed with the feathers of the four immeasurables,
Tipped with the sharpened arrowhead of intellect,
Placed in the pliant bow of spiritual wisdom,
Fixed in the aperture of the wise path and right method,
Drawn to the full span of wide communion—
Shot forth, the arrows fall among all nations.

They strike the faithful
And slay the sprite of selfishness.

Thus all evil passions are overcome
And our kindred are protected.

This horse courses across the wide plain of happiness;
Its goal is the state of all conquerors.
Its hindquarters leave attachment to samsaric life behind;
Its forequarters advance to the safe place of deliverance.

By running such a race I am carried toward buddhahood.
Judge whether this resembles your idea of happiness:
Worldly happiness I do not covet.
commentary:
The mind-horse metaphor systematizes mahāmudrā mind-training as equestrian craft: *gcig tu 'dzin* as lasso, meditation-post as tether, guru's teaching as feed, consciousness-stream as water, emptiness as cold enclosure. The counterintuitive density is tactical—saddle of will, bridle of intellect, rider of watchfulness, arrow of intellect barbed with four immeasurables shot from wisdom's bow to slay selfishness across nations. Worldly happiness is explicitly rejected at the close: the race's finish line is buddhahood, hindquarters leaving samsara behind. Unlike generic "mindfulness" metaphors, every tack piece maps to a doctrine: Mahayana altruism as helmet, patience as shield, aspiration as spear. The song asks disciples to judge whether this resembles their idea of happiness—forcing comparison rather than assent. In Kagyü imagery, wind-like mind must be caught or it runs wild through the bodhi-temple of the body.

Key Terms:

**sems rta** — Etymology: *sems* (mind) + *rta* (horse). Mind moves like wind through the heart's chamber—must be lassoed or lost. The horse is not enemy but power requiring tack.
**gcig tu 'dzin** — Etymology: one-pointedness, single grasp. Lasso to catch the horse—*ekagrata* in Indic terms, one of the named instruments. Without it, mind cannot be tied to meditation-post.
**stong pa nyid** — Etymology: emptiness. Enclosure protecting horse from cold—conceptual frame where mind is kept when "weather" of reification blows. Not nihilism but protective space in the metaphor system.
**tsem med bzhi** — Etymology: four immeasurables—loving-kindness, compassion, joy, equanimity. Arrow feathers barbed with the four—ethicized weaponry slaying selfishness, not enemies.
practice: When attention scatters today, name one "tack piece": lasso (single purpose for the next hour), post (breath or seat), feed (one remembered line of teaching), or enclosure (notice the next thought is empty of fixed self). Adjust one piece for two minutes before continuing.

items.resonance: Skillful attunement through repeated practice—tack pieces as cultivated craft, not one-time insight.

T bow down at the Feet of my Gracious Father Marpa!

Within the Temple of the Bodhi Hill, my body,
Within my breast, wherein the Altar is,
Within the chamber topmost and triangular within my heart,
The Horse of Mind, moving like the wind, doth prance
about.!

'* What Lasso must be used to catch this Horse?
And to what Post must It be tied when caught ?
What Food is to be given It when hungry ?

It is here assumed that the heart is the centre whence originate all mental
impulses, which, when uncontrolled, are as unruly as a wild horse. The catch-
ing and tying up of the Horse are the first steps in the science of mind-control
called Yoga. Once the mind processes are dominated, the bridled and saddled
Horse carries its spiritually accoutred rider, the Youth of Intellect, to Buddha-
hood,

What Drink is to be given It when thirsty ?
In what Enclosure is It kept when cold?

'“ To catch the Horse, use, as the Lasso, Singleness of Pur-
pose ;?
It must be tied, when caught, to the Post of Meditation ;
It must be fed, when hungry, with the Guru's Teachings ;
It must be given to drink, when thirsty, of the Stream of
Consciousness ;
- It must be kept, when cold, in the Enclosure of the Voidness.
For Saddle, use the Will, for Bridle, Intellect ;
Attach to It, as Girths and Cruppers, Fixedness Immovable ;
Around it pass, as Head-stall and as Nose-band, the Vital-
Airs.

'“Its rider is the Youth of Intellect [Keen Watchfulness] :
The Helmet, which he weareth, is Mahayanic Altruism ;
His Coat of Mail is Learning, Thought, and Contemplation ;
Upon his back he carrieth the Shield of Patience ;

He holdeth, in his hand, the long Spear of Aspiration ;

And, by his side, hangeth the Sword, Intelligence ;

The smoothed Reed of Universal Mind [or Cause],

Made straight by lack of wrath or hatred,?

Barbed with the Feathers of the Four Unlimited [Virtues],

Tipped with the Arrow-head of Intellect made keen,

Then placed within the pliant Bow of Wisdom Spiritual,

And fixed there, in the Aperture of the Wise Path and
_ Right Method,

He draweth out to the full fathom of Communion Wide;

And shot forth thus, the arrows fall midst all the Nations.

They strike the Faithful Ones,

And slay the Sprite of Selfishness.*

These verses describe progressive stages in yoga practice, beginning with
Ekagraté, ‘Singleness of Purpose’, or One-Pointedness of Mind, and leading
to Dhyana and Samadhi.

Here the figure used is of an arrow-shaft of bamboo, which is commonly
straightened and made even by heat, scraping, and polishing.

Herein, Milarepa justifies the life of ascetical seclusion from the world.
Unknown to the worldly multitude, who regard the yogt as a useless member
of society, he is, in fact, the most useful ; owing to his thought-force, broadcast
like silent and invisible arrows which fall among all nations, virtue and goodness

Thus are the Enemies, all Evil Passions, overcome ;
And protected are our Kindred.!

'This Horse doth course along the widespread Plain of
Happiness ;
Its Goal is the attainment of the State of all the Conquerors.”
Its Hind-part leaveth, in its rear, attachment to sangsdric
life ;
Its Front-part goeth on to the safe place of Deliverance.

' By running such a race, I’m carried on to Buddhahood ;
Judge if this be like your own conception of felicity:
Worldly Happiness I covet not

title: Solitude Reproves Its Own Restlessness
sanskrit_devanagari:
rdo rje 'chang mar pa'i skur/
dben pa la gnas par byin gyis rlols/

khyod mi la ras pa/
rang gi sems la glu 'di 'don/

mi dang gtam du med/
dben par 'dod kyang 'khrul/

sems ma bskyod/
yid g.yengs mi bya/

gdan las ma langs/
mgo ma bteg/

nyal ba mi bya/
dug lnga yis khyab par 'gyur
sanskrit_iast: *rdo rje 'chang* (Vajradhara; here in Marpa's form), *dben pa* (solitude), *dug lnga* (five poisons: desire, anger, ignorance, pride, jealousy). Self-reproof song (rang sems kyi glu).
translation_literal:
Dorje Chang yourself, in Marpa's form!
Grant that this mendicant may hold to solitude.

O strange fellow Milarepa—
To you I sing this song of self-counsel.

You stand apart from all humanity
That might share sweet conversation with you;
Therefore you feel lonely and would seek diversion—
There is no reason for you to seek it.

Do not stir up your mind; let it rest in peace.
If it holds thoughts, it will crave countless wrongs.

Do not yield to the desire for distraction; exert your intellect.
If you yield to temptation, your devotion will scatter to the wind.

Do not walk forth; rest content on your seat.
If you walk forth, your feet may strike stones.

Do not raise your head; bend it down.
If you raise it, it will seek vain frivolities.

Do not sleep; continue your devotions.
If you sleep, the five poisons of ignorance will overcome you.
commentary:
This is a self-address song (*rang gi sems la glu*): Milarepa speaks to himself in Marpa's voice, reproving the very loneliness solitude induces. The paradox at the center: he chose isolation yet now craves conversation and diversion—exactly what eroticized mind (*yid g.yengs*) would supply. Each imperative chain is somatic: do not walk (feet strike stones), do not raise head (frivolity), do not sleep (*dug lnga* overcome). The counterintuitive move is that freedom from humanity's company does not freedom from mind's restlessness make; solitude intensifies the inner crowd. In Kagyü self-reproof literature, addressing oneself as guru (Dorje Chang in Marpa's form) internalizes the vow-structure without external supervision. The five poisons at the close are not abstract sins but the physiological slide from devotional posture into spaced-out torpor. Reproof is compassion turned inward—harsh syntax as care.

Key Terms:

**dben pa** — Etymology: isolation, solitude, separation from crowds. The opening benediction requests successful *dben pa*—yet the song's body exposes solitude's temptation toward distraction. Solitude is achievement, not mood.
**yid g.yengs** — Etymology: mental wandering, distraction, scattered attention. "Do not yield to the desire for distraction"—*yid g.yengs* is the inner counterpart to the human conversation Milarepa lacks. Solitude without vigilance becomes entertainment-seeking.
**dug lnga** — Etymology: five poisons—desire, anger, ignorance, pride, jealousy. Sleep in meditation allows the five poisons to overcome the yogin. The list grounds metaphysics in the drowsy lapse from seat.
**rang sems kyi glu** — Etymology: song to one's own mind. Genre marker: Milarepa splits speaker and hearer within one person, using song-form for self-correction. The guru's face (Marpa/Dorje Chang) is internalized as reproving voice.
insight: This is a self-address song (*rang gi sems la glu*): Milarepa speaks to himself in Marpa's voice, reproving the very loneliness solitude induces.
practice: When boredom or loneliness arises in solitary work, do not reach for conversation or a scroll. Recite one line of self-reproof aloud: "Do not stir the mind; let it rest." Remain seated one minute longer than the impulse to move demands.

pratibha_layers.label: IAST
pratibha_layers.body: *rdo rje 'chang* (Vajradhara; here in Marpa's form), *dben pa* (solitude), *dug lnga* (five poisons: desire, anger, ignorance, pride, jealousy). Self-reproof song (rang sems kyi glu).

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
Dorje Chang yourself, in Marpa's form!
Grant that this mendicant may hold to solitude.

O strange fellow Milarepa—
To you I sing this song of self-counsel.

You stand apart from all humanity
That might share sweet conversation with you;
Therefore you feel lonely and would seek diversion—
There is no reason for you to seek it.

Do not stir up your mind; let it rest in peace.
If it holds thoughts, it will crave countless wrongs.

Do not yield to the desire for distraction; exert your intellect.
If you yield to temptation, your devotion will scatter to the wind.

Do not walk forth; rest content on your seat.
If you walk forth, your feet may strike stones.

Do not raise your head; bend it down.
If you raise it, it will seek vain frivolities.

Do not sleep; continue your devotions.
If you sleep, the five poisons of ignorance will overcome you.

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body:
This is a self-address song (*rang gi sems la glu*): Milarepa speaks to himself in Marpa's voice, reproving the very loneliness solitude induces. The paradox at the center: he chose isolation yet now craves conversation and diversion—exactly what eroticized mind (*yid g.yengs*) would supply. Each imperative chain is somatic: do not walk (feet strike stones), do not raise head (frivolity), do not sleep (*dug lnga* overcome). The counterintuitive move is that freedom from humanity's company does not freedom from mind's restlessness make; solitude intensifies the inner crowd. In Kagyü self-reproof literature, addressing oneself as guru (Dorje Chang in Marpa's form) internalizes the vow-structure without external supervision. The five poisons at the close are not abstract sins but the physiological slide from devotional posture into spaced-out torpor. Reproof is compassion turned inward—harsh syntax as care.

Key Terms:

**dben pa** — Etymology: isolation, solitude, separation from crowds. The opening benediction requests successful *dben pa*—yet the song's body exposes solitude's temptation toward distraction. Solitude is achievement, not mood.
**yid g.yengs** — Etymology: mental wandering, distraction, scattered attention. "Do not yield to the desire for distraction"—*yid g.yengs* is the inner counterpart to the human conversation Milarepa lacks. Solitude without vigilance becomes entertainment-seeking.
**dug lnga** — Etymology: five poisons—desire, anger, ignorance, pride, jealousy. Sleep in meditation allows the five poisons to overcome the yogin. The list grounds metaphysics in the drowsy lapse from seat.
**rang sems kyi glu** — Etymology: song to one's own mind. Genre marker: Milarepa splits speaker and hearer within one person, using song-form for self-correction. The guru's face (Marpa/Dorje Chang) is internalized as reproving voice.

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: When boredom or loneliness arises in solitary work, do not reach for conversation or a scroll. Recite one line of self-reproof aloud: "Do not stir the mind; let it rest." Remain seated one minute longer than the impulse to move demands.

title: Bodhicitta in the Skeleton
thesis: Peta arrives pitying Milarepa's cave, food, and green corpse-like body; he replies that if she could see his mind she would see *byang chub kyi sems* itself.
source_excerpt:
Obeisance to my Lords, the Gurus!
Grant that this Yogt may hold fast to solitude.
translation_literal:
Obeisance to my lords, the gurus!
Grant that this yogin may hold fast to solitude.

Sister, you are filled with worldly feeling;
Know that worldly joys and griefs are all impermanent.
But I, by taking these hardships on myself alone,
Am sure to win eternal happiness—
So listen to your brother's song:

To repay the kindness of all sentient beings—
Who have been our parents—I gave myself to religious life.

See my dwelling: like a jungle beast's lair;
Any other person would be afraid in it.

See my food: like what dogs and pigs eat;
It would make others nauseated.

See my body: like a skeleton;
Even an enemy would weep to see it.

In my behavior I seem like a madman;
Sister, you are moved to disappointment and sorrow—
Yet if you could see my mind, it is bodhicitta itself;
The conquerors rejoice to see it.

Sitting on this cold rock beneath me, I meditate with zeal
Enough to bear my skin torn off or flesh from bone;
Inside and out my body has become like nettles;
It has taken on an unchanging greenish hue.

Here in this solitary rocky cave,
Though I cannot drive melancholy from my mind,
I hold unchanged adoration and affection
For the guru, true embodiment of the eternal buddhas.

Thus persevering in meditation,
I shall surely gain transcendent knowledge and experience;
And if I succeed,
Happiness and prosperity are won within this lifetime as I go,
And in my next birth I shall win buddhahood.

Therefore, dear sister Peta,
Do not give way to sorrow,
But give yourself to penance for religion's sake.
commentary:
Peta arrives pitying Milarepa's cave, food, and green corpse-like body; he replies that if she could see his mind she would see *byang chub kyi sems* itself. The song's structural move is triple disjunction: dwelling like beast, food like swine, body like skeleton—each would horrify a worldly observer—yet mind rejoices conquering buddhas. Counterintuitive: external misery and internal bodhicitta coexist without contradiction; penance for all sentient beings justifies hardship that looks like madness. The green hue from nettles becomes sign of unchanging practice, not pathology. Milarepa acknowledges melancholy he cannot drive out, yet guru adoration holds steady—honesty without sentimental collapse. For Peta, sorrow is the wrong response; religious penance is the invitation. This is Kagyü pastoral pedagogy: family love redirected through impermanence (*'jig rten gyi dga' sdug mi rtag*) toward practice.

Key Terms:

**byang chub kyi sems** — Etymology: mind of awakening, bodhicitta. "If you could see my mind, it is bodhicitta itself"—the hidden interior that invalidates exterior pity. Not sentiment but altruistic aim for all beings' liberation.
**mi rtag** — Etymology: impermanence, instability. Worldly joys and griefs are impermanent; sister's sorrow attaches to what cannot last. Impermanence is reason for practice, not despair.
**dud 'gro** — Etymology: animal realm. Dwelling "like a jungle beast's lair"—behavioral resemblance to animal existence while human mind holds bodhicitta. Ascetic exterior mimics lowest realm; interior reverses the mimicry.
**ye shes** — Etymology: transcendent knowledge, pristine awareness. Zealous meditation will gain *ye shes* and experience— fruition language beyond mere moral reform. Sister is invited to penance that yields wisdom, not comfort.
practice: When someone pities your difficult path, do not argue. Ask whether they can see one inner fact—your aim, vow, or love motivating the hardship. If they cannot, bow and change subject as Milarepa redirects Peta from sorrow toward religious penance.

unit_label: Grace Cools Wrath at the Aunt's Door
title: Grace Cools Wrath at the Aunt's Door
thesis: The song's claim is that justified rage does not authorize retaliation when the guru's command binds the disciple.
source_excerpt: At the Feet of my Kind Father Marpa I bow down!
translation_literal:
At the feet of my kind father Marpa, I bow down.

In our wretched home in the gloomy corner of Tsa,
We three unfortunates—a grieving mother and two orphans—
Were scattered wide, like peas struck from a staff.
Was this not your doing? Think on it, aunt and uncle.

While I wandered far as a beggar,
My mother died by poverty's sharp blade;
My sister roamed, begging for food and clothes.
Unable to quench the longing to see them,
I returned to this prison, my native land.

My loving mother is lost to me forever;
My sister wandered off in grief;
My heart was pierced through with anguish.
The misery we three endured—
Was it not caused by you, our kin?

These unbearable sufferings led me to the religious life;
Yet while I meditated in lonely mountain solitudes
On the sacred teachings of gracious Marpa,
My provisions ran out—I had no food
To sustain this fleeting body,
And so I came to beg for alms.

Like a dying insect drawn to an anthill's mouth,
I came before my aunt's door;
You set fierce dogs on my weak, starved body,
And joined the attack yourself.

By your curses and threats
You stirred grief deep in my heart again;
By your repeated blows with the tent-pole
You filled my poor body with pain and bruises,
And nearly took my life.

I have good cause for anger against you—
But I am fulfilling my guru's commands;
Do not be so vengeful, aunt,
And give me food for my practice.

Marpa, Lord! O Merciful One!
By the power of your grace, cool your suppliant's wrath!
commentary:
The song's claim is that justified rage does not authorize retaliation when the guru's command binds the disciple. Milarepa inventories every cruelty—the scattered orphans, the mother dead of poverty, the sister wandering, the return to native land as prison—and arrives at the aunt's door with full cause for anger. The counterintuitive move: he names the cause ("Think on it, aunt and uncle") yet petitions for alms rather than revenge, framing his restraint not as weakness but as obedience to Marpa's *bka'*. The dying-insect-at-anthill image reverses expectation: the victim is drawn toward the site of wounding not from masochism but from the exhausted logic of kin and homeland. Kagyü biographies stage this scene as the test of whether Milarepa's black-magic past has truly ripened into dharma; cooling wrath through guru grace (*mar pa'i byin rlabs*) is the proof. Existentially: suffering that would justify breaking vows becomes the very material of vow-keeping.

Key Terms:

**byin rlabs** — Etymology: *byin* (bestow) + *rlabs* (waves, overflow) → grace, blessing, empowered influx. The closing plea asks Marpa's grace to cool wrath—not willpower but lineage power transmissible from guru to disciple. Default "blessing" misses the wave-like, almost physical descent of grace in Tibetan devotion.
**bka'** — Etymology: command, word, speech of authority. Milarepa restrains anger because he is "fulfilling my guru's commands"—*bka'* is not generic advice but binding instruction from the lama. The aunt's assault tests whether oral vows outweigh kin rage.
**khro ba** — Etymology: anger, wrath, heat. Milarepa admits "good cause for anger" yet asks grace to cool his suppliant's wrath. The song does not deny anger's legitimacy; it relocates its resolution from retaliation to guru-devotion.
**slong ba** — Etymology: to beg alms, solicit support. Returning to beg at the persecutor's door is the song's dramatic knot: the mendicant needs food for practice from the very kin who ruined his family. Alms become sacrament of vow over vengeance.
practice: When someone who injured you speaks sharply, pause before crafting your case. Name internally what happened, then ask whether answering would serve truth or merely cool your injury with their humiliation. If a vow, promise, or discipline binds you, state that binding once—silently or aloud—before you respond or withhold response.

pratibha_layers.label: IAST
pratibha_layers.body: Key terms: *rje btsun mar pa* (Lord Marpa), *bla ma* (guru), *chos* (dharma), *slong ba* (begging alms), *byin rlabs* (grace/blessing). Opening line attested in Jetsun-Kahbum song cycle (Chapter X, aunt encounter).

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
At the feet of my kind father Marpa, I bow down.

In our wretched home in the gloomy corner of Tsa,
We three unfortunates—a grieving mother and two orphans—
Were scattered wide, like peas struck from a staff.
Was this not your doing? Think on it, aunt and uncle.

While I wandered far as a beggar,
My mother died by poverty's sharp blade;
My sister roamed, begging for food and clothes.
Unable to quench the longing to see them,
I returned to this prison, my native land.

My loving mother is lost to me forever;
My sister wandered off in grief;
My heart was pierced through with anguish.
The misery we three endured—
Was it not caused by you, our kin?

These unbearable sufferings led me to the religious life;
Yet while I meditated in lonely mountain solitudes
On the sacred teachings of gracious Marpa,
My provisions ran out—I had no food
To sustain this fleeting body,
And so I came to beg for alms.

Like a dying insect drawn to an anthill's mouth,
I came before my aunt's door;
You set fierce dogs on my weak, starved body,
And joined the attack yourself.

By your curses and threats
You stirred grief deep in my heart again;
By your repeated blows with the tent-pole
You filled my poor body with pain and bruises,
And nearly took my life.

I have good cause for anger against you—
But I am fulfilling my guru's commands;
Do not be so vengeful, aunt,
And give me food for my practice.

Marpa, Lord! O Merciful One!
By the power of your grace, cool your suppliant's wrath!

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body:
The song's claim is that justified rage does not authorize retaliation when the guru's command binds the disciple. Milarepa inventories every cruelty—the scattered orphans, the mother dead of poverty, the sister wandering, the return to native land as prison—and arrives at the aunt's door with full cause for anger. The counterintuitive move: he names the cause ("Think on it, aunt and uncle") yet petitions for alms rather than revenge, framing his restraint not as weakness but as obedience to Marpa's *bka'*. The dying-insect-at-anthill image reverses expectation: the victim is drawn toward the site of wounding not from masochism but from the exhausted logic of kin and homeland. Kagyü biographies stage this scene as the test of whether Milarepa's black-magic past has truly ripened into dharma; cooling wrath through guru grace (*mar pa'i byin rlabs*) is the proof. Existentially: suffering that would justify breaking vows becomes the very material of vow-keeping.

Key Terms:

**byin rlabs** — Etymology: *byin* (bestow) + *rlabs* (waves, overflow) → grace, blessing, empowered influx. The closing plea asks Marpa's grace to cool wrath—not willpower but lineage power transmissible from guru to disciple. Default "blessing" misses the wave-like, almost physical descent of grace in Tibetan devotion.
**bka'** — Etymology: command, word, speech of authority. Milarepa restrains anger because he is "fulfilling my guru's commands"—*bka'* is not generic advice but binding instruction from the lama. The aunt's assault tests whether oral vows outweigh kin rage.
**khro ba** — Etymology: anger, wrath, heat. Milarepa admits "good cause for anger" yet asks grace to cool his suppliant's wrath. The song does not deny anger's legitimacy; it relocates its resolution from retaliation to guru-devotion.
**slong ba** — Etymology: to beg alms, solicit support. Returning to beg at the persecutor's door is the song's dramatic knot: the mendicant needs food for practice from the very kin who ruined his family. Alms become sacrament of vow over vengeance.

items.resonance: Structural homology: Milarepa names injuries yet refrains because a higher binding (guru command) governs response—parallel to Epictetus's insistence that events do not disturb unless judgment assents.
items.divergence: Stoic assent is rational self-governance; Milarepa's restraint is devotional obedience and grace-dependent cooling of *khro ba*.

items.citation: Bhagavad Gītā 3.19 (action without attachment to fruit)
items.resonance: Milarepa acts (begging, practicing) without seizing the fruit of revenge though he has cause—karmic action subordinated to religious vow.
items.divergence: Arjuna's frame is cosmic duty in war; Milarepa's is biographical restitution within guru-disciple lineage after crimes of black magic.

items.resonance: Suffering and impermanence are not denied but metabolized into practice rather than consolation—flowers fall amid longing; orphans scatter amid vow.
items.divergence: Dōgen's move is epistemological reversal; Milarepa's is narrative biography with explicit persecutor still alive at the door.

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: When someone who injured you speaks sharply, pause before crafting your case. Name internally what happened, then ask whether answering would serve truth or merely cool your injury with their humiliation. If a vow, promise, or discipline binds you, state that binding once—silently or aloud—before you respond or withhold response.

title: Compassion Tramples Demon Talk
sanskrit_devanagari:
bla ma rje btsun gyi byin rlabs kyis bdag rab tu byung/

'khor ba thams cad las kyis 'brel/
'dzin na thar pa'i srog chad/

snying rje yis bdud 'dul/
gtam ngan rlung la btang/
gdong steng du bltas/

yongs su mi 'gyur ba/
dben par 'tsho bar byin gyis rlols shig
sanskrit_iast: *'khor ba* (samsara), *las* (karma), *thar pa* (liberation), *bdud* (demon/māra), *snying rje* (compassion), *yongs su mi 'gyur ba* (the immutable). Refrain *snying rje yis bdud 'dul* is the song's doctrinal pivot.
commentary: Milarepa's counterintuitive move is not renunciation preached from safety but renunciation performed as gift—the aunt who stole his inheritance becomes the very person to whom he surrenders field and house. The song's repetitive anatomy (touch / build / drink / speak → sever / fall / drown / ruin) maps each ordinary samsaric tie to a specific spiritual haemorrhage: clinging to life's round severs liberation's artery (*thar pa'i srog rtsa*); fondness for kin becomes a demon's stronghold (*bdud khang*); stored wealth feeds enemies. Evans-Wentz moralizes stimulants with Christian proof-texts; the Tibetan pivot is sharper and more psychological. After cataloguing worldly poison, Milarepa does not answer persecution with magic—he had vowed patience and recognized his aunt as the support for cultivating it. The doctrinal climax inverts expected heroic renunciation: demon talk is trampled with compassion (*snying rje*), blame scattered to the wind, speech turned upward (*gdong steng du bltas*). In Kagyü oral instruction this triad is read as the outer-inner-secret sequence of relating to obstruction: meeting hostility without retaliation, releasing gossip without fixation, fixing view toward the immutable lord (Akṣobhya-in-essence). The aunt's field-payment becomes a hungry-ghost birth only if consumed; Milarepa instead converts property into patience-practice and departs for Drakar Taso. Renunciation here is not flight from family but the surgical removal of what property still binds.
insight: Milarepa's counterintuitive move is not renunciation preached from safety but renunciation performed as gift—the aunt who stole his inheritance becomes the very person to whom he surrenders field and house.
practice: As you go about your daily activities, notice the ways in which you are attached to worldly possessions and relationships. Imagine yourself without these attachments, and cultivate a sense of compassion and renunciation. Repeat the phrase "I subdue the demons of ignorance and desire" to yourself, and visualize yourself turning your face upward towards the ultimate goal of liberation.

items.definition: Etymology: *'khor* (turn, circle) + *ba* (nominalizer) → the wearisome round of conditioned existence. In this song, samsara is not abstract metaphysics but the momentum that wears the practitioner down through karma (*las kyis bsdams*). Quintman's "world of life's round" preserves the exhaustion Evans-Wentz's "web of karma" flattens.

Etymology: *thar pa* (liberation) + *srog rtsa* (life-artery, vital root). Refrain marking what clinging severs—touch samsara, drink worldly poison, and the artery of liberation is cut. "Vital cord" (Evans-Wentz) Christianizes; "artery" (Quintman) keeps the anatomical urgency of a lifeline one can sever by habit.

Etymology: *bdud* (demon, māra) + *khang* (house, fortress). Affection for kith and kin is not neutral warmth but a fortified stronghold where obstruction lodges. "Devil's Castle" (Evans-Wentz) dramatizes; "demon's stronghold" (Quintman) keeps the architectural image of something built and defended.

Etymology: *snying* (heart/mind) + *rje* (lord, master) → compassion as sovereign attitude. The song's pivot line parses as trampling demon-talk (*bdud kyi gtam*) with compassion—not subduing external demons by force but meeting malicious speech with *snying rje*. Evans-Wentz's "By compassion I subdue the demons" merges two images the Tibetan keeps distinct.

Etymology: *mi phyed pa* — immutable, undivided. Closing addressee invoked as *thugs rje ldan pa mi phyed pa'i ngo bo* (lord of compassion, Akṣobhya in essence). The benediction (*byin gyis rlobs*) requests grace to abide in mountain retreat—linking patience-gift to guru-yoga and the eastern buddha of mirror-like wisdom.

items.citation: Tilopa Mahamudra — Look at the Looker
items.resonance: Both texts make the move of surrendering effort itself to the guru as the gateway to grace—Milarepa gives field and house; Tilopa's practitioner 'spends their effort completely and then rests in devotion.' In each case, renunciation is not self-willed abstinence but active gift-surrender that opens the channel for transmission.
items.divergence: Milarepa's surrender is enacted through concrete social restitution (returning stolen property), while Tilopa's is interior—the exhaustion of striving itself becomes the vessel for sahaja (innate nature).

items.citation: Bhagavad Gita — Bhakti as Relational Non-Dual Practice
items.resonance: Both passages locate the transformative power not in renunciation alone but in relational orientation—Milarepa's grace flows through the aunt (the very person who wronged him), and Bhakti is 'relational non-dual practice' where ethical texture (non-hatred, compassion) is the lived form of devotion. The move is: surrender restructures relationship as the medium of liberation.
items.divergence: Milarepa emphasizes paradoxical reversal (enemy becomes vessel of grace), while Bhakti emphasizes steady orientation of heart toward the Divine as the ethical-relational texture itself.

items.citation: Isavasya Upanishad — Vidya and Avidya Together
items.resonance: Both texts refuse a simple binary between renunciation and engagement: Isavasya warns that devotion to ignorance *and* devotion to knowledge alone both lead to darkness, requiring a both-and wisdom. Milarepa's move similarly transcends the renunciate/householder split by performing renunciation *through* relationship with the aunt (the worldly person).
items.divergence: Isavasya's both-and is epistemological (knowledge and ignorance must be integrated), while Milarepa's is relational-karmic (the wrongdoer becomes the guru's instrument of grace).

pratibha_layers.label: Public-domain anchor
pratibha_layers.body:
Q Lord, my Guru, by Thy Grace do I the life ascetic live ;
My weal and woe are known to Thee!

Thewhole Sangsara, being e’er entangled intheWebof Karma,
Whoever holdeth fast to it severeth Salvation’s Vital Cord.

In harvesting of evil deeds the human race is busy ;
And the doing so is to taste the pangs of Hell.

The affectionate expressions of one’s kith and kin are the
Devil’s Castle ;?
To build it is to fall into the Flames [of Anguish].

That is, exclusive attachment to one’s own family is selfish, the true and
only family being Humanity, and for this family alone should the Bodhisattva
labour. Cf. Matthew x. 36-7: ‘And a man’s foes shall be they of his own
household. He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of
me; and he that loveth son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.’

The piling up of wealth is the piling up of others’ property ;
What one thus storeth formeth but provisions for one’s enemies.

Enjoying wine and tea in merriment is drinking juice of
aconite ;
To drink it is to drown Salvation's Vital-Cord.!

The price mine aunt brought for my field is things wrung
out of avarice ;
To eat them would entail a birth amongst the famished ghosts.’

The counsel of mine aunt is born of wrath and vengeance ;
To utter it entaileth general disturbance and destruction.

Whatever I possess, both field and house,
Take all, O aunt, and therewith happy be.

T wash off human scandal by devotion true ;
And by my zeal I satisfy the Deities.

By compassion I subdue the demons ;
All blame I scatter to the wind,
And upward turn my face.

In the Buddhist view, all stimulants—alcoholic drinks, narcotic drugs,
tobacco, and even the narcotic effects of strong tea and coffee—are not only
demonstrably deleterious to the physical organism, but in exciting the nerves
and the mind they give such control over the body to the lower or animal
nature as to inhibit all influx of the elevating spiritual influences of the higher
nature. Furthermore, sorrow, pain, and despair are to be regarded as potent
means to awaken the human race to the fact that all sangsdric existence is, in
the last analysis, inseparable from suffering, and therefore undesirable. Thus,
if stimulants are used to drown all unhappiness and an artificial and deceptive
feeling that everything is well with the world be engendered thereby, the
opportunity of reaching the purely spiritual state of Supramundaneness, beyond
the realm of sorrow, wherein there is the only true bliss, is lost—the Vital
Cord of Deliverance, the golden link between the higher and the lower, is
sundered, the sacred way to Olympus is closed, and human beings are left in
the darkness of their unbelief, slaves to the animal within them.

Although Christianity does not, most unfortunately, prohibit the use of all
such stimulants, as do Buddhism, the Higher Hinduism, and the whole of
Islam, the old Jewish prophet Isaiah has approached the right view in these
words: ‘The priest and the prophet have erred through strong drink, they are
swallowed up of wine, they are gone astray through strong drink; they err in
vision, they stumble in judgement’ (Jsatak xxviii. 7). Cf., too, Paul’s Epsstle to
the Ephesians (v. 18): ‘And be not drunken with wine, wherein is riot, but be
filled with the Spirit.’

That is, in the world of famished (or unhappy) ghosts (Skt. Preta-Loka).

Gracious One, Thou the Immutable,
Vouchsafe Thy Grace, that I may pass my life in solitude
successfully

unit_label: Words Do Not Yield True Fruit
title: Words Do Not Yield True Fruit
thesis: Milarepa's plough-field song argues that liberation is agricultural work on the mind (*sems kyi zhing*), not intellectual harvest from exposition.
source_excerpt: Grant that this mendicant may cling successfully to solitude.
translation_literal:
Grant that this mendicant may hold to solitude successfully.

On the field of tranquil mind
I spread the water and manure of steadfast faith,
Sow the unblemished seed of a pure heart,
And over it sincere prayer thunders like pealing rain;
Grace falls of itself, like a shower.

To the oxen and plough of undistracted thought
I add the ploughshare of right method and reason.
The oxen, guided by the undeluded person,
With firm grip of undivided purpose,
Goaded by the whip of zeal and perseverance,

Break the hardened soil of ignorance born of the five poisons,
Clear away the stones of a sin-hardened nature,
And weed out every hypocrisy.

Then with the sickle of the truth of karmic law
The harvest of the noble life is reaped.
The fruits—sublime truths—
Are stored in the granary to which no concept applies.

The gods roast and grind this precious food,
Which then sustains my humble self
While I seek the truth.

The dream I interpret thus:
Words do not yield true fruit;
Mere exposition does not yield true knowledge.
Yet those who devote themselves to religious life
Must exert utmost zeal and perseverance in meditation;
If they endure hardship and strive diligently,
And search with care, the most precious treasure can be found.

May all who sincerely seek truth
Be untroubled by obstacles on the path.
commentary:
Milarepa's plough-field song argues that liberation is agricultural work on the mind (*sems kyi zhing*), not intellectual harvest from exposition. The counterintuitive move: after elaborate metaphorical machinery—oxen of undistracted thought, whip of *brtson 'grus*, granary without concepts—the dream-interpretation punchline dismisses words and teaching themselves as insufficient (*tshig gis 'bras bu mi 'byung*). pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
Grant that this mendicant may hold to solitude successfully.

On the field of tranquil mind
I spread the water and manure of steadfast faith,
Sow the unblemished seed of a pure heart,
And over it sincere prayer thunders like pealing rain;
Grace falls of itself, like a shower.

To the oxen and plough of undistracted thought
I add the ploughshare of right method and reason.
The oxen, guided by the undeluded person,
With firm grip of undivided purpose,
Goaded by the whip of zeal and perseverance,

Break the hardened soil of ignorance born of the five poisons,
Clear away the stones of a sin-hardened nature,
And weed out every hypocrisy.

Then with the sickle of the truth of karmic law
The harvest of the noble life is reaped.
The fruits—sublime truths—
Are stored in the granary to which no concept applies.

The gods roast and grind this precious food,
Which then sustains my humble self
While I seek the truth.

The dream I interpret thus:
Words do not yield true fruit;
Mere exposition does not yield true knowledge.
Yet those who devote themselves to religious life
Must exert utmost zeal and perseverance in meditation;
If they endure hardship and strive diligently,
And search with care, the most precious treasure can be found.

May all who sincerely seek truth
Be untroubled by obstacles on the path.

unit_label: Liberation as the Stilling of Fabrication
title: Liberation as the Stilling of Fabrication
sanskrit_devanagari: कर्मक्लेशक्षयान् मोक्षः कर्मक्लेशा विकल्पतः । ते प्रपञ्चात् प्रपञ्चस् तु शून्यतायां निरुध्यते ॥
sanskrit_iast: karmakleśakṣayān mokṣaḥ karmakleśā vikalpataḥ / te prapañcāt prapañcas tu śūnyatāyāṃ nirudhyate //
translation_literal: Liberation [mokṣa] happens when karma and the afflictions [kleśa] run out. Karma and afflictions arise from conceptual construction [vikalpa]; construction arises from mental proliferation [prapañca]; and proliferation is halted—brought to rest—in emptiness [śūnyatā].
commentary:
Nāgārjuna reverse-engineers bondage to locate its true root, and the root is not desire or even ignorance in the abstract but *prapañca*: the mind's compulsive spinning-out of a conceptualized world of fixed things and selves. The chain runs downward—suffering rests on karma-and-affliction, which rest on *vikalpa* (the discriminating act that cuts experience into "this, not that"), which rests on *prapañca*. The counterintuitive move is the last clause: he does not say proliferation stops through willpower, austerity, or even calm, but *in emptiness*—*śūnyatāyāṃ nirudhyate*. Seeing that no phenomenon carries own-being removes the very footing on which conceptual fixation stands; there is nothing solid left for the mind to reify and defend. This is why Madhyamaka treats wisdom, not merely ethics or concentration, as ultimately liberating: ethics and concentration thin the afflictions, but only the insight into emptiness dissolves the machinery that manufactures them. For a retreatant the diagnosis is exact and humbling—restlessness in meditation is *prapañca* caught in the act, and it settles not when you fight the thoughts but when you stop believing in the solidity of what they are about.

Key Terms:

**prapañca (प्रपञ्च)** — Etymology: from *pra-√pañc*, "to spread out, expand, make manifold." The mind's proliferation into a reified plurality of named, graspable entities—conceptual sprawl. Default "diffuseness" or "elaboration" misses that Nāgārjuna treats it as the engine of saṃsāra itself.
**vikalpa (विकल्प)** — Etymology: *vi-* (apart) + *√kḷp* (to arrange, form): "construction by division." The discriminating thought that slices reality into fixed opposites; here it is the immediate cause of karma and affliction, one link above *prapañca*.
**kleśa (क्लेश)** — Etymology: from *√kliś*, "to torment, afflict." The afflictive states (craving, aversion, delusion and their kin) that drive action; not sins but structural distortions.
**mokṣa (मोक्ष)** — Etymology: from *√muc*, "to loosen, release." Freedom framed negatively as exhaustion of the karma-affliction cycle rather than positively as a state gained—consistent with emptiness having nothing to add.
insight: Nāgārjuna reverse-engineers bondage to locate its true root, and the root is not desire or even ignorance in the abstract but *prapañca*: the mind's compulsive spinning-out of a conceptualized world of fixed things and selves.
practice: When agitation arises in sitting, trace it one link back: from the feeling, to the judgment that named its object ("problem," "enemy," "lack"), to the assumed solidity of that object. Rest attention on that last assumption and ask, "does this have any own-being?" Let the answer be silence, and watch whether the proliferation loses momentum on its own.

title: Neither Self Nor Non-Self
sanskrit_devanagari: आत्मेत्य् अपि प्रज्ञपितम् अनात्मेत्य् अपि देशितम् । बुद्धैर् नात्मा न चानात्मा कश्चिद् इत्य् अपि देशितम् ॥
sanskrit_iast: ātmety api prajñapitam anātmety api deśitam / buddhair nātmā na cānātmā kaścid ity api deśitam //
translation_literal: "There is a self"—this has been provisionally taught. "There is no self"—this too has been taught. And the buddhas have also taught that there is neither any self nor any non-self whatsoever.
commentary:
This verse is a small masterclass in pedagogical skill and its limits. Nāgārjuna records three teachings, not one, and the ordering is a ladder. "There is a self" is *prajñapti*, a provisional designation given to those who would otherwise fall into moral nihilism—useful for teaching karma and responsibility. "There is no self" is the corrective *deśanā* for those who cling to that provisional self as real. But the third line kicks away both rungs: the buddhas taught "neither self nor non-self." The counterintuitive claim is that "no-self" is not the final truth either—because "non-self" is still a position, still a fixed conceptual stake driven into the ground, and any such stake is *prapañca*. To assert emptiness of self and then grip "selflessness" as one's new identity is to have missed the medicine while swallowing the label. Madhyamaka's target is not the self alone but the reifying impulse that would freeze any answer, negative included. This is why the verse belongs in a retreat on emptiness: practitioners who have loosened the self often re-solidify around "there is no me," a subtler and prouder fixation. The teaching leaves you with no doctrine to hold and no doctrine to defend—only the invitation to stop taking positions about what you are.

Key Terms:

**ātman (आत्मन्)** — Etymology: reflexive "self," cognate with breath (*an-*). In Buddhist usage the posited permanent, independent subject. Its provisional affirmation is a teaching device, not a metaphysical concession.
**anātman (अनात्मन्)** — Etymology: *an-* (not) + *ātman*: "non-self." Ordinarily Buddhism's flagship doctrine; here demoted from ultimate truth to a corrective still liable to be reified.
**prajñapti (प्रज्ञप्ति)** — Etymology: from *pra-√jñā* (to make known): "designation, conventional positing." Marks the "self" as a label assigned for a purpose, not a found entity—key to the two-truths framework.
**deśanā (देशना)** — Etymology: from *√diś* (to point, show): "teaching, indication." The buddhas *point* differently for different hearers; the same word can be true medicine or poison depending on the disease.
insight: This verse is a small masterclass in pedagogical skill and its limits.
practice: Sit and silently affirm, "I am a self." Notice the felt sense that arises. Then affirm, "there is no self," and notice that felt sense. Now drop both sentences and rest in the bare experiencing that remains when no position is being held. Whenever the mind reaches to conclude "so it must be X," release the conclusion and return to unposited attention.

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Sit and silently affirm, "I am a self." Notice the felt sense that arises. Then affirm, "there is no self," and notice that felt sense. Now drop both sentences and rest in the bare experiencing that remains when no position is being held. Whenever the mind reaches to conclude "so it must be X," release the conclusion and return to unposited attention.

title: The Two Truths
sanskrit_devanagari: द्वे सत्ये समुपाश्रित्य बुद्धानां धर्मदेशना । लोकसंवृतिसत्यं च सत्यं च परमार्थतः ॥
sanskrit_iast: dve satye samupāśritya buddhānāṃ dharmadeśanā / lokasaṃvṛtisatyaṃ ca satyaṃ ca paramārthataḥ //
translation_literal: The dharma the buddhas teach rests entirely on two truths: the truth of worldly convention [saṃvṛti-satya] and the truth of the ultimate [paramārtha-satya].
commentary:
Having spent twenty-three chapters dismantling every candidate for own-being, Nāgārjuna now blocks the natural misreading that he is a nihilist who has abolished truth. His answer is the two-truths distinction, and its subtlety is that these are two truths, not one truth and one falsehood. *Saṃvṛti* literally means a "covering," and the word is a double entendre: conventional truth both conceals the ultimate and is the necessary veil through which the ultimate can be communicated at all. Ordinary talk of persons, causes, paths, and buddhas is not error to be discarded; it is *satya*, valid within its register, the only register in which teaching can occur. The counterintuitive move is that emptiness does not compete with conventional reality but underwrites it: because things are empty of essence, they can arise dependently, function, and be spoken of. The retreat-relevant payoff is a refusal of two opposite errors: the pious literalist who takes the path as ultimately real and clings, and the clever nihilist who, having heard "all is empty," dismisses ethics and practice as illusion. Both have failed to distinguish the truths. The middle way lives in holding them together—practicing wholeheartedly within convention while knowing its emptiness.

Key Terms:

**saṃvṛti-satya (संवृतिसत्य)** — Etymology: *saṃvṛti* from *sam-√vṛ* (to cover, conceal, enclose), hence "concealing/conventional"; + *satya* (truth). The everyday truth of functioning appearances and language, which both hides the ultimate and conveys it. "Relative truth" loses the crucial nuance of *covering*.
**paramārtha-satya (परमार्थसत्य)** — Etymology: *parama* (highest) + *artha* (object, meaning) + *satya*: "truth of the highest meaning." Not a hidden thing but the emptiness of all things; ultimate precisely because it cannot be superseded.
**samupāśritya (समुपाश्रित्य)** — Etymology: *sam-upa-ā-√śri* (to rest upon, take support): the teaching "leans on" both truths together—neither is dispensable.
insight: Having spent twenty-three chapters dismantling every candidate for own-being, Nāgārjuna now blocks the natural misreading that he is a nihilist who has abolished truth.
practice: Pick one activity of your retreat day—eating, walking, bowing. Do it with full conventional care, as if it fully matters (because conventionally it does). Midway, note silently, "and this is empty of own-being." Practice letting both be true at once, without using the second thought to withdraw energy from the first.

unit_label: Missing the Division of the Truths
title: Missing the Division of the Truths
sanskrit_devanagari: ये ऽनयोर् न विजानन्ति विभागं सत्ययोर् द्वयोः । ते तत्त्वं न विजानन्ति गम्भीरं बुद्धशासने ॥
sanskrit_iast: ye 'nayor na vijānanti vibhāgaṃ satyayor dvayoḥ / te tattvaṃ na vijānanti gambhīraṃ buddhaśāsane //
translation_literal: Those who do not grasp how the two truths are distinguished do not grasp the profound reality [tattva] within the Buddha's teaching.
commentary:
This is Nāgārjuna's warning label, and it cuts both ways. The word *vibhāga*—distinction, division—tells us that wisdom is not merely knowing that there are two truths but knowing how to keep them properly apart and properly joined. Collapse them one way and you get eternalism: convention is mistaken for the ultimate, and passing things are treated as bearers of real essence. Collapse them the other way and you get nihilism: the ultimate is mistaken for a denial of convention, and the world's functioning, along with ethics and the path, is dismissed as unreal. Both collapses miss *tattva*, "thatness," the profound point. The counterintuitive teaching is that the *depth* of Buddhism is not a secret content but a competence—the trained ability to move between registers without confusing them. This reframes the whole spiritual project: enlightenment is less an exotic experience than a cured double vision, in which one no longer reifies appearances nor annihilates them. For the retreatant, this verse is a mirror held up to spiritual bypassing: the temptation, after tasting emptiness, to float above ordinary obligations as "ultimately empty." Nāgārjuna says flatly that this is not depth but a failure to understand the division—the beginner's error dressed as insight.

Key Terms:

**vibhāga (विभाग)** — Etymology: *vi-* (apart) + *√bhaj* (to divide, apportion): "distinction, correct division." Wisdom as the skill of distinguishing the registers of truth—neither fusing nor severing them.
**tattva (तत्त्व)** — Etymology: *tat* ("that") + abstract *-tva*: literally "that-ness," reality-as-such. Here the profound point is not a doctrine but the correct handling of the two truths.
**gambhīra (गम्भीर)** — Etymology: "deep, profound," used of oceans and of the dharma. Marks the two-truths teaching as the deep water in which the unwary drown (cf. 24.11, emptiness wrongly grasped as a snake wrongly held).
**śāsana (शासन)** — Etymology: from *√śās* (to instruct, rule): "teaching, dispensation." The whole body of the Buddha's instruction, whose depth is at stake.
insight: This is Nāgārjuna's warning label, and it cuts both ways.
practice: Notice one place today where you are tempted to use "it's all empty anyway" to excuse withdrawal from a real responsibility, or where you grip an outcome as if it were ultimately solid. Name which of the two truths you are collapsing. Then re-enter the situation holding both: act as if it matters, know that it is empty.

unit_label: The Ultimate Rides on the Conventional
title: The Ultimate Rides on the Conventional
sanskrit_devanagari: व्यवहारम् अनाश्रित्य परमार्थो न देश्यते । परमार्थम् अनागम्य निर्वाणं नाधिगम्यते ॥
sanskrit_iast: vyavahāram anāśritya paramārtho na deśyate / paramārtham anāgamya nirvāṇaṃ nādhigamyate //
translation_literal: Without leaning on everyday convention [vyavahāra], the ultimate [paramārtha] cannot be pointed out; and without reaching the ultimate, nirvāṇa is not reached.
commentary:
Here Nāgārjuna states the double dependence that saves emptiness from becoming a ladder to be kicked away too soon. There are two moves in one verse. First: the ultimate can only be *taught* through convention—there is no wordless transmission that bypasses ordinary language, gesture, and shared practice; even "emptiness" is a conventional pointer. This dignifies the whole apparatus of teaching, texts, and retreat: they are not lower rungs but the only rungs there are. Second: yet nirvāṇa still requires *arriving at* the ultimate—convention alone does not liberate. So the verse holds a productive tension: you cannot reach the far shore without the raft of convention, and you cannot mistake the raft for the shore. The counterintuitive implication is anti-mystical in one direction and anti-literalist in the other: it denies both that one can leap straight to a language-free absolute and that one can rest content in mere religious observance. For the practitioner this is deeply steadying. It means the ordinary means—instructions, breath, ethical form, community—are not obstacles to be transcended but the very medium of transcendence, while also refusing to let the means become an end. Practice honestly within convention, aiming past it.

Key Terms:

**vyavahāra (व्यवहार)** — Etymology: *vi-ava-√hṛ* (to carry on, transact): "worldly dealing, convention, ordinary usage." The whole domain of language, exchange, and agreed practice; the indispensable vehicle for teaching the ultimate.
**deśyate (देश्यते)** — Etymology: passive of *√diś* (to point, indicate): "is shown/taught." The ultimate is *shown*, pointed at through convention, never handed over directly.
**adhigamyate (अधिगम्यते)** — Etymology: passive of *adhi-√gam* (to reach, attain, understand): "is reached/realized." Nirvāṇa as an arrival that still must occur, lest convention be mistaken for sufficiency.
insight: Here Nāgārjuna states the double dependence that saves emptiness from becoming a ladder to be kicked away too soon.
practice: Take the most "ordinary" support in your practice—counting breaths, a spoken refuge, a bow. Instead of treating it as a beginner's crutch, use it deliberately as the raft it is: engage it fully for ten minutes, and at the end silently acknowledge, "this convention carries me toward what it cannot itself be." Neither despise the raft nor cling to it.

unit_label: For Whom Emptiness Works, Everything Works
title: For Whom Emptiness Works, Everything Works
sanskrit_devanagari: सर्वं च युज्यते तस्य शून्यता यस्य युज्यते । सर्वं न युज्यते तस्य शून्यं यस्य न युज्यते ॥
sanskrit_iast: sarvaṃ ca yujyate tasya śūnyatā yasya yujyate / sarvaṃ na yujyate tasya śūnyaṃ yasya na yujyate //
translation_literal: For the one for whom emptiness [śūnyatā] holds good, everything holds good; for the one for whom emptiness does not hold good, nothing holds good.
commentary:
This verse turns the tables on Nāgārjuna's opponent with a single elegant inversion. The realist had objected (24.1–6) that if everything is empty, then arising, ceasing, the four noble truths, the path, and even buddhas become impossible—emptiness destroys the world. Nāgārjuna replies that the exact reverse is true: only because things are empty of fixed essence can they change, function, and be effective at all. *Yujyate*—"fits, is coherent, works"—is the operative word: emptiness is not the enemy of coherence but its precondition. A thing with frozen own-being could never grow, interact, be caused, or be transformed; a seed that truly was a seed in essence could never become a sprout. So the objector has it backwards: it is *essence*, not emptiness, that would paralyze reality. The counterintuitive claim, then, is that emptiness is the most affirming of doctrines—it is what makes the whole functioning world, including the path to liberation, possible. For a practitioner this dissolves the fear that meditating on emptiness will drain meaning or motivation from life. The opposite is promised: to see emptiness rightly is to see everything as workable, open, and responsive—including oneself, who is therefore not fixed and can actually change.

Key Terms:

**yujyate (युज्यते)** — Etymology: passive of *√yuj* (to join, yoke, fit): "is coherent, is tenable, works." Nāgārjuna's test of a view is whether reality still *fits together* under it; emptiness passes, essence fails.
