items.definition: √cit ‘perceive/be aware’ → consciousness itself, the self-luminous awareness that is the true nature within every being → ‘mind/thought’ is the trap; cit is knowingness as such
tat + -maya → consisting of that → 'made of that' — the contemplation that all things are composed of nothing but consciousness → ‘absorbed’ trance-word misses being made of the object/source

√bhū causative → bringing-into-being / creative contemplation → sustained, felt contemplation that turns an idea into lived realization → ‘meditation’ is too generic; here imaginative saturation that makes real

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.citation: Plotinus Enneads — Ennead V, Tractate 1, Section 12
items.resonance: Both texts identify a structural blindness: the soul/awareness continuously performs its nature, but ordinary perception misses it because attention is absorbed in external content. Turning attention inward (to the knower rather than the known) reveals what was always operating.
items.divergence: Plotinus frames this as the soul's continuous noetic activity obscured by sensory focus; Vijnana Bhairava locates the same awareness identically in all bodies as a direct recognition, emphasizing non-dual recognition over Plotinian hierarchical emanation.

items.resonance: Both passages move from recognizing a universal principle (awareness/Consciousness) to a transformative assimilation: when attention stabilizes on the fundamental attribute itself rather than its modifications, the knower realizes identity with the whole.
items.divergence: Pratyabhijnahrdayam emphasizes the power of Consciousness to assimilate the universe through recognition; Vijnana Bhairava emphasizes the sameness of awareness across all beings as the direct insight, with less emphasis on the assimilative act.

items.citation: Tilopa Mahamudra — Mind Is Like the Open Sky
items.resonance: Both use the metaphor of boundlessness (no center, no circumference; same in all bodies) to point toward a nature that cannot be grasped by ordinary spatial or conceptual reference—the knower itself has no fixed location or limit.
items.divergence: Tilopa uses spatial negation (open sky) to dissolve conceptual framing of mind; Vijnana Bhairava uses the ubiquity of awareness across embodied beings to establish its fundamental, unchanging character.

title: Stillness Reveals What Persists Beyond Emotion
sanskrit_devanagari: कामक्रोधलोभमोहमदमात्सर्यगोचरे । बुद्धिं निस्तिमितां कृत्वा तत् तत्त्वम् अवशिष्यते ॥ १०१ ॥
sanskrit_iast: kāmakrodhalobhamohamadamātsaryagocare | buddhiṃ nistimitāṃ kṛtvā tat tattvam avaśiṣyate || 101 ||
translation_literal:
YUKTI #73
When in the field of craving, anger, greed, confusion, intoxicated
excitement, or jealousy, make the mind still & soft [right in the
middle of the emotion]: reality is that which remains [when the
feeling has passed through]. || 101
commentary: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
insight: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

pratibha_layers.body: कामक्रोधलोभमोहमदमात्सर्यगोचरे । बुद्धिं निस्तिमितां कृत्वा तत् तत्त्वम् अवशिष्यते ॥ १०१ ॥
kāmakrodhalobhamohamadamātsaryagocare | buddhiṃ nistimitāṃ kṛtvā tat tattvam avaśiṣyate || 101 ||

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
YUKTI #73
When in the field of craving, anger, greed, confusion, intoxicated
excitement, or jealousy, make the mind still & soft [right in the
middle of the emotion]: reality is that which remains [when the
feeling has passed through]. || 101

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.

items.definition: √budh → discerning intellect → the discerning mind or intellect; here, the faculty to be held motionless within emotion → ‘intellect’ as IQ misses buddhi as the determinative faculty in experience
nis- + timita ‘moist/stilled’ → motionless → unwavering, without ripple or agitation — a perfect inner stillness → ‘inert’ is wrong—unblinking steadiness of awareness

tat + -tva → that-ness/principle → the ultimate reality or true nature that remains when transient states subside → ‘element/truth’ flattens a constitutive principle in the Śaiva map—or true reality vs construct

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.citation: Bhagavad Gita — Mastery of Mind and the Return of Attention
items.resonance: Both texts prescribe iterative return of attention to a stable center as the method for mastery: Yukti 73 stills the mind within emotion itself; Bhagavad Gita repeatedly returns attention from dispersion to center. Both treat attention-discipline as the operative practice, not a one-time achievement.
items.divergence: Yukti 73 emphasizes the knower-as-witness that persists through emotional content; Gita emphasizes the regulated body-habit-attention triad as the vehicle of yoga-mastery, a more embodied and iterative framework.

items.resonance: Both texts identify scattered mind as the condition in which afflictions (kleśa) dominate, and both prescribe gathered concentration as the antidote: Yukti 73 makes the mind 'still & soft' to reveal what remains; Bodhicaryavatara builds energy to steady the mind in concentration, escaping the 'fangs of afflictions.'
items.divergence: Yukti 73 locates clarity in the knower-substrate beneath emotion; Bodhicaryavatara locates it in the stabilized mental state itself, treating concentration as the protective container rather than a window to a transcendent witness.

items.resonance: Both texts identify a substrate that persists when conditions dissolve: Yukti 73 reveals 'that which remains' when feeling passes through; Yoga Sutras 4.11 shows impressions vanish when their four supports (cause, effect, basis, support) are absent, implying a ground that outlasts their configuration.
items.divergence: Yukti 73 treats the remaining reality as conscious witness (the knower); Yoga Sutras 4.11 treats it as the absence of impressions themselves—a negative condition rather than a positive conscious substrate.

title: Illusion's Recognition Dissolves Suffering
sanskrit_devanagari: इन्द्रजालमयं विश्वं व्यस्तं वा चित्रकर्मवत् । भ्रमद् वा ध्यायतः सर्वम् पश्यतश् च सुखोद्गमः ॥ १०२ ॥
sanskrit_iast: indrajālamayaṃ viśvaṃ vyastaṃ vā citrakarmavat | bhramad vā dhyāyataḥ sarvam paśyataś ca sukhodgamaḥ || 102 ||
translation_literal:
YUKTI #74
Contemplating the diverse universe as being similar to a magic
show, or a wondrous painting, or as [constantly] in flux—seeing
everything [in this way], the arising of [true] happiness occurs. || 102
commentary: Read this line as a contemplative pointer: pause interpretation for a moment and let the insight disclose itself directly.
insight: Read this line as a contemplative pointer: pause interpretation for a moment and let the insight disclose itself directly.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

pratibha_layers.body: इन्द्रजालमयं विश्वं व्यस्तं वा चित्रकर्मवत् । भ्रमद् वा ध्यायतः सर्वम् पश्यतश् च सुखोद्गमः ॥ १०२ ॥
indrajālamayaṃ viśvaṃ vyastaṃ vā citrakarmavat | bhramad vā dhyāyataḥ sarvam paśyataś ca sukhodgamaḥ || 102 ||

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
YUKTI #74
Contemplating the diverse universe as being similar to a magic
show, or a wondrous painting, or as [constantly] in flux—seeing
everything [in this way], the arising of [true] happiness occurs. || 102

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body: Read this line as a contemplative pointer: pause interpretation for a moment and let the insight disclose itself directly.

items.definition: Indra’s net/web → magical display → A magician's illusion or conjuring display; here, an image for the world's non-solid, apparent nature → ‘illusion’ as fake misses the sorcerous display-power of manifestation
viśva ‘all/universe’ → the universe or totality of appearances, understood in Trika as the self-display of consciousness → ‘universe’ as container misses the all as content of consciousness
sukha ‘ease’ + udgama ‘rising’ → the welling up or arising of joy that accompanies the release from the world's coercive solidity → ‘rise of pleasure’ hedonizes the upwelling of ease in recognition

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.citation: Nagarjuna Mulamadhyamakakarika — Dependent Arising Is Emptiness Is the Middle Way
items.resonance: Both texts dissolve the apparent multiplicity of phenomena into a unified conceptual framework by reframing how appearance itself is understood: Yukti 74 sees the diverse universe as illusory display (magic show, painting, flux), while Nagarjuna identifies dependent arising with emptiness, making the very mechanism of manifestation reveal non-dual reality.
items.divergence: Vijnana Bhairava emphasizes direct contemplative disclosure of happiness through perceptual shift, whereas Nagarjuna uses logical analysis of the two truths to dismantle conceptual grasping and avoid nihilism.

items.citation: Heraclitus Fragments — The straight and crooked way of the woolcarders is one and the same.”
items.resonance: Both passages collapse apparent opposites into a single underlying reality: Heraclitus identifies the straight and crooked paths as one, while Yukti 74 treats the flux of diverse forms (magic, painting, change) as a unified display—both dissolving dualistic perception into non-dual seeing.
items.divergence: Heraclitus grounds this unity in the logos as cosmic principle, whereas Vijnana Bhairava locates it in the direct experiential recognition that happiness arises when conceptual distinctions are suspended.

title: The Knower Remains Beyond Pleasure and Pain
sanskrit_devanagari: न चित्तं निक्षिपेद् दुःखे न सुखे वा परिक्षिपेत् । भैरवि ज्ञायतां मध्ये किं तत्त्वम् अवशिष्यते ॥ १०३ ॥
sanskrit_iast: na cittaṃ nikṣiped duḥkhe na sukhe vā parikṣipet | bhairavi jñāyatāṃ madhye kiṃ tattvam avaśiṣyate || 103 ||
translation_literal:
YUKTI #75
Do not abandon the heart-mind to either suffering or happiness,
O Bhairavī! In the Center is that reality which remains: let it be
known. || 103
commentary: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
insight: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

pratibha_layers.body: न चित्तं निक्षिपेद् दुःखे न सुखे वा परिक्षिपेत् । भैरवि ज्ञायतां मध्ये किं तत्त्वम् अवशिष्यते ॥ १०३ ॥
na cittaṃ nikṣiped duḥkhe na sukhe vā parikṣipet | bhairavi jñāyatāṃ madhye kiṃ tattvam avaśiṣyate || 103 ||

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
YUKTI #75
Do not abandon the heart-mind to either suffering or happiness,
O Bhairavī! In the Center is that reality which remains: let it be
known. || 103

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.

items.definition: √cit → mind-stream/functional mind → the individuated, fluctuating mind that identifies with passing states → ‘mind’ blurs citta (stream) with cit (knowingness)

madhya ‘middle/center’ → the middle or central ground between two poles, here the awareness underlying both pleasure and pain → ‘center’ as geometry misses the still hinge between movements where awareness opens

tat + -tva → that-ness/principle → reality or essential principle; here the abiding consciousness that remains when the mind stops swinging → ‘element/truth’ flattens a constitutive principle in the Śaiva map—or true reality vs construct

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.resonance: Both texts locate the root of suffering not in external conditions (happiness/suffering themselves) but in the mind's relationship to them—Astavakra traces suffering to worry/judgment, Vijnana Bhairava instructs non-abandonment to either pole, redirecting attention to the witnessing consciousness rather than content.
items.divergence: Astavakra emphasizes cognitive recognition (knowing suffering's cause dissolves it), while Vijnana Bhairava emphasizes sustained non-dual attention to the heart-mind itself as the locus of clarity.

items.resonance: Both dissolve the binary of pleasure and suffering into a unified ground—Yoga Spandakarika names this ground 'profound consciousness' where opposites are revealed as non-dual, and Vijnana Bhairava's instruction not to abandon to either state similarly points toward a consciousness that transcends the duality.
items.divergence: Yoga Spandakarika makes an ontological claim (pleasure/suffering are inherently non-dual), while Vijnana Bhairava prescribes a practice of non-abandonment that reveals this non-duality through attention.

items.citation: Svetasvatara Upanishad — Yoga as Embodied Crossing
items.resonance: Both direct attention inward to the heart as the seat where mind and senses gather, and both frame this gathering as the means by which one transcends affliction—the Svetasvatara through embodied alignment, Vijnana Bhairava through non-dual resting in the heart-mind.
items.divergence: Svetasvatara emphasizes somatic technique (alignment of body, neck, head) as the method, while Vijnana Bhairava emphasizes the non-dual stance of not-abandoning as the direct means.

title: Attention Returns to the Knower
sanskrit_devanagari: विहाय निजदेहस्थं सर्वत्रास्मीति भावयन् । दृढेन मनसा दृष्ट्या नान्येक्षिण्या सुखी भवेत् ॥ १०४ ॥
sanskrit_iast: vihāya nijadehasthaṃ sarvatrāsmīti bhāvayan | dṛḍhena manasā dṛṣṭyā nānyekṣiṇyā sukhī bhavet || 104 ||
translation_literal:
YUKTI #76
Letting go of body-consciousness, and contemplating “I am
everywhere” with firm mind and unwavering viewpoint, one
becomes happy. || 104
commentary: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
insight: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

pratibha_layers.body: विहाय निजदेहस्थं सर्वत्रास्मीति भावयन् । दृढेन मनसा दृष्ट्या नान्येक्षिण्या सुखी भवेत् ॥ १०४ ॥
vihāya nijadehasthaṃ sarvatrāsmīti bhāvayan | dṛḍhena manasā dṛṣṭyā nānyekṣiṇyā sukhī bhavet || 104 ||

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
YUKTI #76
Letting go of body-consciousness, and contemplating “I am
everywhere” with firm mind and unwavering viewpoint, one
becomes happy. || 104

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.

items.definition: causative stem of √bhū → one who brings-into-being → actively contemplating or cultivating a felt sense, not merely thinking about it → not ‘thinking about’—actively causing the Real to present in awareness
sarva + tra ‘there’ → everywhere → everywhere; the all-pervading scope of true awareness → ‘everywhere’ as location misses ubiquity of the Real in every state
sukhin ‘at ease’ + √bhū optative → 'one becomes happy'—the natural ease (ānanda) of consciousness resting in its own fullness → ‘become happy’ self-help misses the verse’s promise of ease-in-being

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.citation: Svetasvatara Upanishad — Yoga as Embodied Crossing
items.resonance: Both texts redirect attention from dispersed sensory engagement toward an integrated inward locus—the heart or the knower—as the gateway to transcendence. In Yukti 76, letting go of body-consciousness and anchoring in 'I am everywhere' parallels the Svetasvatara's gathering of senses and mind into the heart to cross fear.
items.divergence: The Svetasvatara emphasizes embodied alignment and postural discipline as the method, while Vijnana Bhairava works through pure attentional shift and non-dual recognition without requiring physical technique.

items.resonance: Both passages collapse the subject-object duality by revealing consciousness itself as the ground in which all apparent division occurs. Yukti 76's 'I am everywhere' and Spandakarika's recognition that 'pleasure and suffering, subject and object, are nothing other than the space of profound consciousness' make the same move: the knower is not separate from what is known.
items.divergence: Spandakarika frames this as an ontological truth about the nature of reality itself, while Vijnana Bhairava presents it as a direct contemplative realization achieved through deliberate mental steadying and viewpoint-shift.

items.resonance: Both texts identify mental steadiness and unwavering focus as the antidote to fragmentation and suffering. Yukti 76's 'firm mind and unwavering viewpoint' and Shantideva's call to 'steady the mind in gathered concentration' to escape the 'fangs of the afflictions' share the same diagnostic move: scattered attention is the root of bondage.
items.divergence: Shantideva situates this within a Buddhist ethical framework where energy precedes concentration and afflictions are karmic defilements, while Vijnana Bhairava works within a non-dual Tantric metaphysics where steadiness reveals the already-present omnipresence of consciousness.

title: Consciousness Pervades All Manifest Forms
sanskrit_devanagari: घटादौ यच् च विज्ञानम् इच्छाद्यं वा ममान्तरे । नैव सर्वगतं जातम् भावयन् इति सर्वगः ॥ १०५ ॥
sanskrit_iast: ghaṭādau yac ca vijñānam icchādyaṃ vā mamāntare | naiva sarvagataṃ jātam bhāvayan iti sarvagaḥ || 105 ||
translation_literal:
YUKTI #77
“Consciousness, Will, and so on are not only in me, but are in
everything, including inanimate objects.” Contemplating in this
way that everything manifest is manifest everywhere, one
[experiences oneself] as all-pervasive. || 105
commentary: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
insight: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

pratibha_layers.body: घटादौ यच् च विज्ञानम् इच्छाद्यं वा ममान्तरे । नैव सर्वगतं जातम् भावयन् इति सर्वगः ॥ १०५ ॥
ghaṭādau yac ca vijñānam icchādyaṃ vā mamāntare | naiva sarvagataṃ jātam bhāvayan iti sarvagaḥ || 105 ||

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
YUKTI #77
“Consciousness, Will, and so on are not only in me, but are in
everything, including inanimate objects.” Contemplating in this
way that everything manifest is manifest everywhere, one
[experiences oneself] as all-pervasive. || 105

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.

items.definition: vi- + √jñā → discriminative/special knowing → the awareness or consciousness that reveals any object or state; here, the single knowing common to outer things and inner feelings → ‘wisdom/science’ misses vijñāna as consciousness in its knowing function (and VBT’s title-term)

gone-to-all / all-pervasive → all-pervading; consciousness as that which is everywhere and which the meditator recognizes as their own true nature → static ‘everywhere’ misses the dynamic pervasion named

√iṣ ‘wish’ → will/desire → desire or will; taken as a representative inner movement, contrasted with the outer object (pot) → ‘desire’ as craving misses icchā-śakti: free will-to-appear of consciousness

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.citation: Tantrasara — The Three Śaktis and the Twelve Kālīs
items.resonance: Both texts move from recognizing a universal principle (Consciousness/Śakti) as substrate to reorienting attention inward to perceive it structurally present in all experience. The shift is from intellectual acknowledgment to direct recognition through the architecture of perception itself.
items.divergence: Yukti 77 emphasizes the all-pervasive nature of consciousness as the ground of manifestation; Tantrasara emphasizes learning to recognize Śakti's presence within the specific layers and structures of one's own experiential apparatus.

items.resonance: Both texts perform the same inversion: setting aside the object-domain (body/passing content) to rest attention on the knowing principle itself (consciousness/the knower), with the claim that this reorientation alone liberates.
items.divergence: Yukti 77 arrives at all-pervasiveness through this turn; Astavakra Gita emphasizes immediate freedom and peace as the direct result of the shift in identification.

title: Attention to the Knower Itself
sanskrit_devanagari: ग्राह्यग्राहकसंवित्तिः सामान्या सर्वदेहिनाम् । योगिनां तु विशेषोऽस्ति सम्बन्धे सावधानता ॥ १०६ ॥
sanskrit_iast: grāhyagrāhakasaṃvittiḥ sāmānyā sarvadehinām | yogināṃ tu viśeṣo'sti sambandhe sāvadhānatā || 106 ||
translation_literal:
YUKTI #78
The awareness of knower and known is common to all embodied
beings, but for yogīs there is this difference: they pay careful
attention to the connection. || 106
commentary: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
insight: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

pratibha_layers.body: ग्राह्यग्राहकसंवित्तिः सामान्या सर्वदेहिनाम् । योगिनां तु विशेषोऽस्ति सम्बन्धे सावधानता ॥ १०६ ॥
grāhyagrāhakasaṃvittiḥ sāmānyā sarvadehinām | yogināṃ tu viśeṣo'sti sambandhe sāvadhānatā || 106 ||

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
YUKTI #78
The awareness of knower and known is common to all embodied
beings, but for yogīs there is this difference: they pay careful
attention to the connection. || 106

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.

items.definition: √grah ‘grasp’ → grasped / grasper → the object grasped and the subject who grasps — the two poles of ordinary perception → ‘object/subject’ philosophy-speak misses the lived grasping pair
sam- + √vid → unified knowing → unified, whole awareness; the knowing that spans and underlies both subject and object → ‘consciousness’ generic misses whole awareness spanning subject and object

sa-avadhāna ‘with attention’ + -tā → steady, careful alertness — the continuous vigilance that is the actual practice of this verse → ‘mindfulness’ brand misses steady vigilance as the verse’s actual practice

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.citation: Plotinus Enneads — Ennead V, Tractate 1, Section 12
items.resonance: Both texts identify a structural blindness: the soul/awareness continuously performs its native act, but ordinary perception misses it because attention is absorbed in external content. The yogī's difference (like the soul's awakening) lies in redirecting perception from the object-stream to the subject's own continuous operation.
items.divergence: Plotinus frames this as the soul's metaphysical continuity obscured by sense-focus; the Vijnana Bhairava frames it as a yogic discipline of attention to the knower-known connection itself, grounded in non-dual awareness rather than Neoplatonic emanation.

items.citation: Tilopa Mahamudra — Look at the Looker
items.resonance: Both texts prescribe a reversal of attentional direction: from the content of experience to the looker/knower itself. The yogī's 'careful attention to the connection' parallels the instruction to 'look at the looker'—a reflexive turn that reveals what is already present but unnoticed.
items.divergence: Tilopa's method emphasizes guru-devotion and the spontaneous (sahaja) arising of innate nature; the Vijnana Bhairava emphasizes the yogī's own disciplined attention to the structural fact of knower-known, without invoking grace or the guru's role as primary catalyst.

title: Recognizing Consciousness Beyond Your Own Body
sanskrit_devanagari: स्ववद् अन्यशरीरेऽपि संवित्तिम् अनुभावयेत् । अपेक्षां स्वशरीरस्य त्यक्त्वा व्यापी दिनैर् भवेत् ॥ १०७ ॥
sanskrit_iast: svavad anyaśarīre'pi saṃvittim anubhāvayet | apekṣāṃ svaśarīrasya tyaktvā vyāpī dinair bhavet || 107 ||
translation_literal:
YUKTI #79
Cultivate the felt-sense that the consciousness in another’s body
is the same as one’s own. Releasing obsession with one’s own
body, one experiences one’s all-pervasiveness within days. || 107
commentary: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
insight: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

pratibha_layers.body: स्ववद् अन्यशरीरेऽपि संवित्तिम् अनुभावयेत् । अपेक्षां स्वशरीरस्य त्यक्त्वा व्यापी दिनैर् भवेत् ॥ १०७ ॥
svavad anyaśarīre'pi saṃvittim anubhāvayet | apekṣāṃ svaśarīrasya tyaktvā vyāpī dinair bhavet || 107 ||

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
YUKTI #79
Cultivate the felt-sense that the consciousness in another’s body
is the same as one’s own. Releasing obsession with one’s own
body, one experiences one’s all-pervasiveness within days. || 107

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.

items.definition: sam- + √vid → unified awareness → sentient awareness, the living fact of being conscious — here recognized as one, not many → same as samvitti: whole knowing, not a mental content
pervader → pervasive, all-extending; the natural condition of consciousness once its bodily limit is dropped → ‘that which pervades’—awareness as pervader, not a substance spread in space

apa- + √īkṣ ‘look toward’ → dependence/expectation → dependence or reference-point; the mental anchoring of awareness to 'my body,' which the practice releases → ‘expectation’ as psychology misses ontological reliance that binds awareness

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.resonance: Both texts move from recognizing consciousness as universal to assimilating or identifying with that universality: Yukti 79 cultivates felt-sense of identical consciousness across bodies; Pratyabhijnahrdayam 15 describes obtaining the Power of Consciousness and assimilating the universe to oneself through unity-experience.
items.divergence: Yukti 79 emphasizes the immediate felt-sense of sameness in another's body as the method; Pratyabhijnahrdayam frames this as a power obtained and then extended outward to assimilate the universe, making it more cosmological than phenomenological.

items.resonance: Both texts use a structural reversal: instead of consciousness being located in the body, the body/universe appears within consciousness. Yukti 79 shifts attention from content to knower; Astavakra Gita 15.7 reframes the universe as appearance within you (like waves in ocean), inverting the usual subject-object relation.
items.divergence: Yukti 79 works through intersubjective recognition (consciousness in another); Astavakra Gita works through a non-dual collapse of inside/outside, making the universe itself the appearance rather than focusing on shared consciousness between persons.

title: Attention Returns to the Knower Itself
sanskrit_devanagari: निराधारं मनः कृत्वा विकल्पान् न विकल्पयेत् । तदात्मपरमात्मत्वे भैरवो मृगलोचने ॥ १०८ ॥
sanskrit_iast: nirādhāraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā vikalpān na vikalpayet | tadātmaparamātmatve bhairavo mṛgalocane || 108 ||
translation_literal:
YUKTI #80
Making the mind supportless, one should not assemble mental
constructs. O doe-eyed goddess, [the state called] Bhairava is that
of [experiencing] the supreme Self in oneself. || 108
commentary: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
insight: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

pratibha_layers.body: निराधारं मनः कृत्वा विकल्पान् न विकल्पयेत् । तदात्मपरमात्मत्वे भैरवो मृगलोचने ॥ १०८ ॥
nirādhāraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā vikalpān na vikalpayet | tadātmaparamātmatve bhairavo mṛgalocane || 108 ||

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
YUKTI #80
Making the mind supportless, one should not assemble mental
constructs. O doe-eyed goddess, [the state called] Bhairava is that
of [experiencing] the supreme Self in oneself. || 108

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.

items.definition: nir- + ādhāra ‘support’ → supportless; the mind deprived of any object or prop to rest upon → ‘unsupported’ as precarious misses abiding without extrinsic prop

vi- + √kḷp ‘fashion’ → alternative construct → a mental construct or discursive thought; the faculty that divides awareness into this-and-that → ‘thought’ is too broad; dualizing ideation that splits seamless awareness
parama + ātman → the supreme Self, recognized as identical with one's own individual self (ātman) → Vedāntic ‘Higher Self’ baggage may over-specify this verse’s pointer

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.citation: Tilopa Mahamudra — Mind Is Like the Open Sky
items.resonance: Both texts dissolve the constructed scaffolding of mind by redirecting attention away from bounded form toward an unbounded, centerless awareness. Vijnana Bhairava's 'making the mind supportless' and Tilopa's 'mind has no center and no circumference' share the move of negating structural containment as the path to clarity.
items.divergence: Vijnana Bhairava emphasizes the cessation of mental construct-assembly as technique, while Tilopa uses spatial metaphor (space, sky) to point directly to the nature of mind itself—one is procedural, the other descriptive-pointing.

items.resonance: Both texts locate liberation in a reversal of attention from external content to the knower's own nature. Vijnana Bhairava's 'clarity grows when attention returns to the knower' and Spandakarika's 'reveals to the tantrika his own nature' both make the self-disclosure of consciousness the fruit of redirected awareness.
items.divergence: Vijnana Bhairava frames this as negation (unsupporting the mind), while Spandakarika frames it as positive attainment ('supreme nectar, immortality')—one via subtraction, one via fullness.

title: Becoming Śiva Through Conviction of Identity
sanskrit_devanagari: सर्वज्ञः सर्वकर्ता च व्यापकः परमेश्वरः । स एवाहं शैवधर्मा इति दार्ढ्याच् छिवो भवेत् ॥ १०९ ॥
sanskrit_iast: sarvajñaḥ sarvakartā ca vyāpakaḥ parameśvaraḥ | sa evāhaṃ śaivadharmā iti dārḍhyāc chivo bhavet || 109 ||
translation_literal:
YUKTI #81
“The Highest Divinity is omniscient, omnipotent, and all-
pervading; and I am he who possesses Śiva’s qualities.” Stabilizing
this conviction, one becomes Śiva. || 109
commentary: Read this line as a contemplative pointer: pause interpretation for a moment and let the insight disclose itself directly.
insight: Read this line as a contemplative pointer: pause interpretation for a moment and let the insight disclose itself directly.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

pratibha_layers.body: सर्वज्ञः सर्वकर्ता च व्यापकः परमेश्वरः । स एवाहं शैवधर्मा इति दार्ढ्याच् छिवो भवेत् ॥ १०९ ॥
sarvajñaḥ sarvakartā ca vyāpakaḥ parameśvaraḥ | sa evāhaṃ śaivadharmā iti dārḍhyāc chivo bhavet || 109 ||

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
YUKTI #81
“The Highest Divinity is omniscient, omnipotent, and all-
pervading; and I am he who possesses Śiva’s qualities.” Stabilizing
this conviction, one becomes Śiva. || 109

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body: Read this line as a contemplative pointer: pause interpretation for a moment and let the insight disclose itself directly.

items.definition: √dṛh ‘be firm’ → firmness → firmness or steadiness; the unshakable conviction that makes the identification with Śiva transformative rather than merely conceptual → ‘firmness’ as grit misses stabilized abiding of recognition

all-knower / all-doer → 'All-knowing' and 'doer of all' — two defining powers of Śiva, contrasted with the felt limitations of ordinary selfhood → divine epithets that here name capacities of recognized consciousness
Śiva + dharma ‘nature/law’ → the essential nature of Śiva; here, the recognition that one's own true nature is identical with it → ‘Śaiva religion’ institutionalizes the nature proper to Śiva

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.citation: Svetasvatara Upanishad — The Cosmic Person Beyond and Within
items.resonance: Both passages establish identity between the individual and an all-pervading divine principle (Śiva) that dwells simultaneously transcendent and immanent—the target stabilizes conviction in this identity as a contemplative act, while Svetasvatara locates Śiva as the omnipresent Lord in the heart-cave of all beings.
items.divergence: The Vijnana Bhairava frames this as a first-person recognition-stabilization (aham) requiring sustained conviction, whereas Svetasvatara presents it as a metaphysical fact about cosmic structure that the seeker must discern.

items.citation: Nagarjuna Mulamadhyamakakarika — The Stilling of All Grasping Is Peace
items.resonance: Both texts identify a supreme state (śiva/peace) as the cessation of a particular cognitive or grasping activity—the target achieves Śiva-hood through stabilizing non-dual conviction, while Nagarjuna reaches śiva through the stilling of all conceptual proliferation and grasping.
items.divergence: The Vijnana Bhairava posits an affirmative identification with divine qualities as the means, whereas Nagarjuna's approach is fundamentally apophatic, reaching peace through the negation of all conceptual elaboration.

title: Waves Arise Lawfully From Their Source
sanskrit_devanagari: जलस्येवोर्मयो वह्नेर् ज्वालाभङ्ग्यः प्रभा रवेः । ममैव भैरवस्यैता विश्वभङ्ग्यो विभेदिताः ॥ ११० ॥
sanskrit_iast: jalasyevormayo vahner jvālābhaṅgyaḥ prabhā raveḥ | mamaiva bhairavasyaitā viśvabhaṅgyo vibheditāḥ || 110 ||
translation_literal:
YUKTI #82
“Just as waves [arise] from water, undulating flames from fire, and light-
rays from the sun, the various kinds of ‘waves’ of the universe arise
from me, Bhairava.” || 110
commentary: The teaching frames change as lawful and intelligible, inviting steadiness within transformation.
insight: The teaching frames change as lawful and intelligible, inviting steadiness within transformation.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

pratibha_layers.body: जलस्येवोर्मयो वह्नेर् ज्वालाभङ्ग्यः प्रभा रवेः । ममैव भैरवस्यैता विश्वभङ्ग्यो विभेदिताः ॥ ११० ॥
jalasyevormayo vahner jvālābhaṅgyaḥ prabhā raveḥ | mamaiva bhairavasyaitā viśvabhaṅgyo vibheditāḥ || 110 ||

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
YUKTI #82
“Just as waves [arise] from water, undulating flames from fire, and light-
rays from the sun, the various kinds of ‘waves’ of the universe arise
from me, Bhairava.” || 110

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body: The teaching frames change as lawful and intelligible, inviting steadiness within transformation.

items.definition: √bhañj ‘break’ → inflection/curve/mode → a bend, curl, or mode; here the world as an inflection or wave-form of consciousness rather than a separate substance → ‘gesture/style’ aestheticizes the subtle mode by which spanda appears

vi- + √bhid → divided/differentiated (pl.) → made distinct or differentiated—the many appearances are genuinely diversified expressions of the one, not illusory → ‘divided’ as broken misses differentiation within undivided ground

Trika absolute: terrifyingly free consciousness → the absolute consciousness that is the practitioner's own true self, from which all appearances stream forth → not a sectarian deity-badge—the very form of awareness the practice discloses

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.resonance: Both texts model transformation as lawful emanation from a single source-element: fire transmutes into sea, earth, lightning (Heraclitus); waves, flames, and light-rays emanate from water, fire, and sun respectively (Bhairava). Each uses elemental cascades to render multiplicity intelligible as ordered process, not chaos.
items.divergence: Heraclitus grounds transformation in cosmic conflict and strife (polemos); Bhairava grounds it in non-dual consciousness (Bhairava as source) and treats change as a play of manifestation rather than agonistic necessity.

items.resonance: Both texts locate the intelligibility of transformation in succession and phase-structure: Patañjali identifies successive phases as the cause of successive transformations; Bhairava frames the universe's waves as arising lawfully from a single source, inviting steadiness *within* transformation by grasping its structural order.
items.divergence: Patañjali's framework is epistemological and technical (explaining how yogic perception grasps transformation); Bhairava's is metaphysical and devotional (asserting the non-dual source from which all phases emanate).

title: Stillness Emerges From Exhausted Motion
sanskrit_devanagari: भ्रान्त्वा भ्रान्त्वा शरीरेण त्वरितम् भुवि पातनात् । क्षोभशक्तिविरामेण परा संजायते दशा ॥ १११ ॥
sanskrit_iast: bhrāntvā bhrāntvā śarīreṇa tvaritam bhuvi pātanāt | kṣobhaśaktivirāmeṇa parā saṃjāyate daśā || 111 ||
translation_literal:
YUKTI #83
Whirling quickly around and around with the body and then falling
to the ground, by the cessation of the power of excitation, the
Supreme State arises. || 111
commentary: Read this line as a contemplative pointer: pause interpretation for a moment and let the insight disclose itself directly.
insight: Read this line as a contemplative pointer: pause interpretation for a moment and let the insight disclose itself directly.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

pratibha_layers.body: भ्रान्त्वा भ्रान्त्वा शरीरेण त्वरितम् भुवि पातनात् । क्षोभशक्तिविरामेण परा संजायते दशा ॥ १११ ॥
bhrāntvā bhrāntvā śarīreṇa tvaritam bhuvi pātanāt | kṣobhaśaktivirāmeṇa parā saṃjāyate daśā || 111 ||

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
YUKTI #83
Whirling quickly around and around with the body and then falling
to the ground, by the cessation of the power of excitation, the
Supreme State arises. || 111

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body: Read this line as a contemplative pointer: pause interpretation for a moment and let the insight disclose itself directly.

items.definition: agitation + power → the energy of agitation or churning; here the physical and mental disturbance deliberately provoked and then allowed to subside → not ‘anxiety energy’—the power of stir as a face of Śakti

vi- + √ram → pause/cessation → cessation, the falling away or coming to rest of activity — the crucial pause in which awareness opens → ‘pause’ as break misses the rest-point that discloses the ground
parā + daśā → the supreme state or highest condition of consciousness that arises when agitation stops → ‘highest stage’ ladder-think misses the supreme phase of consciousness

items.resonance: Both texts identify a dynamic surge or movement of consciousness itself as the ultimate principle: Yukti 83 shows the Supreme State arising through cessation of excitation (śakti's power), while Śiva Sūtra names this very surge of awareness as Bhairava. Each treats consciousness not as static witness but as an active, self-recognizing force.
items.divergence: Yukti 83 emphasizes the *cessation* of movement leading to revelation, whereas Śiva Sūtra identifies the surge itself as divine; one privileges the still point after kinetic collapse, the other the pulsation as primary.

items.citation: Svetasvatara Upanishad — Yoga as Embodied Crossing
items.resonance: Both employ embodied technique—whirling/falling in Yukti 83, aligned posture and sense-gathering in Śvetāśvatara—as a method to cross from ordinary consciousness into a transcendent state. The body's organized action or surrender becomes the gateway to the Supreme.
items.divergence: Yukti 83 uses spontaneous collapse and cessation of excitation as the trigger, while Śvetāśvatara prescribes deliberate alignment and concentration; one is surrender through disorientation, the other disciplined gathering.

items.resonance: Both point to a state in which the ordinary mind-function ceases and a higher consciousness emerges: Yukti 83's Supreme State arises when excitation-power ends, and Patañjali's samādhi is the state where the mind becomes 'seeded' (stabilized in its source). Each describes a threshold where conditioned mental activity yields to a deeper principle.
items.divergence: Patañjali frames this as the mind's own refined state (seeded in its own nature), while Yukti 83 emphasizes śakti's power and its cessation as the mechanism; one is internalist, the other explicitly energetic.

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

title: Knowing Itself Emerges When Effort Dissolves
sanskrit_devanagari: आधारेष्व् अथवाऽशक्त्याऽज्ञानाच् चित्तलयेन वा । जातशक्तिसमावेशक्षोभान्ते भैरवं वपुः ॥ ११२ ॥
sanskrit_iast: ādhāreṣv athavā'śaktyā'jñānāc cittalayena vā | jātaśaktisamāveśakṣobhānte bhairavaṃ vapuḥ || 112 ||
translation_literal:
YUKTI #84
Through incapacity regarding the loci (ādhāras), or through the
dissolution of the mind due to unknowing, [then,] at the end of the
excitation of absorption in energy produced [by trying to figure it
out], Bhairava-nature [is revealed]. || 112
commentary: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
insight: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

pratibha_layers.body: आधारेष्व् अथवाऽशक्त्याऽज्ञानाच् चित्तलयेन वा । जातशक्तिसमावेशक्षोभान्ते भैरवं वपुः ॥ ११२ ॥
ādhāreṣv athavā'śaktyā'jñānāc cittalayena vā | jātaśaktisamāveśakṣobhānte bhairavaṃ vapuḥ || 112 ||

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
YUKTI #84
Through incapacity regarding the loci (ādhāras), or through the
dissolution of the mind due to unknowing, [then,] at the end of the
excitation of absorption in energy produced [by trying to figure it
out], Bhairava-nature [is revealed]. || 112

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.

items.definition: ā- + √dhṛ → support/base → inner support-centers along the body's axis where breath and awareness can be gathered and held → ‘support’ as prop misses the base the practice uses or relinquishes

citta + laya ‘dissolution’ → dissolution or absorption of mental activity, the settling of the thinking mind into stillness → ‘mind-dissolution’ can sound blank-out; here functional mind settles into source

sam- + ā- + √viś ‘enter’ → immersion/possession → immersion or absorption; here the spontaneous influx of śakti that occurs when effortful grasping ceases → ‘possession’ occultizes free immersion of awareness in its own fullness

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.citation: Bhagavad Gita — Mastery of Mind and the Return of Attention
items.resonance: Both texts locate realization through iterative return of attention to a stable center rather than through dramatic cognitive breakthrough. Yukti 84 reveals Bhairava-nature when mental excitation dissolves and attention turns inward to the knower; Bhagavad Gita describes yoga-mastery as repeatedly returning attention from dispersion to center.
items.divergence: Vijnana Bhairava emphasizes the cessation of effort and unknowing as the gateway, while Bhagavad Gita stresses disciplined habituation and regulated practice as the method.

items.resonance: Both texts paradoxically describe how striving toward the ultimate reveals it: Yukti 84 shows that dissolution of mental effort (unknowing) at the end of absorption-excitation reveals Bhairava-nature; Yoga Spandakarika describes how ardent striving toward the supreme tremor makes it appear, like an object seen more clearly through focused effort.
items.divergence: Vijnana Bhairava frames the revelation as occurring through the *cessation* of excitation and unknowing, while Yoga Spandakarika frames it as the fruit of sustained ardent striving.

items.resonance: Both texts identify the inward stabilization of attention as the pivot between affliction and liberation. Yukti 84 turns attention from content to knower; Bodhicaryavatara warns that a scattered mind lives in affliction and prescribes gathered concentration as the remedy.
items.divergence: Vijnana Bhairava emphasizes the spontaneous revelation of one's nature through this turn, while Shantideva emphasizes the ethical and soteriological necessity of building energy and steadying the mind against kleśa.

title: Stillness of Gaze Reveals Radical Freedom
sanskrit_devanagari: सम्प्रदायम् इमम् देवि शृणु सम्यग् वदाम्य् अहम् । कैवल्यं जायते सद्यो नेत्रयोः स्तब्धमात्रयोः ॥ ११३ ॥
sanskrit_iast: sampradāyam imam devi śṛṇu samyag vadāmy aham | kaivalyaṃ jāyate sadyo netrayoḥ stabdhamātrayoḥ || 113 ||
translation_literal:
YUKTI #85
O goddess, listen to this traditional teaching: I will speak it
accurately. For one whose eyes are unmoving, radical freedom can
arise in a moment. || 113
commentary: Read this line as a contemplative pointer: pause interpretation for a moment and let the insight disclose itself directly.
insight: Read this line as a contemplative pointer: pause interpretation for a moment and let the insight disclose itself directly.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

pratibha_layers.body: सम्प्रदायम् इमम् देवि शृणु सम्यग् वदाम्य् अहम् । कैवल्यं जायते सद्यो नेत्रयोः स्तब्धमात्रयोः ॥ ११३ ॥
sampradāyam imam devi śṛṇu samyag vadāmy aham | kaivalyaṃ jāyate sadyo netrayoḥ stabdhamātrayoḥ || 113 ||

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
YUKTI #85
O goddess, listen to this traditional teaching: I will speak it
accurately. For one whose eyes are unmoving, radical freedom can
arise in a moment. || 113

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body: Read this line as a contemplative pointer: pause interpretation for a moment and let the insight disclose itself directly.

items.definition: kevala ‘alone’ → aloneness/isolation of puruṣa → absolute freedom or aloneness; here, the direct recognition that awareness was never bound by objects → classical Sāṅkhya isolation—check whether this verse uses it or revises it
sam- + pra- + √dā → tradition/transmission → a teaching handed down through direct transmission from teacher to student → ‘sect/tradition’ institutionalizes living transmission
sadyas ‘immediately’ → at once, immediately — signaling a sudden rather than gradual awakening → ‘at once’ marketing misses the instantaneous character of recognition claimed

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.citation: Tantrasara — Śiva’s Play of Veiling and Revealing
items.resonance: Both passages mark a shift from abstract teaching to direct, personalized transmission: Vijnana Bhairava's 'let the insight disclose itself directly' and Tantrasara's 'The teaching now becomes personal' both suspend mediated explanation in favor of immediate recognition.
items.divergence: Vijnana Bhairava emphasizes spontaneous disclosure through pause, while Tantrasara frames personalization as a deliberate pedagogical turn within a structured tantric system.

items.resonance: Both passages identify freedom as obscured by mental-representational entanglement and propose direct insight as liberation: Vijnana Bhairava's 'let the insight disclose itself' mirrors Yoga Spandakarika's recognition that forgetting 'innate freedom' occurs through capture in subtle energies and mental forms.
items.divergence: Vijnana Bhairava treats direct disclosure as the method itself, while Yoga Spandakarika diagnoses the problem (entanglement) and implies recovery through recognizing what is already present.

title: Silence Reveals What Words Conceal
sanskrit_devanagari: संकोचं कर्णयोः कृत्वा ह्य् अधोद्वारे तथैव च । अनच्कम् अहलं ध्यायन् विशेद् ब्रह्म सनातनम् ॥ ११४ ॥
sanskrit_iast: saṃkocaṃ karṇayoḥ kṛtvā hy adhodvāre tathaiva ca | anackam ahalaṃ dhyāyan viśed brahma sanātanam || 114 ||
translation_literal:
YUKTI #86
Closing the ears and likewise the ‘lower gate’, meditating on [the
sound] without vowel or consonant [? ahala], one may enter the
eternal Absolute. || 114
commentary: Read this line as a contemplative pointer: pause interpretation for a moment and let the insight disclose itself directly.
insight: Read this line as a contemplative pointer: pause interpretation for a moment and let the insight disclose itself directly.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

pratibha_layers.body: संकोचं कर्णयोः कृत्वा ह्य् अधोद्वारे तथैव च । अनच्कम् अहलं ध्यायन् विशेद् ब्रह्म सनातनम् ॥ ११४ ॥
saṃkocaṃ karṇayoḥ kṛtvā hy adhodvāre tathaiva ca | anackam ahalaṃ dhyāyan viśed brahma sanātanam || 114 ||

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
YUKTI #86
Closing the ears and likewise the ‘lower gate’, meditating on [the
sound] without vowel or consonant [? ahala], one may enter the
eternal Absolute. || 114

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body: Read this line as a contemplative pointer: pause interpretation for a moment and let the insight disclose itself directly.

items.definition: an-ac ‘without vowels’ + a-hal ‘without consonants’ → 'without vowel, without consonant' — sound prior to articulation, the unstruck resonance underlying all speech → not linguistic trivia—the phonemic void where mantra dissolves into pure resonance

adhas ‘below’ + dvāra ‘door’ → the 'lower gate' at the base of the trunk (muladhara region), sealed to stop the downward leak of prāṇa → not a mere anatomical lower aperture—the practice gate at the root

√nad ‘sound’ → resonance → inner subtle sound; here the undivided vibration of consciousness that becomes audible when external hearing is stilled → ‘sound’ as acoustic misses subtle resonance prior to ordinary hearing

items.citation: Mandukya Upanishad and Gaudapada Karika — Verse 7 · Turīya — The Fourth
items.resonance: Both texts use systematic negation to point toward a non-dual awareness that transcends all categorical divisions (sensory, conceptual, dualistic). The Vijnana Bhairava's 'sound without vowel or consonant' and the Mandukya's 'not inwardly conscious, not outwardly conscious' both dissolve the subject-object distinction through apophatic precision.
items.divergence: The Mandukya employs a fourfold negation to isolate turīya (the fourth state) as a metaphysical category; the Vijnana Bhairava uses sensory closure as a direct contemplative method to collapse the distinction itself in lived experience.

items.resonance: Both texts locate liberation in a sudden recognition (pratyabhijñā / direct disclosure) where the meditator realizes their own authorship or agency as consciousness itself, collapsing the gap between knower and known through introversion.
items.divergence: The Pratyabhijnahrdayam emphasizes intellectual recognition of authorship leading to ascent; the Vijnana Bhairava uses sensory negation and silence as the portal, privileging non-conceptual disclosure over cognitive realization.

items.resonance: Both passages describe a transformation of mental condition into unified consciousness where opposites (repressed/revived, sound/silence, multiplicity/unity) become equally present and transparent to awareness without hierarchy or preference.
items.divergence: Patañjali frames this as a sequential state-transformation within samādhi; the Vijnana Bhairava treats it as immediate recognition through sensory closure, emphasizing simultaneity over progression.

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

title: Gazing Into Emptiness Dissolves Thought
sanskrit_devanagari: कूपादिके महागर्ते स्थित्वोपरि निरीक्षणात् । अविकल्पमतेः सम्यक् सद्यस् चित्तलयः स्फुटम् ॥ ११५ ॥
sanskrit_iast: kūpādike mahāgarte sthitvopari nirīkṣaṇāt | avikalpamateḥ samyak sadyas cittalayaḥ sphuṭam || 115 ||
translation_literal:
YUKTI #87
Standing above a deep well, chasm, or the like and gazing into it,
one’s mind becomes completely free of thought, and suddenly
dissolves into clarity. || 115
commentary: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
insight: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

pratibha_layers.body: कूपादिके महागर्ते स्थित्वोपरि निरीक्षणात् । अविकल्पमतेः सम्यक् सद्यस् चित्तलयः स्फुटम् ॥ ११५ ॥
kūpādike mahāgarte sthitvopari nirīkṣaṇāt | avikalpamateḥ samyak sadyas cittalayaḥ sphuṭam || 115 ||

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
YUKTI #87
Standing above a deep well, chasm, or the like and gazing into it,
one’s mind becomes completely free of thought, and suddenly
dissolves into clarity. || 115

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Commentary
pratibha_layers.body: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.

items.definition: vi- + √kḷp ‘fashion’ → alternative construct → the mind's habitual conceptual activity — naming, dividing, judging; here the technique targets the mind already loosened from it (avikalpa) → ‘thought’ is too broad; dualizing ideation that splits seamless awareness
citta + laya ‘dissolution’ → the dissolving or melting away of the busy thinking mind into its silent ground → ‘mind-dissolution’ can sound blank-out; here functional mind settles into source

pratibha_layers.label: Practice (Abhyasa)
pratibha_layers.body: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

items.citation: Bhagavad Gita — Mastery of Mind and the Return of Attention
items.resonance: Both texts locate liberation in the iterative return of attention from dispersed content to a stable center or knower. Yukti 87 dissolves thought by redirecting gaze inward; the Gita prescribes repeated restoration of attention from dispersion to center as the method of yoga-mastery.
items.divergence: The Gita emphasizes disciplined habituation and bodily regulation as scaffolding for attention; Yukti 87 relies on a spontaneous precipice-induced collapse of thought into clarity, requiring no prior practice.

items.citation: Tilopa Mahamudra — Mind Is Like the Open Sky
items.resonance: Both texts describe the knower or mind as boundless and unlocatable—without circumference or fixed position. Yukti 87's clarity emerges when attention turns to the knower itself; Tilopa's mind has no center and no circumference, resisting spatial or conceptual containment.
items.divergence: Tilopa uses spatial negation (space as metaphor) to point to mind's nature; Yukti 87 uses a concrete perceptual technique (gazing into a void) to trigger the experiential recognition of that boundlessness.

items.resonance: Both texts identify scattered attention as the root vulnerability to suffering and prescribe gathered concentration as the remedy. Shantideva warns that a scattered mind lives 'between the fangs of the afflictions'; Yukti 87 shows how focused inward attention dissolves the thought-content that binds consciousness.
items.divergence: Shantideva frames concentration as a prerequisite built through vīrya (energy/effort) within a moral framework; Yukti 87 presents it as an immediate, spontaneous outcome of a specific perceptual gesture.

title: The Mind Finds Only Śiva Everywhere
sanskrit_devanagari: यत्र यत्र मनो याति बाह्ये वाभ्यन्तरेऽपि वा । तत्र तत्र शिवावास्था व्यापकत्वात् क्व यास्यति ॥ ११६ ॥
sanskrit_iast: yatra yatra mano yāti bāhye vābhyantare'pi vā | tatra tatra śivāvāsthā vyāpakatvāt kva yāsyati || 116 ||
translation_literal:
YUKTI #88
Wherever the mind goes, externally or even internally, it
[discovers] nothing but the state of Śiva. Since [that state] is all-
pervasive, where else could the mind go? || 116
commentary: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
insight: The emphasis turns inward: clarity grows when attention returns to the knower rather than the passing content.
practice: Read this passage slowly three times. Pause for one minute and write one sentence about how to apply it today.

pratibha_layers.body: यत्र यत्र मनो याति बाह्ये वाभ्यन्तरेऽपि वा । तत्र तत्र शिवावास्था व्यापकत्वात् क्व यास्यति ॥ ११६ ॥
yatra yatra mano yāti bāhye vābhyantare'pi vā | tatra tatra śivāvāsthā vyāpakatvāt kva yāsyati || 116 ||

pratibha_layers.label: Pratibha Translation
pratibha_layers.body:
YUKTI #88
Wherever the mind goes, externally or even internally, it
